chapters.title: Turn an Orbital Position Into a Direction in the Sky
chapters.label: sec:e1-look-angles
chapters.html:
Fig. 14 shows the change of viewpoint behind antenna pointing. Orbital radius answers where the satellite lies relative to Earth. The observer instead needs a ray from the station to the satellite. That ray’s length is slant range, and its orientation relative to the local horizon supplies elevation [source].

Use a spherical Earth, a surface station and a satellite outside Earth. The station and satellite-subpoint coordinates are (Le,ℓe)(L_e,\ell_e) and (Ls,ℓs)(L_s,\ell_s), respectively. Latitudes LL are north-positive and longitudes ℓ\ell are east-positive; west is negative. They are geocentric latitudes under this spherical model. The satellite subpoint, SSP, is Earth’s surface intersection with the radial line from Earth’s center through the spacecraft. Use radians in numerical trigonometric functions.

The dot product of the two radial unit directions gives central angle: cos⁡γ=sin⁡Lesin⁡Ls+cos⁡Lecos⁡Lscos⁡(ℓs−ℓe).\begin{equation} \cos\gamma=\sin L_e\sin L_s +\cos L_e\cos L_s\cos(\ell_s-\ell_e). \end{equation} The last cosine uses a longitude difference. For an equatorial satellite on the station’s meridian, γ=|Le|\gamma=|L_e|. Away from that meridian, retain the longitude term.

Let RER_E be Earth’s radius, rsr_s satellite geocentric radius and dd the station-to-satellite distance. The law of cosines gives d=rs2+RE2−2rsREcos⁡γ.\begin{equation} d=\sqrt{r_s^2+R_E^2-2r_sR_E\cos\gamma}. \end{equation} The surface arc REγR_E\gamma is a different distance. Radio propagation time and free-space spreading use dd. Resolve the same ray along local up and local horizontal: u=rscos⁡γ−RE,q=rssin⁡γ.\begin{equation} u=r_s\cos\gamma-R_E,\qquad q=r_s\sin\gamma. \end{equation} Both are in meters and q≥0q\ge0 for 0≤γ≤π0\le\gamma\le\pi. Signed elevation follows directly: El=atan2⁡(u,q)=atan2⁡(cosγ−RErs,sinγ).\begin{equation} E_l=\operatorname{atan2}(u,q) =\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\cos\gamma-\frac{R_E}{r_s},\sin\gamma\right). \end{equation} This two-argument arctangent retains the upward or downward sign. It returns radians, with 90∘90^\circ at zenith and 0∘0^\circ at the ideal horizon.

For a fresh illustrative station (28∘,−60∘)(28^\circ,-60^\circ) and GEO SSP (0∘,−75∘)(0^\circ,-75^\circ), central separation is about 31.5∘31.5^\circ, slant range about 36900 km and elevation about 53.3∘53.3^\circ. This GEO station will reappear in the radio link budget, where the slant range sets the spreading loss.

Teach it. Point to four different objects in the drawing: orbital radius, altitude, slant range and central angle. Explain why a station directly below a satellite sees 90∘90^\circ elevation even though γ=0\gamma=0.

Use the Horizon to Decide Visibility

Fig. 15 shows why a nearby low satellite can be invisible from a station that can still see a much more distant GEO satellite. Visibility is a geometric obstruction test: the straight ray must leave the surface above the local tangent. With a spherical surface station, that is u≥0u\ge0, so cos⁡γ≥RErs,γ≤γh=cos⁡−1(RErs).\begin{equation} \cos\gamma\ge\frac{R_E}{r_s},\qquad \gamma\le\gamma_h=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_E}{r_s}\right). \end{equation} At the horizon the triangle has a right angle at the station and dh=rs2−RE2d_h=\sqrt{r_s^2-R_E^2}. For a 900 km circular altitude the horizon central separation is about 28.8∘28.8^\circ; at GEO it is about 81.3∘81.3^\circ. A higher orbit sees a larger geometric part of Earth, while its greater range penalizes the radio link.

The lecture also gives an inverse-cosine elevation expression [source]: Emag=cos⁡−1[sin⁡γ1+(RE/rs)2−2(RE/rs)cos⁡γ].\begin{equation} E_{\mathrm{mag}}=\cos^{-1}\!\left[ \frac{\sin\gamma}{\sqrt{1+(R_E/r_s)^2-2(R_E/r_s)\cos\gamma}} \right]. \end{equation} Its principal value equals |El||E_l| for this geometry. Above the horizon it agrees with signed elevation. Below the horizon it returns a positive magnitude. Keeping this form together with the visibility test is valid; alternatively restore the sign from uu. The atan2 form incorporates that sign in one calculation.

A specified minimum elevation mask Emin>0E_{\min}>0 is stricter than geometric visibility. Terrain, obstructions, atmospheric effects and link quality can motivate it. Earth oblateness, station altitude and refraction require richer models than the spherical surface triangle. Clamp computed inverse-trigonometric inputs to their mathematical domain only for tiny floating-point roundoff, rather than concealing an inconsistent geometry.

Teach it. Explain why a positive value from the inverse-cosine formula alone cannot establish visibility. Predict what increasing a station’s minimum-elevation requirement does to its usable coverage.

Project the Ray Onto Local East, North and Up

Fig. 16 shows why latitude and longitude are inputs to a look-angle calculation rather than the final pointing angles. A station at another location has another local horizon and another north direction. The satellite position is unchanged, but its coordinates in that local basis change [source].

First put both positions in the same Earth-centered, Earth-fixed frame. With a spherical surface station, write 𝒓e=RE(cos⁡Lecos⁡ℓecos⁡Lesin⁡ℓesin⁡Le),𝒓s=rs(cos⁡Lscos⁡ℓscos⁡Lssin⁡ℓssin⁡Ls).\begin{equation} \mathbf{r}_e=R_E \begin{pmatrix}\cos L_e\cos\ell_e\\\cos L_e\sin\ell_e\\\sin L_e\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{r}_s=r_s \begin{pmatrix}\cos L_s\cos\ell_s\\\cos L_s\sin\ell_s\\\sin L_s\end{pmatrix}. \end{equation} Each entry is in meters. The station’s local basis is 𝒆̂=(−sin⁡ℓe,cos⁡ℓe,0),𝒏̂=(−sin⁡Lecos⁡ℓe,−sin⁡Lesin⁡ℓe,cos⁡Le),𝒖̂=(cos⁡Lecos⁡ℓe,cos⁡Lesin⁡ℓe,sin⁡Le).\begin{align} \hat{\mathbf{e}}&=(-\sin\ell_e,\cos\ell_e,0),\\ \hat{\mathbf{n}}&=(-\sin L_e\cos\ell_e,-\sin L_e\sin\ell_e,\cos L_e),\\ \hat{\mathbf{u}}&=(\cos L_e\cos\ell_e,\cos L_e\sin\ell_e,\sin L_e). \end{align} The vectors have unit length and are mutually perpendicular. Subtract toward the satellite, 𝒅=𝒓s−𝒓e\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{r}_s-\mathbf{r}_e, then take the projections dE=𝒆̂⋅𝒅,dN=𝒏̂⋅𝒅,dU=𝒖̂⋅𝒅.\begin{equation} d_E=\hat{\mathbf{e}}\cdot\mathbf{d},\quad d_N=\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\mathbf{d},\quad d_U=\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\mathbf{d}. \end{equation} Range is d=dE2+dN2+dU2d=\sqrt{d_E^2+d_N^2+d_U^2}, horizontal magnitude is q=dE2+dN2q=\sqrt{d_E^2+d_N^2} and El=atan2⁡(dU,q)E_l=\operatorname{atan2}(d_U,q). These projections reproduce the triangle’s elevation while retaining the horizontal direction needed for azimuth.

Subtracting an Earth-fixed station from an inertial satellite position would mix frames. Rotate the positions into one frame first. A ray used for transmission from satellite toward ground reverses the subtraction; its angles belong to the satellite’s antenna frame. Ground elevation is not automatically the satellite’s off-axis angle.

Teach it. Explain which step changes the origin and which changes the axes. Predict what happens to all three signed components if the ray direction is reversed.

Keep Azimuth’s Convention and Quadrant

Fig. 17 shows why an acute angle alone cannot tell a dish where to point. The course’s geographic bearing is measured clockwise from north: 0∘0^\circ north, 90∘90^\circ east, 180∘180^\circ south and 270∘270^\circ west. Define the convention before using an inverse trigonometric function [source].

The full bearing is Az=wrap⁡[0,2π)[atan2⁡(dE,dN)].\begin{equation} A_z=\operatorname{wrap}_{[0,2\pi)} \bigl[\operatorname{atan2}(d_E,d_N)\bigr]. \end{equation} East comes first and North second because the zero direction is north. A convenient dimensionless version uses Δℓ=ℓs−ℓe\Delta\ell=\ell_s-\ell_e: eh=cos⁡Lssin⁡Δℓ,nh=sin⁡Lscos⁡Le−cos⁡Lssin⁡Lecos⁡Δℓ,dE=rseh,dN=rsnh.\begin{align} e_h&=\cos L_s\sin\Delta\ell,\\ n_h&=\sin L_s\cos L_e-\cos L_s\sin L_e\cos\Delta\ell,\\ d_E&=r_se_h,\qquad d_N=r_sn_h. \end{align} The station’s radial position has zero East and North projections, so the common positive factor rsr_s cancels from azimuth. Signs identify the quadrant before any numerical inverse function is evaluated. The illustrative station/SSP pair used above has eh<0e_h<0 and nh<0n_h<0, so the bearing is southwest, about 209.7∘209.7^\circ.

The lecture’s northward test can be rearranged, away from latitude poles, as tan⁡Lecos⁡Δℓ<tan⁡Ls.\begin{equation} \tan L_e\cos\Delta\ell<\tan L_s. \end{equation} Multiplying by cos⁡Lecos⁡Ls>0\cos L_e\cos L_s>0 for ordinary interior latitude values gives nh>0n_h>0. The sine/cosine form stays bounded near the poles, while the tangent form becomes singular. At a geographic pole the numerical latitude basis still needs a chosen reference meridian to define local north/east.

At zenith, dE=dN=0d_E=d_N=0, so azimuth is physically undefined even if a programming library returns a number for atan2(0,0)(0,0). Near zenith, tiny horizontal errors can produce a large bearing change without a large change in actual pointing direction. The instructor’s timed-exam guidance emphasizes simple look-angle triangles; the ENU form supports understanding and simulation rather than implying that every exam problem requires a long 3-D calculation [source].

Teach it. Place a satellite ray in each of the four horizontal quadrants and predict its bearing interval. Explain the difference between an undefined bearing at zenith and an invisible ray below the horizon.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, ASD05 Look Angles, supplied ASD5include.pdf and linked lecture recording. Lecture recording.

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, supplied pre-Exam-1 class transcript, “Exam Scope and Wire Antennas.” Exam boundary and customized-formula-sheet guidance.

chapters.title: Keep the Whole Spacecraft Working
chapters.label: sec:e1-spacecraft
chapters.html:
Fig. 18 shows why a good radio specification can still produce an unusable spacecraft. More transmitted power demands electrical input, heat removal, solar collection and eclipse storage. A larger antenna can reduce RF-power demand while adding pointing and structural demands [source].

Start with coverage, lifetime, orbit and allowable mass. At a defined electrical bus, a useful accounting identity is Pbus(t)=∑jPj(t),Ebus=∫Pbus(t)dt.\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{bus}}(t)=\sum_jP_j(t),\qquad E_{\mathrm{bus}}=\int P_{\mathrm{bus}}(t)\,dt. \end{equation} Power is in watts; energy is in joules with seconds or Wh with hours. Every load must refer to that bus, including conversion losses needed to supply equipment at other voltages. Average power determines interval energy; simultaneous peak power sets current-handling requirements.

For an illustrative amplifier with RF output 40 W and DC input 100 W, efficiency is 0.4 and approximately 60 W becomes device heat. The power subsystem supplies 100 W. Antenna efficiency and feeder losses are additional interfaces. Carry every efficiency once at its defined boundary.

Teach it. Trace a proposed doubling of RF output through electrical input, eclipse energy, solar recharge, waste heat and launch mass.

Pay for a Maneuver With Momentum and Propellant

Fig. 19 shows what an orbit-transfer calculation has left unpaid. Propulsion must provide the required Δv\Delta v while accelerating both hardware and remaining propellant. Conservation of momentum relates thrust and expelled mass [source]: F=ṁpve,Isp=Fṁpg0=veg0.\begin{equation} F=\dot m_pv_e,\qquad I_{\mathrm{sp}}=\frac{F}{\dot m_pg_0}=\frac{v_e}{g_0}. \end{equation} Thrust FF is in N, expelled mass rate ṁp>0\dot m_p>0 in kg/s, effective exhaust speed vev_e in m/s and reference g0=9.80665g_0=9.80665 m/s2^2. Specific impulse is in seconds. Effective exhaust speed can include pressure thrust; physical nozzle speed alone may require another term.

Incremental momentum accounting gives dv=−vedm/mdv=-v_e\,dm/m, where vehicle mass decreases. Integrate between total masses immediately before and after the burn: Δv=veln⁡m0mf,mp=mf(eΔv/ve−1).\begin{equation} \Delta v=v_e\ln\frac{m_0}{m_f},\qquad m_p=m_f(e^{\Delta v/v_e}-1). \end{equation} Final mass can include fuel reserved for later burns. With the same vev_e and no discarded stages, successive mass ratios multiply. For illustrative mf=200m_f=200 kg, ve=2400v_e=2400 m/s and Δv=600\Delta v=600 m/s, m0=256.8m_0=256.8 kg and consumed propellant is 56.8 kg.

Launch also incurs gravity, drag and steering losses. Earth’s eastward surface speed ωEREcos⁡L\omega_ER_E\cos L can assist an appropriate eastward launch; it does not eliminate orbital-energy requirements. Staging discards hardware that no longer contributes useful thrust.

Teach it. Explain why fuel for burn two belongs in burn one’s final mass, and why high specific impulse alone does not establish whether a vehicle can lift off.

Trade Electrical Power Against Thrust and Time

Fig. 20 shows why an efficient electric thruster may need a long maneuver. High exhaust speed gives substantial momentum per propellant mass, but kinetic energy per mass grows with speed squared [source]. Pjet=12ṁpve2=12Fve.\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{jet}}=\frac12\dot m_pv_e^2=\frac12Fv_e. \end{equation} For defined efficiency ηt=Pjet/Pelec\eta_t=P_{\mathrm{jet}}/P_{\mathrm{elec}}, F=2ηtPelecve,ṁp=2ηtPelecve2.\begin{equation} F=\frac{2\eta_tP_{\mathrm{elec}}}{v_e},\qquad \dot m_p=\frac{2\eta_tP_{\mathrm{elec}}}{v_e^2}. \end{equation} This is an explanatory energy-flow model, rather than a complete thruster specification. Ionization, beam divergence, neutralization and auxiliaries belong consistently inside ηt\eta_t or in separate losses.

At 1 kW input, ηt=0.6\eta_t=0.6 and ve=30v_e=30 km/s, thrust is 0.04 N and flow is 1.33×10−61.33\times10^{-6} kg/s. A small force can accumulate useful impulse over time in orbit. For approximately constant mass, Δv≃Ft/m\Delta v\simeq Ft/m with tt in seconds; use the rocket equation when mass changes substantially.

Ion and Hall thrusters accelerate charged particles electrically and require charge management. Chemical engines typically supply much greater thrust for short maneuvers. Long low-thrust transfers use different trajectories from an impulsive Hohmann construction.

Teach it. At fixed power and efficiency, predict the thrust and mass-flow changes when exhaust speed doubles. Name a mission constraint that might favor lower specific impulse.

Keep Pointing Separate From Orbital Position

Fig. 21 shows why the correct orbit alone cannot establish communication. Position determines where the target lies; attitude determines where the hardware points. Panels, antennas, radiators and sensors can prefer different directions [source].

Attitude is body orientation in a stated frame. Reaction wheels turn the body through opposite internal angular-momentum changes. Persistent disturbance torque can saturate wheel storage, requiring momentum unloading. Thrusters provide external torque; magnetic torquers depend on the local magnetic field. Spin stabilization averages some disturbances but complicates antenna accommodation and solar collection. Three-axis stabilization supplies controlled body directions using sensors and actuators.

Station keeping changes an orbit; attitude control changes orientation. A force applied off center can affect both. For a simple panel a 30∘30^\circ sun-angle error gives collection factor cos⁡30∘=0.866\cos30^\circ=0.866. Antenna pointing loss follows its own pattern rather than automatically following that same cosine. Radiator performance depends on the surfaces it views.

Teach it. Distinguish a failure repaired by changing the orbit, turning the body, or recomputing the ground-station pointing direction.

Read a Solar Cell’s Actual Operating Point

Fig. 22 shows why a cell’s largest current and voltage cannot be used as though they occur together. The load selects a point on the current–voltage curve; maximum-power-point control seeks the largest product [source]. Pmp=VmpImp,FF=PmpVocIsc,ηcell=PmpSA.\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{mp}}=V_{\mathrm{mp}}I_{\mathrm{mp}},\quad \mathrm{FF}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{mp}}}{V_{\mathrm{oc}}I_{\mathrm{sc}}},\quad \eta_{\mathrm{cell}}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{mp}}}{SA}. \end{equation} Voltage is in V, current in A, irradiance SS in W/m2^2 and illuminated area AA in m2^2. Fill factor FF and efficiency are dimensionless. FF compares the actual operating rectangle with endpoint scales; efficiency compares electrical output with incoming optical power.

The illustrative normalized curve i=1−v10i=1-v^{10} has maximum at vmp=11−1/10≃0.787v_{\mathrm{mp}}=11^{-1/10}\simeq0.787 and imp=10/11≃0.909i_{\mathrm{mp}}=10/11\simeq0.909, giving FF≃0.715\simeq0.715. These values validate the diagram, not a semiconductor device model. Series cells add voltage; matched parallel strings add current. Shading, mismatch, packaging and converters can lower delivered array output. Cell efficiency alone excludes those system losses.

Teach it. Locate the two endpoints and maximum-power point. Explain why bus-voltage regulation and cell-side operating-point control can be different jobs.

Collect Enough Sunlight at End of Life

Fig. 23 shows why an array rating must name illumination, orientation and mission age. An edge-on working panel intercepts little direct sunlight; a sun-facing panel may have degraded or be at an unfavorable temperature [source] [source]. S(DS)=S1(1AUDS)2,Parray,bus=S(DS)Aηcellmax⁡(0,cos⁡α)flossfEOL.\begin{align} S(D_S)&=S_1\left(\frac{1\,\mathrm{AU}}{D_S}\right)^2,\\ P_{\mathrm{array,bus}}&=S(D_S)A\eta_{\mathrm{cell}} \max(0,\cos\alpha)f_{\mathrm{loss}}f_{\mathrm{EOL}}. \end{align} Solar distance DSD_S and reference distance use matching units; S1S_1 is irradiance at 1 AU. Angle α\alpha lies between panel normal and direction toward the Sun. Dimensionless factors describe stated array-to-bus losses and retained end-of-life output.

Assume S=1361S=1361 W/m2^2, A=1.5A=1.5 m2^2, ηcell=0.28\eta_{\mathrm{cell}}=0.28, α=40∘\alpha=40^\circ, floss=0.85f_{\mathrm{loss}}=0.85 and fEOL=0.8f_{\mathrm{EOL}}=0.8. Delivered power is approximately 298 W. These are illustrative inputs, not a selected flight design. A rating already incorporating EOL or conversion losses requires those factors only once.

A supplied temperature correction might be fT=1+aT(T−Tref)f_T=1+a_T(T-T_{\mathrm{ref}}), with aTa_T in K−1^{-1}; apply it only over its valid range. Multi-junction cells collect different spectral bands, but their efficiency still needs a stated optical/electrical boundary. Solar generation weakens continuously with distance rather than ending abruptly beyond a particular planet.

Teach it. Explain how a 20% output reduction changes required area, and distinguish that reduction from a 20% margin applied to demand.

Store Energy Through the Dark Interval

Fig. 24 shows the interval a solar-only spacecraft cannot meet directly from its array. Eclipse duration comes from geometry; required stored energy comes from integrating the actual bus load. Heaters and standby hardware may remain active with the transmitter silent [source] [source].

For a circular orbit, Sun in the orbital plane, spherical Earth and parallel illumination, central-eclipse duration is te=Tπsin⁡−1(REr).\begin{equation} t_e=\frac{T}{\pi}\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R_E}{r}\right). \end{equation} The shadowed arc spans twice the half-angle sin⁡−1(RE/r)\sin^{-1}(R_E/r). The illustrative 900 km circle gives about 35 min. A different Sun–orbit plane angle can shorten or remove eclipse; penumbra and seasonal detail need a richer model.

For the energy/current calculations here, use an ideal constant-voltage battery whose terminal energy exchange equals its stored-energy exchange; ηc\eta_c and ηd\eta_d represent conversion-path efficiencies between battery terminals and bus. Let DallowD_{\mathrm{allow}} be the allowed capacity fraction removed per cycle: Ebus,e=∫eclipsePbusdt,Eremoved=Ebus,eηd,\begin{equation} E_{\mathrm{bus,e}}=\int_{\mathrm{eclipse}}P_{\mathrm{bus}}\,dt,\qquad E_{\mathrm{removed}}=\frac{E_{\mathrm{bus,e}}}{\eta_d}, \end{equation} Ecap≥MmarginEbus,eηdDallow.\begin{equation} E_{\mathrm{cap}}\ge\frac{M_{\mathrm{margin}}E_{\mathrm{bus,e}}}{\eta_dD_{\mathrm{allow}}}. \end{equation} Chosen margin Mmargin≥1M_{\mathrm{margin}}\ge1 is dimensionless. Capacity EcapE_{\mathrm{cap}} is available full capacity at the evaluated age and temperature. If it is fraction fcapf_{\mathrm{cap}} of beginning-of-life nameplate capacity, require Ecap,BOL≥Ecap/fcapE_{\mathrm{cap,BOL}}\ge E_{\mathrm{cap}}/f_{\mathrm{cap}}.

The figure’s bus demand is 80×0.6=4880\times0.6=48 Wh and removed energy 53.33 Wh. With allowed depth of discharge 0.5 and margin 1.2, minimum evaluated capacity is 128 Wh. The depicted choice is 200 Wh at that condition. Since SOC=Estored/Ecap\mathrm{SOC}=E_{\mathrm{stored}}/E_{\mathrm{cap}}, its drop is 53.33/200=0.26753.33/200=0.267. At fixed 24 V battery voltage, discharge current is 80/(0.9×24)=3.7080/(0.9\times24)=3.70 A. A higher simultaneous peak requires its own current check.

Teach it. Explain why efficiency divides bus energy, and why sufficient capacity does not establish acceptable peak current or cycle life.

Recharge Before the Next Eclipse

Fig. 25 shows the second storage condition: surviving one eclipse is insufficient if subsequent sunlight cannot restore its deficit. The array supplies current operations while charging for the next dark interval [source].

Define Psurplus,bus=Parray,bus−Pload,sunP_{\mathrm{surplus,bus}}=P_{\mathrm{array,bus}}-P_{\mathrm{load,sun}}. For charging efficiency ηc\eta_c from bus surplus to stored energy and constant available time trt_r, ηcPsurplus,bustr≥Eremoved,\begin{equation} \eta_cP_{\mathrm{surplus,bus}}t_r\ge E_{\mathrm{removed}}, \end{equation} Parray,bus≥Pload,sun+Eremovedηctr.\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{array,bus}}\ge P_{\mathrm{load,sun}} +\frac{E_{\mathrm{removed}}}{\eta_ct_r}. \end{equation} Use hours with Wh. Restoring 53.33 Wh over 2 h at ηc=0.9\eta_c=0.9 needs 29.63 W bus surplus. Adding the simultaneous 60 W load gives at least 89.63 W array bus output under the evaluated illumination.

A current limit can be stricter. At battery terminal voltage VbV_b and allowed charging current Ic,maxI_{c,\max}, a constant-voltage approximation gives Pstored,charge≤min⁡(ηcPsurplus,bus,VbIc,max).\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{stored,charge}}\le \min\!\left(\eta_cP_{\mathrm{surplus,bus}},V_bI_{c,\max}\right). \end{equation} Actual voltage, acceptance and taper depend on chemistry, temperature and SOC. Integrate the permitted charging profile when supplied. Unused sunlight can be curtailed rather than overcharging storage. Repeat this cycle at end of life after generation and usable capacity have changed.

Teach it. Explain why dividing eclipse energy by the entire orbital period can underestimate recharge power. Identify when adding solar area ceases to shorten recharge time.

Carry Waste Heat to a Radiating Surface

Fig. 26 shows why thermal control belongs in the electrical budget. Most spacecraft electrical energy ultimately becomes heat. Radiating surfaces remove it, while eclipse heaters may be needed to keep hardware sufficiently warm [source].

Structures conduct heat internally; vacuum has no surrounding-air convection. A simple lumped balance is CthdTdt=Pabs+Pdiss−ϵσAT4.\begin{equation} C_{\mathrm{th}}\frac{dT}{dt}=P_{\mathrm{abs}}+P_{\mathrm{diss}}-\epsilon\sigma AT^4. \end{equation} Effective heat capacity CthC_{\mathrm{th}} is in J/K, absolute temperature TT in K, powers in W, area AA in m2^2 and emissivity ϵ\epsilon dimensionless. The Stefan–Boltzmann constant is σ=5.670374419×10−8\sigma=5.670374419\times10^{-8} W/(m2^2K4^4). Here PabsP_{\mathrm{abs}} includes absorbed environmental inputs, while the last term is outgoing radiation. If using net exchange ϵσA(T4−Tenv4)\epsilon\sigma A(T^4-T_{\mathrm{env}}^4) instead, remove the same ambient absorption from PabsP_{\mathrm{abs}} to avoid counting it twice.

The steady cold-background illustration has Teq=[Pabs+PdissϵσA]1/4.\begin{equation} T_{\mathrm{eq}}=\left[\frac{P_{\mathrm{abs}}+P_{\mathrm{diss}}}{\epsilon\sigma A}\right]^{1/4}. \end{equation} For 100 W heat, ϵ=0.8\epsilon=0.8 and A=0.3A=0.3 m2^2, Teq=292.8T_{\mathrm{eq}}=292.8 K. Celsius cannot enter the fourth power. A real radiator requires view factors, surface absorptivity, solar/Earth radiation and conductive paths.

Finite heat capacity means temperature responds over time rather than instantly following eclipse. Heater energy increases storage demand; increased amplifier DC input usually increases heat. Different components have different safe temperature ranges.

Teach it. Predict how equilibrium temperature changes when heat input doubles, then explain why one surface temperature cannot certify every component’s peak temperature.

Match Radiation Protection to Its Failure Mechanism

Fig. 27 shows why different radiation failures require different controls. Correcting a memory bit does not reverse accumulated transistor changes or repair a damaged solar-cell lattice [source].

Single-event effects follow individual energetic interactions. An upset can change a bit; latch-up can create excessive current requiring rapid protection and possibly power cycling. Total ionizing dose accumulates and shifts device characteristics. Displacement damage disrupts material structure and can reduce semiconductor or photovoltaic performance. Orbit, shielding, device design and exposure affect each mechanism differently.

Redundancy has a stated failure model. For three independent identical channels, each wrong with probability pp, a perfect majority voter fails when at least two channels are wrong: pmajority=3p2(1−p)+p3=3p2−2p3.\begin{equation} p_{\mathrm{majority}}=3p^2(1-p)+p^3=3p^2-2p^3. \end{equation} At illustrative p=0.01p=0.01, this is 0.000298 per evaluated event. It is not a flight reliability estimate: shared power, clocks, correlated exposure or a failed voter violate its assumptions. Extra channels also add mass, power and heat. Shielding, qualified components, current protection and error correction address different parts of the problem.

Teach it. Match memory correction, current limiting, shielding and device qualification to the mechanisms they can address. Explain why a generic “radiation-proof” label supplies too little information.

Distinguish a Relay From a Receiver That Makes Decisions

Fig. 28 shows two different satellite jobs. A bent-pipe relay forwards an information-bearing waveform without interpreting every bit. A regenerative payload estimates digital information and retransmits according to those decisions [source].

A low-noise amplifier handles the weak receive input; later power amplification supplies transmitted RF output. Mixing produces sum and difference frequencies; filters select the desired translated band. An intermediate frequency can make filtering and amplification convenient before another conversion.

An ideal linear amplifier multiplies both signal and in-band noise by gain gg: gC/(gN)=C/NgC/(gN)=C/N. Real hardware adds noise. Gain alone cannot recover an uplink signal-to-noise ratio already lost. Regeneration can avoid forwarding that analog noise when decisions are correct, but a wrong detected bit does not become correct merely by retransmission.

Regeneration adds format support, processing demand and latency. Bent-pipe operation retains waveform flexibility within bandwidth and linearity limits. Both require power, cooling, pointing and reliability. Later radio chapters quantify noise and received power at explicit terminal planes.

Teach it. Explain which payload must understand the modulation and which can forward it without decoding. Identify weak-signal handling and large electrical heat loads in each architecture.

Compare Energy Sources by Their Mechanism

Fig. 29 shows why generation and storage specifications answer different questions. Solar arrays produce while illuminated. Batteries supply stored energy until recharged. Fuel cells consume reactants and require tanks and support hardware. RTGs depend on decay rather than sunlight [source].

For an ideal hydrogen/oxygen cell, 2H2+O2→2H2O2\mathrm{H}_2+\mathrm{O}_2\rightarrow2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}. With both tabulated electrode values given as reduction potentials, Ecell=Ecathode−Eanode,ΔG=−nFFEcell.\begin{equation} E_{\mathrm{cell}}=E_{\mathrm{cathode}}-E_{\mathrm{anode}},\qquad \Delta G=-nF_FE_{\mathrm{cell}}. \end{equation} Potential EcellE_{\mathrm{cell}} is in volts, ΔG\Delta G is J per mole of balanced reaction, nn is its electron-transfer count and FF≃96485F_F\simeq96485 C/mol is Faraday’s constant. For the reaction as written, n=4n=4. Operating losses lower the loaded voltage, and supporting hardware reduces net system output.

An RTG supplies long-lived electrical output through thermoelectric conversion, with substantial heat still needing accommodation. Solar output depends on illumination, orientation and aging. Batteries depend on cycle life, temperature, power capability and SOC range. Select among mechanisms using the energy timeline and mission constraints.

Teach it. Explain which sources require sunlight, periodic recharge, supplied reactants or a continuing thermal source.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, ASD06 Spacecraft Subsystems, supplied ASD6include.pdf and linked lecture recording. Lecture recording.

  • ECE 6390, supplied Photovoltaic Notes, battery comparison chart and first-seven-class transcripts.

chapters.title: Follow the Electromagnetic Wave
chapters.label: sec:e1-waves
chapters.html:
Fig. 30 shows the rules that connect a driven antenna to the fields surrounding it. A satellite radio link carries energy through changing electric and magnetic fields. Before turning that energy into a link budget, identify what the fields measure, which sources are present, and what the material permits [source].

The electric field 𝑬\boldsymbol{E} is force per unit electric charge, measured in volts per metre. The magnetic field 𝑯\boldsymbol{H} is measured in amperes per metre. Electric flux density 𝑫\boldsymbol{D} has units C/m2^2 and magnetic flux density 𝑩\boldsymbol{B} has units tesla. For the linear, isotropic material model used here, 𝑫=ϵ𝑬,𝑩=μ𝑯.\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{D}=\epsilon\boldsymbol{E},\qquad \boldsymbol{B}=\mu\boldsymbol{H}. \end{equation} Permittivity ϵ\epsilon is in F/m and permeability μ\mu in H/m. These material relations accompany Maxwell’s equations: ∇⋅𝑫=ρv,∇⋅𝑩=0,∇×𝑬=−∂𝑩∂t,∇×𝑯=𝑱+∂𝑫∂t.\begin{align} \nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{D}&=\rho_v,&\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{B}&=0,\\ \nabla\times\boldsymbol{E}&=-\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{B}}{\partial t},& \nabla\times\boldsymbol{H}&=\boldsymbol{J}+\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{D}}{\partial t}. \end{align} ρv\rho_v is free-charge density in C/m3^3; 𝑱\boldsymbol{J} is free-current density in A/m2^2. Divergence measures net local outward flux. Curl measures local circulation, with its vector normal to that circulation according to the right-hand rule. Zero magnetic divergence requires zero net flux through a closed surface; it allows a nonzero magnetic field through parts of that surface.

The displacement-current term ∂𝑫/∂t\partial\boldsymbol{D}/\partial t is essential in a charging capacitor. Conduction current enters its wire, while changing electric flux spans its insulating gap. Both enter the magnetic-circulation law. Charge conservation gives a useful check: ∇⋅𝑱=−∂ρv∂t.\begin{equation} \nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{J}=-\frac{\partial\rho_v}{\partial t}. \end{equation} If more charge leaves a small region than enters, its stored charge decreases. A source-free propagation region can still contain a wave launched by an antenna elsewhere. To use the simple lossless wave equations below, exclude both local free sources and conduction loss; zero charge density by itself would not exclude a conducting current 𝑱=σ𝑬\boldsymbol{J}=\sigma\boldsymbol{E}.

Represent One Frequency by Amplitude and Phase

Fig. 31 shows how a phasor saves repeated sinusoidal bookkeeping. A steady-frequency field may have a different amplitude and phase at every position, but its common time dependence is known. Store those spatial amplitudes and phases, then restore the oscillation when needed.

Use the ejωte^{j\omega t} convention throughout, with j2=−1j^2=-1 and ω=2πf\omega=2\pi f. A tilde denotes a complex peak-amplitude phasor: 𝑬(𝒓,t)=ℜ{𝑬̃(𝒓)ejωt}.\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{E}(\boldsymbol{r},t)=\Re\!\left\{ \widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}(\boldsymbol{r})e^{j\omega t}\right\}. \end{equation} For a scalar component Ẽx=Aejψ\widetilde E_x=Ae^{j\psi}, this becomes Ex(t)=Acos⁡(ωt+ψ)E_x(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\psi). AA is the component’s peak amplitude; ψ\psi is a phase in radians. The imaginary coordinate records phase rather than an additional physical electric field. For example, Ẽx=2ejπ/3\widetilde E_x=2e^{j\pi/3} V/m gives Ex(0)=1E_x(0)=1 V/m and a peak magnitude of 2 V/m.

Time differentiation becomes multiplication by jωj\omega. This changes the source-free curl equations into ∇×𝑬̃=−jωμ𝑯̃,∇×𝑯̃=jωϵ𝑬̃.\begin{align} \nabla\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}&=-j\omega\mu\widetilde{\boldsymbol{H}},\\ \nabla\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{H}}&=j\omega\epsilon\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}. \end{align} The minus sign in the electric-field equation belongs to the stated time convention. A source using e−jωte^{-j\omega t} will carry corresponding sign changes. Keep a single convention through the entire calculation.

Phasor addition also explains interference. Two co-polarized plane waves traveling in the same direction in the same lossless medium, each with peak field AA and a fixed relative phase Δψ\Delta\psi, have summed amplitude 2A|cos⁡(Δψ/2)|2A|\cos(\Delta\psi/2)|. Their combined power is proportional to 4A2cos⁡2(Δψ/2)4A^2\cos^2(\Delta\psi/2). In phase, the field doubles and its local power becomes four times that of either contribution alone; opposite phases produce cancellation. The sources’ complete spatial interference redistributes energy, so one observation point is insufficient to infer total radiated power.

Connect the Double Curl to a Standing Wave

Fig. 32 shows a field changing across space and a pair of waves that can produce it. The electric field points along xx but varies along zz. Its first curl points along yy and its second returns to xx.

In a homogeneous, source-free, lossless region, take the curl of the electric-field curl equation and substitute the magnetic-field equation: ∇×(∇×𝑬̃)=ω2μϵ𝑬̃=k2𝑬̃.\begin{equation} \nabla\times(\nabla\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}) =\omega^2\mu\epsilon\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}=k^2\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}. \end{equation} The vector identity ∇×(∇×𝑬̃)=∇(∇⋅𝑬̃)−∇2𝑬̃\begin{equation} \nabla\times(\nabla\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}) =\nabla(\nabla\cdot\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}})-\nabla^2\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}} \end{equation} then gives the Helmholtz equation, ∇2𝑬̃+k2𝑬̃=0,k=ωμϵ.\begin{equation} \nabla^2\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}+k^2\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}=0, \qquad k=\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}. \end{equation} Homogeneous permittivity and zero free charge give ∇⋅𝑬̃=0\nabla\cdot\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}=0. The same equation holds for 𝑯̃\widetilde{\boldsymbol{H}}. It states the allowed spatial variation at one frequency; sources and boundaries determine which allowed solution occurs.

For the figure’s example 𝑬̃=𝒙̂E0cos⁡(kz)\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}=\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}E_0\cos(kz), the divergence is zero because ExE_x does not vary with xx. Yet ∇×𝑬̃=−𝒚̂kE0sin⁡(kz),∇×∇×𝑬̃=𝒙̂k2E0cos⁡(kz).\begin{align} \nabla\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}&=-\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}kE_0\sin(kz),\\ \nabla\times\nabla\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}} &=\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}k^2E_0\cos(kz). \end{align} To realize this field, send two waves with electric components Acos⁡(ωt∓kz)A\cos(\omega t\mp kz) along +z+z and −z-z in the same lossless medium. Their electric fields point along the same axis, but reversing travel reverses the magnetic direction. Adding each pair gives Ex(z,t)=2Acos⁡(kz)cos⁡(ωt),Hy(z,t)=(2A/η)sin⁡(kz)sin⁡(ωt).\begin{align*} E_x(z,t)&=2A\cos(kz)\cos(\omega t),\\ H_y(z,t)&=(2A/\eta)\sin(kz)\sin(\omega t). \end{align*} Here E0=2AE_0=2A and η\eta is the medium’s wave impedance. At z=0z=0 the electric field oscillates and the magnetic field vanishes. At z=λ/4z=\lambda/4 their roles reverse. The two time factors peak a quarter period apart, so their product averages to zero: equal waves carry equal power in opposite directions. Fig. 43 shows the voltage envelope on a lossless feed line. At an open end the voltage peaks and current vanishes.

Read a Plane Wave’s Direction and Companion Field

Fig. 33 shows the geometry behind a uniform traveling plane wave: electric field, magnetic field and propagation form a mutually perpendicular triad. The local oscillation travels through space; the field’s transverse direction describes its polarization.

For the simple lossless medium, v=1μϵ,λ=vf,k=2πλ,η=μϵ.\begin{equation} v=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}},\quad \lambda=\frac vf,\quad k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},\quad \eta=\sqrt{\frac\mu\epsilon}. \end{equation} vv is phase velocity in m/s, λ\lambda wavelength in metres, kk wavenumber in rad/m, and η\eta intrinsic impedance in ohms. In free space v=c≃2.998×108v=c\simeq2.998\times10^8 m/s and η0≃376.73Ω\eta_0\simeq376.73~\Omega. Intrinsic impedance describes the electric-to-magnetic field ratio; it is not a dissipative resistor in the propagation path.

A plane wave is 𝑬̃(𝒓)=𝑬0e−jk𝒌̂⋅𝒓,𝒌̂⋅𝑬0=0.\begin{equation} \widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}(\boldsymbol{r})=\boldsymbol{E}_0 e^{-jk\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}},\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\boldsymbol{E}_0=0. \end{equation} 𝒌̂\hat{\boldsymbol{k}} is a unit vector giving direction of travel. Restore time to get phase ωt−k𝒌̂⋅𝒓\omega t-k\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}. Keeping that phase constant while increasing time moves the point in the positive 𝒌̂\hat{\boldsymbol{k}} direction. An antenna looking back toward the source points along −𝒌̂-\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}; that is the direction of arrival.

The companion field follows directly: 𝑯̃=1η𝒌̂×𝑬̃.\begin{equation} \widetilde{\boldsymbol{H}}=\frac1\eta \hat{\boldsymbol{k}}\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}. \end{equation} Use a cross product and the stated propagation direction, with no complex conjugation in this conversion. For example, take 𝒌̂=(2,−1,2)/3\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}=(2,-1,2)/3 and 𝑬0=(1,2,0)\boldsymbol{E}_0=(1,2,0) V/m. Their dot product is zero and the companion amplitude is (−4,2,5)/(3η0)(-4,2,5)/(3\eta_0) A/m. This vector test checks transverse geometry as well as field magnitude.

At 2 GHz in free space, λ≃0.150\lambda\simeq0.150 m and k≃41.9k\simeq41.9 rad/m. An extra path length of λ/4\lambda/4 gives an extra delay Δt=λ/(4c)\Delta t=\lambda/(4c) and a received phasor phase lag kΔd=π/2k\Delta d=\pi/2. A path-length change can therefore matter greatly to interference even when it is tiny compared with the total satellite range.

Describe Polarization at One Fixed Point

Fig. 34 shows the question polarization answers: how does the electric-field direction change with time at one location? Looking along a wave’s spatial field-tip curve answers a different question, so fix the observation point before following the tip.

Write the two transverse components as Ex=Acos⁡u,Ey=bAcos⁡(u+δ),u=ωt−kz.\begin{equation} E_x=A\cos u,\qquad E_y=bA\cos(u+\delta), \qquad u=\omega t-kz. \end{equation} bb is their dimensionless amplitude ratio and δ\delta their relative phase. In-phase or opposite-phase components trace a line. Equal amplitudes with relative phase ±π/2\pm\pi/2 trace a circle. More general nondegenerate combinations trace an ellipse. A common phase added to both components shifts the time origin; their relative phase controls the shape and rotation.

For b=1b=1 and δ=π/2\delta=\pi/2, 𝑬=A(𝒙̂cos⁡u−𝒚̂sin⁡u)\boldsymbol{E}=A(\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}\cos u-\hat{\boldsymbol{y}}\sin u). Its magnitude is always AA, although each component oscillates. For b=1/2b=1/2 with the same relative phase, the ellipse’s principal axes have ratio two. A circular or elliptical handedness label must specify whether one looks along propagation or back toward the transmitter; reversing the viewpoint reverses the apparent rotation.

The receiver responds to the field component that matches its receiving polarization. Aligned linear antennas can collect the available co-polarized power. Rotating one by 90∘90^\circ ideally rejects it; an ideal linear receiver accepts half of a circularly polarized wave’s power. Section V turns this picture into a coupling factor and distinguishes polarization mismatch from pointing or port-impedance mismatch.

Convert Fields Into Transported Power

Fig. 35 shows the two conversions that bridge field calculations and radio engineering: average a squared oscillation to obtain power, then track that power as it spreads across a growing area.

The instantaneous Poynting vector is 𝑺=𝑬×𝑯\boldsymbol{S}=\boldsymbol{E}\times\boldsymbol{H}, in W/m2^2. Using peak phasors, its time average is ⟨𝑺⟩=12ℜ{𝑬̃×𝑯̃*}.\begin{equation} \langle\boldsymbol{S}\rangle=\frac12\Re\!\left\{ \widetilde{\boldsymbol{E}}\times\widetilde{\boldsymbol{H}}^{\,*}\right\}. \end{equation} The conjugate belongs in this power calculation. For a uniform plane wave in the stated lossless medium, ⟨𝑺⟩=𝑬0⋅𝑬0*2η𝒌̂.\begin{equation} \langle\boldsymbol{S}\rangle= \frac{\boldsymbol{E}_0\cdot\boldsymbol{E}_0^*}{2\eta}\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}. \end{equation} The numerator is the sum of squared component magnitudes. Peak phasors require the factor one half; RMS phasors already include that averaging. For a linearly polarized wave with peak field 2 V/m, the average free-space flux is 22/(2η0)=5.312^2/(2\eta_0)=5.31 mW/m2^2. In the earlier vector example, the squared norm is five, giving 6.646.64 mW/m2^2 in direction 𝒌̂\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}.

A circularly polarized field with each component’s peak equal to AA has phasor norm squared 2A22A^2, so its average flux is A2/ηA^2/\eta. Here the total real field has constant magnitude AA. Declaring whether an amplitude refers to one component, vector norm or RMS value prevents a factor-of-two error.

Connect a Local Plane Wave to Spherical Spreading

Fig. 36 shows how the plane-wave idealization can describe the neighborhood of a distant receiver. A source can send a spherical wave over the complete link while its field is nearly uniform in direction and amplitude across a small receiving antenna.

In a lossless radiation zone, field amplitude is proportional to 1/r1/r and outward flux to 1/r21/r^2. Integrating the outward flux over a sphere gives the same radiated power at every such radius. For isotropic radiation the flux is uniform, so the integral is simply flux times 4πr24\pi r^2. Doubling distance therefore halves field amplitude and quarters power flux. A globally uniform plane wave has no spreading in its idealized infinite transverse extent; the local approximation does not remove the real source’s range dependence.

An isotropic source of radiated power PP would produce S=P/(4πr2)S=P/(4\pi r^2). Real antennas redistribute that power by direction, which motivates directivity and gain. The next chapter connects their pattern to current on a wire, then Section VI follows the directional flux into receiving-antenna power.

Pause and teach it.

Explain the physical meaning and units of 𝑬\boldsymbol{E}, 𝑯\boldsymbol{H}, 𝒌̂\hat{\boldsymbol{k}} and ⟨𝑺⟩\langle\boldsymbol{S}\rangle for one plane wave. Identify which cross product needs a conjugate, why one has a factor one half, and why the antenna’s viewing direction reverses the propagation vector. Then explain how a source-free region can still carry energy.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, supplied WAV01–WAV03 recordings: Maxwell’s equations, scalar wave equation and plane waves. Maxwell; wave equation; plane waves.

chapters.title: Turn Wire Current Into an Antenna Pattern
chapters.label: sec:e1-antennas
chapters.html:
Fig. 37 shows why antenna geometry creates directionality. Each piece of alternating current contributes a field. Their amplitudes, orientations and path phases determine which directions reinforce and which cancel. Far from the source, those summed fields become locally transverse traveling waves [source].

An antenna links a guided circuit to radiation. Near its metal, charges, currents and stored reactive energy matter. The simple plane-wave relation E/H=ηE/H=\eta applies to its radiation zone, rather than every point next to the wire. ANT5 organizes analysis around a known source current, a known aperture field, or a numerical coupled field/current solution. Exam 1 emphasizes the first route and the meaning of supplied results; apertures, dishes and array synthesis belong to the next exam [source].

For source coordinate 𝒓′\boldsymbol{r}' and distant observer 𝒓\boldsymbol{r}, the useful distance approximation is ∥𝒓−𝒓′∥≃r−𝒓̂⋅𝒓′.\begin{equation} \|\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{r}'\|\simeq r-\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}'. \end{equation} Use rr in slowly varying amplitude factors, but retain the dot product in phase. A small fraction of the large range can still be a significant fraction of wavelength. Removing that phase would remove the interference responsible for the pattern.

The course’s engineering far-field criterion is r>max⁡(λ,Da2λ),\begin{equation} r>\max\!\left(\lambda,\frac{D_a^2}{\lambda}\right), \end{equation} where DaD_a is the largest source dimension, not directivity. It is a practical approximation that improves with distance; other references use different numerical factors or tolerances. For a zz-directed wire, spherical θ\theta is measured from +z+z, while ϕ\phi is azimuth around that axis. Thus θ=90∘\theta=90^\circ is broadside to the wire. Keep this polar angle distinct from a station’s elevation above its horizon.

Choose the Current Model Before Its Radiation Resistance

Fig. 38 shows why a wire’s total length alone does not determine how strongly it radiates. The current distribution also matters. The Hertzian element uses a uniform current as an ideal building block; a short center-fed open wire tapers toward zero at its ends.

Let L≪λL\ll\lambda be complete tip-to-tip length and I0I_0 the feed-current peak. The uniform-current integral is I0LI_0L; a triangular distribution has half that integrated current moment. In the short-source approximation, field is proportional to that moment and radiated power to its square. Consequently, Rrad,Hertzian=80π2(L/λ)2,Rrad,short=20π2(L/λ)2.\begin{align} R_{\mathrm{rad,Hertzian}}&=80\pi^2(L/\lambda)^2,\\ R_{\mathrm{rad,short}}&=20\pi^2(L/\lambda)^2. \end{align} Radiation resistance is defined through power carried away by waves: Prad=12Ipeak2Rrad=Irms2Rrad.\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{rad}}=\tfrac12 I_{\mathrm{peak}}^2R_{\mathrm{rad}} =I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R_{\mathrm{rad}}. \end{equation} It is an equivalent circuit representation of radiation, separate from resistance that heats the conductor. Peak and RMS currents require their corresponding power expression.

For the illustrative electrical length L/λ=0.05L/\lambda=0.05, the uniform model gives Rrad=1.974ΩR_{\mathrm{rad}}=1.974~\Omega, while the triangular model gives 0.493Ω0.493~\Omega. Both have the peak-normalized power pattern sin⁡2θ\sin^2\theta: strongest broadside and zero along the wire axis. Their complete directivity is D(θ)=1.5sin⁡2θD(\theta)=1.5\sin^2\theta, with peak 1.5 or 1.76 dBi. Sharing a normalized pattern therefore does not imply sharing radiation resistance or efficiency.

Electrically small means size is small relative to wavelength, rather than merely small in metres. Small wires also tend to have important reactive input impedance and limited useful matching bandwidth. A matching network can transform the input impedance at a selected frequency; it does not convert conductor heating into radiation. If the example triangular wire has an independently assumed 1Ω1~\Omega loss resistance, its radiation efficiency is only 0.493/(0.493+1)=0.3300.493/(0.493+1)=0.330, even after a perfect port match.

Picture the Half-Wave Dipole in Three Dimensions

Fig. 39 shows the full shape that a single two-dimensional antenna cut can hide. The dipole radiates around its wire axis, with little radiation toward either wire end. Rotating around the wire changes azimuth without changing the ideal pattern.

An ideal thin center-fed half-wave dipole has nominal total length λ/2\lambda/2 and an approximately sinusoidal current amplitude, I(z)=I0cos⁡(kz),|z|≤λ/4.\begin{equation} I(z)=I_0\cos(kz),\qquad |z|\le\lambda/4. \end{equation} Its center feed is a current maximum; each open end is a current node. Over this single standing-wave hump the ideal current shares a common phase. Its amplitude varies along the wire, while a traveling-wave phase progression would be a different current model.

Integrating the contributions gives radiation-zone angular field shape F(θ)=cos⁡[(π/2)cos⁡θ]sin⁡θ,pn(θ)=|F(θ)|2.\begin{equation} F(\theta)=\frac{\cos[(\pi/2)\cos\theta]}{\sin\theta}, \qquad p_n(\theta)=|F(\theta)|^2. \end{equation} FF is field-amplitude shape and pnp_n is peak-normalized power. At broadside F=1F=1. Along the axis the apparent zero-over-zero has the limit zero, giving the pictured nulls. The result has no ϕ\phi dependence because the ideal geometry is rotationally symmetric.

Its nominal radiation resistance is about 73Ω73~\Omega. Geometric length, input reactance and exact resonant length depend on wire thickness and surroundings; a length exactly λ/2\lambda/2 does not guarantee a purely resistive input. At 2 GHz, the nominal geometric tip-to-tip half wavelength is about 7.5 cm. A practical tuned antenna can be slightly shorter and still represent the same basic radiation model.

Read Pattern Cuts and Half-Power Beamwidth

Fig. 40 shows how the familiar pattern plot depends on which plane is cut. A vertical dipole’s E-plane cut includes the wire axis and varies with polar angle; its broadside H-plane cut sweeps azimuth. These planes are named from the principal electric- and magnetic-field directions in the relevant radiation geometry.

Half-power beamwidth is the angular separation between points on either side of a main maximum where power is one half its peak. In field amplitude, that same level is 1/21/\sqrt2 of peak. In decibels it is 10log⁡10(1/2)=−3.0110\log_{10}(1/2)=-3.01 dB, consistent with 20log⁡10(1/2)20\log_{10}(1/\sqrt2).

For the half-wave shape, the crossings occur at θ=50.96∘\theta=50.96^\circ and 129.04∘129.04^\circ, measured from the wire axis. Their difference is 78.08∘78.08^\circ. The ideal short-dipole sin⁡2θ\sin^2\theta shape has crossings at 45∘45^\circ and 135∘135^\circ, giving 90∘90^\circ. The half-wave pattern is somewhat more concentrated broadside.

Omnidirectional in this context means independent of azimuth. Isotropic means independent of every spatial direction. The dipole is omnidirectional around its wire, while the axial nulls make it strongly nonisotropic. To interpret a supplied plot, first ask which angle varies, which polarization is measured and whether the plotted quantity is field, power, gain or a normalized pattern.

Normalize a Pattern to Obtain Directivity

Fig. 41 shows why a normalized maximum of one cannot simply be inserted as antenna gain. Directivity compares the directional radiated intensity with the average intensity of the same total radiated power distributed over a sphere.

Let SrS_r be radiation-zone outward average flux in W/m2^2. Radiation intensity is U(θ,ϕ)=r2SrU(\theta,\phi)=r^2S_r in W/sr. Total radiated power is Prad=∫02π∫0πU(θ,ϕ)sin⁡θdθdϕ.\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{rad}}=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^\pi U(\theta,\phi)\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi. \end{equation} The factor sin⁡θ\sin\theta belongs to spherical solid angle; uniform steps of polar angle do not cover equal areas near a sphere’s pole and equator. Directivity is D(θ,ϕ)=4πU(θ,ϕ)Prad.\begin{equation} D(\theta,\phi)=\frac{4\pi U(\theta,\phi)}{P_{\mathrm{rad}}}. \end{equation} Its full-sphere average is one. Particular directions can exceed or fall below one because radiated power is redistributed, with no active power amplification implied.

If pnp_n is a peak-normalized power pattern, define beam solid angle ΩA=∫pndΩ\Omega_A=\int p_n\,d\Omega and peak directivity D0=4π/ΩAD_0=4\pi/\Omega_A. For an azimuth-independent dipole, D0=2∫0πpn(θ)sin⁡θdθ.\begin{equation} D_0=\frac{2}{\displaystyle\int_0^\pi p_n(\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta}. \end{equation} The half-wave integral gives D0=1.64092D_0=1.64092, or 2.1509 dBi. Its full directional directivity is therefore 1.64092pn(θ)1.64092p_n(\theta). ANT6’s half-wave table shape must be interpreted with this normalization. A bare squared pattern fraction describes shape, while total radiated-power normalization supplies its peak directivity.

Separate Radiation Loss From Reflection at the Port

Fig. 42 shows the power references behind three often-confused antenna specifications. Directivity uses radiated power, absolute gain uses accepted power, and realized gain uses power incident on a specified port before mismatch [source].

Radiation efficiency is the fraction of accepted input power that radiates: ηrad=PradPacc,G(θ,ϕ)=ηradD(θ,ϕ).\begin{equation} \eta_{\mathrm{rad}}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{rad}}}{P_{\mathrm{acc}}},\qquad G(\theta,\phi)=\eta_{\mathrm{rad}}D(\theta,\phi). \end{equation} For a corresponding series-resistance model, ηrad=RradRrad+Rloss.\begin{equation} \eta_{\mathrm{rad}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{rad}}}{R_{\mathrm{rad}}+R_{\mathrm{loss}}}. \end{equation} Conductor and dielectric loss reduce the useful radiated fraction. They differ from the spatial redistribution described by directivity and from incident power reflected before entering the antenna.

For a real positive reference impedance Z0Z_0, the antenna reflection coefficient and accepted fraction are Γ=ZA−Z0ZA+Z0,PaccPinc=1−|Γ|2.\begin{equation} \Gamma=\frac{Z_A-Z_0}{Z_A+Z_0},\qquad \frac{P_{\mathrm{acc}}}{P_{\mathrm{inc}}}=1-|\Gamma|^2. \end{equation} ZAZ_A may be complex. Squared magnitude is the reflected-power fraction; Γ\Gamma itself is a complex amplitude ratio. Realized gain is Grealized=(1−|Γ|2)ηradD.\begin{equation} G_{\mathrm{realized}}=(1-|\Gamma|^2)\eta_{\mathrm{rad}}D. \end{equation} For |Γ|=0.2|\Gamma|=0.2 and ηrad=0.8\eta_{\mathrm{rad}}=0.8, the incident-to-radiated fraction is 0.96×0.8=0.7680.96\times0.8=0.768. With half-wave peak directivity 1.64092, realized peak gain is 1.26023, or 1.0045 dBi. This lower gain does not require a different normalized angular shape.

An ideal lossless antenna can be badly mismatched; a perfectly matched antenna can dissipate most accepted power as heat. A datasheet’s word “gain” needs its reference checked, because reported measurements may already include mismatch. Applying efficiency again to absolute gain, or mismatch again to realized gain, would count the same reduction twice. Gain referenced to a nominal half-wave dipole uses dBd, with approximately GdBi=GdBd+2.15G_{\mathrm{dBi}}=G_{\mathrm{dBd}}+2.15.

Read a Standing-Wave Ratio as a Match Measurement

Fig. 43 shows what a feed-line measurement reveals. Interference between forward and reflected waves creates a position-dependent envelope, while the voltage at every position still oscillates at the RF frequency.

The maximum and minimum envelope magnitudes are proportional to 1+|Γ|1+|\Gamma| and 1−|Γ|1-|\Gamma|. Thus VSWR=VmaxVmin=1+|Γ|1−|Γ|.\begin{equation} \mathrm{VSWR}=\frac{V_{\max}}{V_{\min}} =\frac{1+|\Gamma|}{1-|\Gamma|}. \end{equation} VSWR is ordinarily a dimensionless linear ratio at least one. Zero reflection gives VSWR 1. Complete reflection gives an infinite ratio in the ideal lossless line. An open end is a voltage maximum and current minimum; their standing-wave peaks are offset by a quarter wavelength. Along the line, adjacent voltage maxima and minima are λg/4\lambda_g/4 apart and successive maxima are λg/2\lambda_g/2 apart. The guided wavelength is λg=vp,line/f\lambda_g=v_{\mathrm{p,line}}/f, using the line’s phase speed.

For an independently assumed tuned antenna ZA=73+j0ΩZ_A=73+j0~\Omega and a 50 Ω\Omega line, |Γ|=23/123=0.187|\Gamma|=23/123=0.187, accepted fraction is 0.965 and VSWR is 1.46. A matching network could improve this at a chosen frequency. This port test alone says little about radiation efficiency or whether the antenna has a null toward the desired satellite.

Project the Field Onto the Receiving Polarization

Fig. 44 shows why pointing and polarization alignment require separate checks. An antenna may face the correct direction while responding to a transverse field axis that poorly matches the incoming electric field.

For two ideal linear polarizations separated by ψ\psi, ppol=cos⁡2ψ,Lpol,dB=−10log⁡10ppol.\begin{equation} p_{\mathrm{pol}}=\cos^2\psi,\qquad L_{\mathrm{pol,dB}}=-10\log_{10}p_{\mathrm{pol}}. \end{equation} The received voltage component is proportional to cos⁡ψ\cos\psi; power squares it. At ψ=45∘\psi=45^\circ, half the co-polarized available power remains and polarization loss is 3.01 dB. At 90∘90^\circ, ideal coupling is zero. Imperfect real antennas can have finite cross-polar response, so a measured null need not be infinitely deep.

An ideal circular-to-linear pair also couples one half of available power, independent of the linear axis’s azimuth in the transverse plane. Matched circular handedness can couple fully under the same viewing convention; opposite handedness ideally rejects the signal. These statements refer to polarization coupling, separate from antenna directionality and load matching.

Reciprocity ties receiving and transmitting behavior for the same reciprocal antenna at the same frequency and environment. Directional gain then determines effective collecting area through Ae=Gλ2/(4π)A_e=G\lambda^2/(4\pi) for the matched co-polarized case. A receiving dipole’s small wire cross-section therefore does not set its effective area; induced current, matching and wave coupling do.

Use Images and Folded Currents to Compare Familiar Antennas

Fig. 45 shows two useful changes to the basic dipole, each with a different electrical consequence. A conducting boundary changes which half of space radiates; folding adds a coupled conductor and changes input impedance [source].

The ideal quarter-wave monopole has an image that reproduces the full half-wave dipole’s field in the upper hemisphere. No power radiates into the lower hemisphere of the ideal infinite conducting plane, so peak directivity doubles to approximately 3.28, or 5.16 dBi. Nominal radiation resistance is half the corresponding dipole value, approximately 36.5Ω36.5~\Omega. The upper pattern retains the dipole shape. Its one-sided interval from the horizon maximum to the half-power direction is about 39∘39^\circ, distinct from the dipole’s two-sided 78∘78^\circ width.

A finite ground plane produces edge diffraction, possible back radiation and shifted maxima; the ideal image model is a reference rather than a promise for every car roof or spacecraft panel. Its physical size relative to wavelength matters.

A half-wave folded dipole with equal, thin, closely spaced conductors retains approximately the ordinary half-wave dipole’s normalized pattern and peak directivity, while its nominal input resistance is about four times as large, roughly 280–300 Ω\Omega. The increased impedance can help match an appropriate load. It does not multiply antenna gain by four, and it is not automatically a better match to a 50 Ω\Omega line. Wire spacing, diameter and nearby materials modify the ideal values.

Use Current Symmetry to Predict Reinforcement and Nulls

Fig. 46 shows the current-based reasoning used in the exam-review lecture. Before evaluating an integral, identify equal contributions, opposite contributions and the path-phase differences toward the proposed observer. The current sketch supplies useful predictions that a numerical field solution can later check [source].

For an observer broadside to the loop plane, symmetric source locations have equal path phase in the ideal model. Like-directed vertical current components can reinforce the corresponding radiation polarization. Symmetric opposite horizontal contributions can cancel. Changing viewing direction introduces unequal phase, so a cancellation in one direction or polarization does not establish zero radiation everywhere.

This example is an electrically large loop, approximately one wavelength around its perimeter, rather than the uniform-current electrically small-loop model. Its precise current distribution and detailed pattern require the corresponding field solution. The lecture’s point is how standing-current symmetry makes some directions and polarizations plausible before computation. A deep null can also help direction finding: rotating the antenna to minimize a received tone can identify an angular direction more sharply than seeking a broad maximum.

Across these examples, current distribution sets the radiation pattern and radiation resistance; losses set the accepted-to-radiated fraction; mismatch sets incident-to-accepted power; and receiving polarization selects a component of the arriving field. Section VI keeps those quantities separate while assembling the complete link.

Pause and teach it.

Explain how two antennas can share a normalized pattern but have different radiation resistance, and how two antennas can have the same VSWR but different gain. Then use a vertical dipole to distinguish an axial null, a polarization null and a mismatch loss. Identify which of those effects a matching network can address.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, supplied ANT5.pdf, ANT6.pdf, wire-antenna classroom transcript and ANT06 Half Wave Dipole lecture. Lecture recording.

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, supplied pre-Exam-1 class transcript, “Exam Scope and Wire Antennas.” Exam boundary and customized-formula-sheet guidance.

chapters.title: Follow Power Through the Radio Link
chapters.label: sec:e1-radio
chapters.html:
Fig. 47 shows how antenna gain connects the preceding chapters to a communications requirement. The orbit and station determine slant range. The antenna directs power toward that station, and the receiver couples a fraction of the arriving wave into its port. A link budget accounts for each step [source].

Let PtP_t be power accepted by the transmit antenna in watts and GtG_t its linear absolute gain toward the receiver. At unobstructed far-field distance dd, the average incident flux is S(d)=PtGt4πd2.\begin{equation} S(d)=\frac{P_tG_t}{4\pi d^2}. \end{equation} SS is W/m2^2 and dd is antenna-to-antenna slant range, rather than satellite altitude or geocentric orbital radius. Effective isotropic radiated power is EIRP=PtGt\mathrm{EIRP}=P_tG_t: the isotropic power that would produce this flux in that direction. A directional antenna can have EIRP greater than its actual total radiated watts because it redistributes energy.

For a reciprocal receiving antenna with matching polarization and conjugately matched load, effective collecting area and gain are related by Ae=Grλ24π,Pr=SAe.\begin{equation} A_e=\frac{G_r\lambda^2}{4\pi},\qquad P_r=S A_e. \end{equation} AeA_e is in m2^2 and describes available power at the receiving terminals. It need not equal the antenna’s visible metal area. Combining the equations gives the free-space Friis transmission relation, Pr=PtGtGr(λ4πd)2ppolL.\begin{equation} P_r=P_tG_tG_r\left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi d}\right)^2 \frac{p_{\mathrm{pol}}}{L}. \end{equation} The polarization-coupling fraction 0≤ppol≤10\le p_{\mathrm{pol}}\le1 is defined in the antenna chapter. L≥1L\ge1 is any separately specified excess power-loss factor. The antennas must be in each other’s far field and the free-space model assumes a clear path. Reflections, obstruction, rain and mispointing need appropriate additional treatment.

Power reference planes keep the accounting physical. Absolute gain already includes radiation efficiency relative to accepted antenna power; realized gain also includes mismatch at its stated reference impedance. If a supplied assembly gain or EIRP includes a feed-cable loss, applying that loss again would count it twice. Identify whether PrP_r means available antenna power or power actually delivered through a receiver mismatch.

Give Every Decibel Its Reference

Fig. 48 shows why the suffix attached to dB matters. A logarithm can express a ratio of two powers or a power relative to a fixed reference. Those uses can share an arithmetic scale while representing different physical quantities.

For a dimensionless positive power ratio qq, qdB=10log⁡10q,q=10qdB/10.\begin{equation} q_{\mathrm{dB}}=10\log_{10}q,\qquad q=10^{q_{\mathrm{dB}}/10}. \end{equation} Gain of +3.01+3.01 dB approximately doubles power; loss of 3.01 dB halves it. A quoted positive loss LdB=10log⁡10LL_{\mathrm{dB}}=10\log_{10}L is subtracted in a budget. A negative gain can describe the same attenuation. Pick one sign convention consistently.

Absolute powers require a reference: PdBW=10log⁡10(P1W),PdBm=10log⁡10(P1mW)=PdBW+30.\begin{align} P_{\mathrm{dBW}}&=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P}{1~\mathrm{W}}\right),\\ P_{\mathrm{dBm}}&=10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P}{1~\mathrm{mW}}\right) =P_{\mathrm{dBW}}+30. \end{align} Thus 25 W is 13.98 dBW or 43.98 dBm. A power of −90-90 dBm is 10−1210^{-12} W, a positive physical power below the reference milliwatt. More negative received dBm means less power; a value such as −79.9-79.9 dBm is greater than −80-80 dBm.

An antenna’s dBi value is a power gain relative to isotropic radiation, not an absolute number of watts. For voltage or field ratios at equal impedance, power is proportional to amplitude squared, so an amplitude ratio uses 20log⁡10|a2/a1|20\log_{10}|a_2/a_1|. If impedances differ, voltage ratio alone does not specify power ratio. Also, add independent powers in linear watts before taking a logarithm; adding two dBm numbers would multiply their referenced powers rather than sum them.

Build a Forward Budget, Then Read It Backward

Fig. 49 shows each power change separately so that the final received value can be checked. This is a declared teaching link, independent of the supplied homework and historical test questions.

Free-space path loss in decibels is LFS=20log⁡10(4πdfc).\begin{equation} L_{\mathrm{FS}}=20\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{4\pi df}{c}\right). \end{equation} With dd in metres, ff in hertz and cc in m/s, the argument is dimensionless. Equivalently, for distance in kilometres and frequency in GHz, LFS≃92.45+20log⁡10dkm+20log⁡10fGHz.\begin{equation} L_{\mathrm{FS}}\simeq92.45+20\log_{10}d_{\mathrm{km}} +20\log_{10}f_{\mathrm{GHz}}. \end{equation} The constant changes with the units. The logarithmic budget is Pr,dBW=Pt,dBW+Gt,dBi+Gr,dBi−LFS−Lother+10log⁡10ppol.\begin{align} P_{r,\mathrm{dBW}}={}&P_{t,\mathrm{dBW}}+G_{t,\mathrm{dBi}}+G_{r,\mathrm{dBi}}\\ &-L_{\mathrm{FS}}-L_{\mathrm{other}}+10\log_{10}p_{\mathrm{pol}}. \end{align} Since ppol≤1p_{\mathrm{pol}}\le1, its logarithmic contribution is nonpositive. Alternatively subtract a positive polarization loss −10log⁡10ppol-10\log_{10}p_{\mathrm{pol}}, using that effect once.

For the plotted link, LFS=164.49L_{\mathrm{FS}}=164.49 dB and Pr=13.98+20+12−164.49−2=−120.51dBW=−90.51dBm.\begin{align} P_r&=13.98+20+12-164.49-2\\ &=-120.51~\mathrm{dBW}=-90.51~\mathrm{dBm}. \end{align} Here the 2 dB term is the complete stated excess loss, with no additional polarization penalty. Free-space loss arises from geometric spreading and the receiving gain-to-area relationship even in a nonabsorbing vacuum; it does not imply that vacuum turns the missing intercepted energy into heat.

An inverse budget starts from the required received power and asks how much path loss is acceptable. Move the known terms to obtain LFS,maxL_{\mathrm{FS,max}}. Then solve for the unknown: dmax=c4πf10LFS,max/20,fmax=c4πd10LFS,max/20.\begin{equation} d_{\max}=\frac{c}{4\pi f}10^{L_{\mathrm{FS,max}}/20},\qquad f_{\max}=\frac{c}{4\pi d}10^{L_{\mathrm{FS,max}}/20}. \end{equation} Enter a required margin by raising the receiver requirement before finding the permitted loss. The customized exam formula sheet supplies relevant equations; recognizing the unknown, units, gain direction and power reference remains the student’s job [source].

Predict the Effect of Range and Frequency

Fig. 50 shows how to check a numerical answer before trusting it. The two factors enter Friis through the same square, provided the stated gains stay fixed.

At fixed frequency and gains, doubling range gives one quarter the received power, a 6.02 dB decrease. Moving a station does not simply substitute satellite altitude for slant range; the look-angle geometry must first supply the new dd. At fixed range and gains, doubling frequency halves wavelength and also quarters received power.

That frequency comparison keeps gain fixed. A different experiment keeps physical antenna dimensions fixed while changing wavelength; gain may then change, together with matching, pointing requirements and atmospheric loss. The formula remains usable, but each frequency-dependent input must be recalculated. The same distinction helps explain why a universal claim that every higher-frequency satellite link is stronger or weaker omits needed design information.

For the running illustrative link, doubling range from 2000 to 4000 km changes received power from −90.51-90.51 to −96.53-96.53 dBm, assuming every other input remains fixed. A receiver threshold of −100-100 dBm would then have 3.47 dB of received-power headroom before any additional required reserve. The threshold here is an independent illustrative assumption, rather than a sensitivity derived from the noise model below.

Count Noise in the Receiver’s Actual Bandwidth

Fig. 51 shows why signal power alone does not determine reception quality. A receiver admits random fluctuations over a band, and their total competing power depends on both noise density and the filter’s equivalent noise bandwidth [source].

For approximately white thermal noise, N=kBTsysBN,kB=1.380649×10−23J/K.\begin{equation} N=k_BT_{\mathrm{sys}}B_N,\qquad k_B=1.380649\times10^{-23}~\mathrm{J/K}. \end{equation} TsysT_{\mathrm{sys}} is equivalent system noise temperature in kelvin, BNB_N is equivalent noise bandwidth in hertz, and NN is noise power in watts, all referred to one stated receiver plane. The units are (J/K)(K)(1/s)=W(\mathrm{J/K})(\mathrm{K})(1/\mathrm{s})=\mathrm{W}. Equivalent bandwidth preserves a real filter’s integrated noise passage as the area of an ideal rectangle; a quoted occupied-signal bandwidth need not equal it.

At an antenna-output reference plane, a useful model is Tsys=TA+Te,rxT_{\mathrm{sys}}=T_A+T_{e,\mathrm{rx}}. Antenna temperature TAT_A represents collected environmental noise; receiver equivalent input temperature TeT_e represents added device noise. Neither is automatically the physical case temperature. Do not add temperatures referred to different circuit locations without translating them.

For the independently assumed Tsys=300T_{\mathrm{sys}}=300 K and BN=1B_N=1 MHz, noise is 4.14×10−154.14\times10^{-15} W, or −113.83-113.83 dBm. Combining this with the running link’s −90.51-90.51 dBm at the same reference plane gives (C/N)dB=Pr,dBm−NdBm=23.32dB.\begin{equation} (C/N)_{\mathrm{dB}}=P_{r,\mathrm{dBm}}-N_{\mathrm{dBm}}=23.32~\mathrm{dB}. \end{equation} Halving noise bandwidth reduces noise by 3.01 dB, provided the desired signal remains properly passed. A bandwidth change can also restrict information rate or distort the signal, so it is not an unconstrained improvement.

At a required C/N of 12 dB, the 2000 km link has 11.32 dB of margin, or 8.32 dB after a 3 dB reserve. Now aim the same equipment at the GEO satellite in Fig. 14. Its 53.3∘53.3^\circ elevation clears the horizon. Holding directional gains, excess loss and receiver noise fixed, the 36875 km slant range costs an additional 20log⁡10(36875/2000)=25.3120\log_{10}(36875/2000)=25.31 dB. Received power falls to −115.82-115.82 dBm, C/N to −2.00-2.00 dB, and the link is 14.00 dB short of threshold before reserve. For an ideal flat AWGN channel, Shannon’s bound is Ccap=Blog⁡2(1+C/N)C_{\mathrm{cap}}=B\log_2(1+C/N) bits/s with a linear C/N inside the logarithm. A practical waveform and receiver have their own rate and error requirements.

Refer Every Receiver Stage’s Added Noise to the Input

Fig. 52 shows why the component near the antenna matters so much. An amplifier multiplies both the input signal and its existing noise, then contributes additional noise. Early useful gain makes a later contribution less significant when referred back to the same input plane.

Noise factor and its decibel form are F=(S/N)in(S/N)out,NF=10log⁡10F.\begin{equation} F=\frac{(S/N)_{\mathrm{in}}}{(S/N)_{\mathrm{out}}},\qquad NF=10\log_{10}F. \end{equation} The standard source reference temperature is T0=290T_0=290 K. Equivalent added input noise temperature follows from Te=(F−1)T0.\begin{equation} T_e=(F-1)T_0. \end{equation} Convert quoted NF to linear FF first; inserting a dB value into this subtraction would mix quantities. The reference T0T_0 belongs to the noise-factor definition. An actual antenna temperature enters the separate system-noise calculation.

For cascaded stages with linear power gains GiG_i, Ftot=F1+F2−1G1+F3−1G1G2+⋯,Te,tot=Te1+Te2G1+Te3G1G2+⋯.\begin{align} F_{\mathrm{tot}}&=F_1+\frac{F_2-1}{G_1} +\frac{F_3-1}{G_1G_2}+\cdots,\\ T_{e,\mathrm{tot}}&=T_{e1}+\frac{T_{e2}}{G_1} +\frac{T_{e3}}{G_1G_2}+\cdots. \end{align} These are Friis noise-cascade equations, describing a different operation from the Friis free-space transmission equation. Gains below one are allowed for passive loss stages. The inputs and outputs must use the matched reference assumptions of the cascade model.

The example LNA has NF 0.8 dB and gain 20 dB, so F1=1.2023F_1=1.2023, G1=100G_1=100 and Te1=58.66T_{e1}=58.66 K. A second stage with NF 7 dB contributes 1163.44/100=11.631163.44/100=11.63 K at the input. The combined receiver has Te=70.29T_e=70.29 K and NF 0.943 dB. These receiver values are a separate example from the previously assumed complete Tsys=300T_{\mathrm{sys}}=300 K.

A matched passive loss L≥1L\ge1 at physical temperature TpT_p has power gain 1/L1/L and equivalent input temperature (L−1)Tp(L-1)T_p. At Tp=T0T_p=T_0, its noise factor is LL. Placing a 2 dB, 290 K loss before this receiver gives Te,front=281.02T_{e,\mathrm{front}}=281.02 K; moving it between the LNA and later stage gives only 78.79 K input-referred total. A front-end filter can still be necessary to prevent a strong interferer from overloading the amplifier. Sensitivity and dynamic range are distinct design checks.

Project Motion Onto the Line of Sight for Doppler

Fig. 53 shows why total spacecraft speed is insufficient to calculate the frequency shift. The important motion changes transmitter–receiver separation. At closest approach in the pictured symmetric model, the satellite still moves quickly while its instantaneous range rate is zero [source].

Define separation and its outward rate in a common coordinate frame: d=∥𝒓R−𝒓T∥,𝒌̂=𝒓R−𝒓Td,ḋ=(𝒗R−𝒗T)⋅𝒌̂.\begin{align} d&=\|\boldsymbol{r}_R-\boldsymbol{r}_T\|,\qquad \hat{\boldsymbol{k}}=\frac{\boldsymbol{r}_R-\boldsymbol{r}_T}{d},\\ \dot d&=(\boldsymbol{v}_R-\boldsymbol{v}_T)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}. \end{align} The unit vector points along propagation from transmitter to receiver. To first order for speeds much smaller than cc, Δf≃−fccḋ=(𝒗T−𝒗R)⋅𝒌̂λ.\begin{equation} \Delta f\simeq-\frac{f_c}{c}\dot d =\frac{(\boldsymbol{v}_T-\boldsymbol{v}_R)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{k}}}{\lambda}. \end{equation} fcf_c and Δf\Delta f are in Hz, velocities in m/s and wavelength in metres. Positive range rate means recession and a negative received-frequency offset. The expression is for one-way reception; a round-trip radar problem has its own path and frequency accounting.

In the figure’s simplified overhead pass, horizontal position is x=vtx=vt and d(t)=h2+v2t2d(t)=\sqrt{h^2+v^2t^2}. Differentiating gives ḋ=v2t/d\dot d=v^2t/d. At 100 s after closest approach, ḋ≃5857\dot d\simeq5857 m/s and the 2 GHz carrier shifts by about −39.1-39.1 kHz. At t=0t=0, the shift crosses zero even though orbital-style track speed remains 7.5 km/s. Earth rotation, curved trajectories and a moving station require their actual common-frame positions and velocities.

Turn Rain Geometry and Statistics Into a Fade Allowance

Fig. 54 shows the connection between look angle and weather loss. A low-elevation ray spends more distance inside the rain. The amount of attenuation per kilometre also depends on rain rate, frequency and polarization [source].

The course’s supplied empirical model is γR=kRRαR,AR=γRLeff.\begin{equation} \gamma_R=k_RR^{\alpha_R},\qquad A_R=\gamma_RL_{\mathrm{eff}}. \end{equation} RR is rain rate in mm/h, γR\gamma_R is specific attenuation in dB/km, LeffL_{\mathrm{eff}} is effective rainy distance in km and ARA_R is total attenuation in dB. Use the fitted kRk_R and exponent αR\alpha_R for the specified frequency and polarization. The units of kRk_R assume the stated rain-rate convention.

For a flat uniform layer with top hRh_R and station altitude hs<hRh_s<h_R, Leff=hR−hssin⁡El,El>0.\begin{equation} L_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{h_R-h_s}{\sin E_l},\qquad E_l>0. \end{equation} ElE_l is elevation above the horizon, as in the look-angle chapter. With the figure’s explicitly assumed coefficients, γR=4.14\gamma_R=4.14 dB/km. At El=30∘E_l=30^\circ, the 3 km vertical layer becomes a 6 km path and loss is 24.84 dB. At zenith the path and loss halve. Near the horizon, curvature and nonuniform rain limit the flat-layer approximation.

For 99.9% rain-only availability, select the rain rate exceeded 0.1% of the time and budget for its modeled loss. That fraction is about 8.8 hours per year in aggregate. A different availability target requires its own exceedance rate.

Absorption and scattering reduce received power. Changes in ionospheric electron density can alter delay or cause scintillation, disturbing ranging and carrier tracking. Faraday rotation changes linear-polarization alignment (Fig. 44). Radiation damage to spacecraft electronics is a separate mechanism (Section III).

Pause and teach it.

Start with the running link’s transmit power and explain every conversion needed to obtain received C/N. At the GEO station, how much extra directional gain would restore the 12 dB requirement with 3 dB reserve? Then predict which quantities change when noise bandwidth halves, a filter moves ahead of the LNA, or elevation drops during rain. For a passing satellite, explain how maximum speed can coexist with zero instantaneous Doppler shift.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, supplied rain-attenuation and Doppler lectures, RF-band reference and space-weather discussion. Rain attenuation; Doppler shift.
