chapters.title: Read This Guide as One Satellite Link
chapters.label: sec:intro
chapters.html:
Fig. 1 shows where each chapter acts on the same physical link. A geostationary satellite radiates a beam toward a ground station; the ground station turns the arriving field back into bits; a separate set of navigation satellites lets a handheld receiver measure where it is. Each chapter answers one question about that picture, and each answer becomes the input to the next chapter.

One running example threads through the guide. A geostationary satellite at Atlanta’s longitude sends a 10 GHz downlink to a 1 m dish in Atlanta. Chapter II gives the dish’s gain, Chapter IV its look angle, slant range and received power, and Chapter VII its noise, symbol-energy ratio and decision quality. Following one set of numbers from antenna to decision shows exactly where each formula’s inputs come from.

Table I collects the running example’s independent choices. Geometry, frequency, antenna efficiency, transmitter settings and receiver assumptions enter at different points; the later chapters calculate their consequences. The model assumes far-field free-space propagation, matched pointing and polarization, and no extra feeder, rain or implementation losses. Those choices isolate the course calculations rather than predict a complete operating satellite link. The symbol rate, received quality ratios and noisy decisions are derived or simulated later; they are not additional measured givens.

chapters.title: A Wave Is an Oscillation That Arrives Somewhere Else
chapters.label: sec:waves
chapters.html:
Fig. 2 shows the field reading at one fixed receiver. Identify its peak height and the time to repeat before writing an equation. Those two visible features become amplitude and frequency; the starting point on the cycle becomes phase. Every antenna, waveform and navigation idea in this guide is built from these three numbers and from what happens to them when a wave travels.

Imagine holding a tiny electric-field meter at one place. A simple radio wave would make its reading rise, pass through zero, reverse, and repeat. Begin with one component of the vector field along a fixed direction. Write that measured component as E(t)=Epkcos⁡(ωt+ϕ0).\begin{equation} E(t)=E_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos(\omega t+\phi_0). \label{eq:realwave} \end{equation}(1) Here EE is electric field in volts per metre (V/m), tt is time in seconds, and EpkE_{\mathrm{pk}} is its peak amplitude. The angular frequency ω\omega tells us how fast the oscillation runs, in radians per second. The initial phase ϕ0\phi_0 tells us where in its cycle the oscillation starts at t=0t=0. A phase of zero starts this cosine at its positive peak; a phase of π\pi starts it at its negative peak. Phase specifies the position within that repeating cycle.

Ordinary frequency ff counts cycles per second, or hertz (Hz). One cycle contains 2π2\pi radians, so ω=2πf\omega=2\pi f. The period Tc=1/fT_c=1/f is the duration of one cycle. The subscript cc will help distinguish this carrier period from a much longer symbol interval later. When a frequency is 10 GHz, the field completes ten billion oscillations each second. Drawing every wiggle would wear out the pencil. This is where the complex exponential earns its keep.

Read the Complex Exponential

Fig. 3 unrolls the rotating complex arrow along a time axis. Its tip traces a helix; the helix seen end-on is the unit circle, its shadow on one wall is the cosine we measure, and its shadow on the floor is the matching sine. The arrow is mathematical bookkeeping: its length stores amplitude and its angle stores phase. This picture lets us add many same-frequency waves without drawing every rapid oscillation.

Euler’s identity gives a compact description of a point moving around the unit circle: ejωt=cos⁡(ωt)+jsin⁡(ωt).\begin{equation} e^{j\omega t}=\cos(\omega t)+j\sin(\omega t). \end{equation} The complex number has magnitude one and angle ωt\omega t. As time increases, that angle increases. Its horizontal, real-axis projection is exactly the cosine we wanted. The operator Re⁡{⋅}\operatorname{Re}\{\cdot\} means “take the real part.” Thus E(t)=Re⁡{Epkejϕ0ejωt}.\begin{equation} E(t)=\operatorname{Re}\{E_{\mathrm{pk}}e^{j\phi_0}e^{j\omega t}\}. \label{eq:phasor} \end{equation}(3) The time-independent complex amplitude Ẽ=Epkejϕ0\widetilde E=E_{\mathrm{pk}}e^{j\phi_0} is the phasor. It stores amplitude in its length and phase in its angle. The shared factor ejωte^{j\omega t} puts the rapid oscillation back when we need the real field. The complex-plane rotation keeps track of the sinusoid’s phase, while the field component oscillates along its chosen physical direction. MIT’s phasor introduction uses the same real-part construction [source].

The phasor representation makes equal-frequency sinusoids easy to combine: add their complex arrows, then take the real part. Multiplying a phasor by ejϕe^{j\phi} rotates it through an added phase ϕ\phi without changing its magnitude. Multiplying it by a positive real number changes its magnitude without rotating it. Those are precisely the two knobs an array feed will give us: amplitude and phase.

Now Let the Oscillation Travel

Fig. 4 draws the whole disturbance at once, as a surface over distance and time. Slicing it at one place gives a receiver’s time trace; slicing it at one instant gives a snapshot in space. The crests run diagonally across the surface, so a receiver farther away meets each crest later. We translate that visible delay into a phase lag while keeping time, distance and angle units separate.

Suppose a wave travels from a source to a receiver a distance RR away. In this section, RR is a path length, in metres, from source to observation point. Later, aa denotes aperture radius.

In free space the propagation speed is c≃3.00×108c\simeq 3.00\times10^8 m/s. The travel time is τ=R/c\tau=R/c, where τ\tau is a delay in seconds. What the receiver sees now is what the source was doing τ\tau seconds ago. Replace tt by t−τt-\tau: E(R,t)=Epkcos⁡[ω(t−Rc)+ϕ0]=Epkcos⁡(ωt−kR+ϕ0),k=ωc.\begin{align} E(R,t)&=E_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos\!\left[\omega\left(t-\frac{R}{c}\right)+\phi_0\right]\\ &=E_{\mathrm{pk}}\cos(\omega t-kR+\phi_0),\qquad k=\frac{\omega}{c}. \end{align} The wavenumber kk measures phase change per metre, in radians/m. The wavelength λ=c/f\lambda=c/f is the distance travelled during one cycle, so k=2π/λk=2\pi/\lambda. Consequently kRkR is a phase angle: radians/m times metres gives radians. The equation above isolates travel phase; we will add spreading loss shortly.

The corresponding exponential separates neatly: ejω(t−R/c)=ejωte−jωR/c=ejωte−jkR.\begin{equation} e^{j\omega(t-R/c)}=e^{j\omega t}e^{-j\omega R/c} =e^{j\omega t}e^{-jkR}. \label{eq:delayphase} \end{equation}(6) The factor e−jkRe^{-jkR} records the travel delay as a phase lag. With real kk, its magnitude is one, so multiplication rotates the phasor through −kR-kR radians while preserving its length.

Put numbers on the scale. At 10 GHz, λ=3.0\lambda=3.0 cm and k=2π/λ≃209k=2\pi/\lambda\simeq209 rad/m, so a path change of only 1 mm rotates the phasor by 0.2090.209 rad, or 12∘12^\circ. Millimetre geometry therefore matters at microwave frequencies; reflector surfaces and array element positions must be accurate to a small fraction of a wavelength.

The minus sign follows from choosing e+jωte^{+j\omega t} for time. A crest keeps the same total phase ωt−kR\omega t-kR. As tt increases, RR must increase to keep that phase unchanged, so the crest moves outward. An author using e−jωte^{-j\omega t} instead will reverse the matching propagation sign. The time and propagation factors must use the matching signs from the chosen convention.

An extra path ΔR\Delta R adds phase −kΔR-k\Delta R. An additional wavelength gives −2π-2\pi, a complete turn back to the same phase. Half a wavelength gives −π-\pi, reversing the field at a given instant. These relative phase shifts determine how contributions reinforce and cancel in aperture and array theory. Figure 5 shows the half- and full-wavelength cases alongside the separate change in amplitude with range.

Spreading Is a Different Part of the Wave

Fig. 5 shows both the phase turn from an extra path and the shrinking amplitude as radiation spreads. Follow the field curve and the power curve separately: doubling range halves one and quarters the other. Propagation phase and geometric dilution enter different factors of the same wave.

An outward spherical wave spreads over a growing area. In a far-field free-space direction, its electric-field amplitude decreases approximately as 1/R1/R, while its power density decreases as 1/R21/R^2. Choose a reference distance RrefR_{\mathrm{ref}} in metres and let Ẽref\widetilde E_{\mathrm{ref}} be the complex field there, in V/m. Its magnitude gives the peak field amplitude at that reference point, and its angle gives the phase there. Along the same direction, Ẽ(R)=ẼrefRrefRe−jk(R−Rref).\begin{equation} \widetilde E(R)=\widetilde E_{\mathrm{ref}}\frac{R_{\mathrm{ref}}}{R} e^{-jk(R-R_{\mathrm{ref}})}. \end{equation} The ratio Rref/RR_{\mathrm{ref}}/R scales the field amplitude as the wave spreads. The exponential supplies the additional phase delay over R−RrefR-R_{\mathrm{ref}}. The two factors change at very different rates: moving one wavelength farther turns the phase by a full cycle while changing a far-field amplitude by only λ/R\lambda/R of itself. In a lossy medium, absorption introduces an additional amplitude attenuation factor; the equation here models free-space propagation.

Read the Dot and Cross Products

Fig. 6 shows the two geometric operations we need next, on one pair of vectors. The dot product reads distance projected along a direction, which lies in the plane of the two vectors. The cross product leaves that plane: it points along the normal, with a length equal to the shaded area and a sign fixed by the right-hand rule.

For ordinary real vectors 𝒂\mathbf{a} and 𝒃\mathbf{b}, write their magnitudes as |𝒂||\mathbf{a}| and |𝒃||\mathbf{b}|, and let ψ\psi be the angle between them in radians. Their dot product is 𝒂⋅𝒃=|𝒂||𝒃|cos⁡ψ.\begin{equation} \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{a}|\,|\mathbf{b}|\cos\psi. \end{equation} The result is a scalar measuring how strongly the vectors align. For a nonzero reference vector 𝒃\mathbf{b}, its unit direction is 𝒃̂=𝒃/|𝒃|\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{b}/|\mathbf{b}|. The signed projection of 𝒂\mathbf{a} along that direction is d=𝒂⋅𝒃̂=|𝒂|cos⁡ψd=\mathbf{a}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}=|\mathbf{a}|\cos\psi, so 𝒂⋅𝒃=|𝒃|d\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=|\mathbf{b}|d. A positive projection points along the reference direction; a negative projection points oppositely. A unit direction dotted with a position vector measured in metres therefore produces a projected distance in metres.

Their cross product 𝒂×𝒃\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} is a vector perpendicular to the plane containing them, with magnitude |𝒂×𝒃|=|𝒂||𝒃|sin⁡ψ.\begin{equation} |\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|=|\mathbf{a}|\,|\mathbf{b}|\sin\psi. \end{equation} Its direction follows the right-hand rule: curl the fingers from 𝒂\mathbf{a} toward 𝒃\mathbf{b} through their smaller angle, and the thumb points along the cross product. Reversing the order reverses its direction. The magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors, with units equal to the product of their units. Both operations return later in this chapter: the dot product converts an element’s position into a path difference toward an observer, and the cross product gives the direction in which a plane wave carries power.

Where Maxwell and Helmholtz Fit in This Story

Fig. 7 shows what spatial derivatives measure before we use them in Maxwell's equations. Divergence adds up the flow through every face of a small closed box; curl adds up the circulation around a small loop and points along the loop’s axis. They describe local variation, so a field may have a large value while one of these derivatives is zero.

The spatial derivative operator is ∇=(∂/∂x,∂/∂y,∂/∂z)\nabla=(\partial/\partial x,\partial/\partial y,\partial/\partial z), where x,y,zx,y,z are Cartesian coordinates in metres. Using its dot or cross form with a field combines derivatives of that field’s components. These operations measure how the field varies around a point.

The travelling cosine satisfies the field equations in a homogeneous, isotropic, source-free, lossless region. Under those conditions, Maxwell’s equations connect a changing electric field to a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field back to an electric field: ∇×𝑬=−μ∂𝑯∂t,∇×𝑯=ϵ∂𝑬∂t.\begin{equation} \nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\mu\frac{\partial\mathbf{H}}{\partial t}, \qquad \nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\epsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}. \end{equation} Here 𝑬\mathbf{E} is electric field in V/m and 𝑯\mathbf{H} is magnetic field in A/m. The material properties are permeability μ\mu (H/m) and permittivity ϵ\epsilon (F/m). In vacuum they are μ0\mu_0 and ϵ0\epsilon_0. The curl operator ∇×\nabla\times describes local circulation of a vector field; the partial derivative ∂/∂t\partial/\partial t describes how the field changes with time at a fixed place. The circulation of each field is linked to the other field’s time variation. This spatial-temporal relationship supports a disturbance that propagates through the region.

The divergence ∇⋅\nabla\cdot measures net outward field through a tiny surrounding surface per unit enclosed volume. In the charge-free uniform medium, ∇⋅𝑬=0\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0: the outward and inward contributions balance locally. That single fact removes one term from the derivation that follows.

Curl Again to Read Spatial Curvature

Fig. 8 shows a concrete nonzero double curl. Starting with 𝑬=E0cos⁡(kz)𝒙̂\mathbf{E}=E_0\cos(kz)\hat{\mathbf{x}}, the first curl is −kE0sin⁡(kz)𝒚̂-kE_0\sin(kz)\hat{\mathbf{y}} and the second is k2E0cos⁡(kz)𝒙̂k^2E_0\cos(kz)\hat{\mathbf{x}}. Curl changes both the component direction and derivative scale: the first curl turns the vertical field into a horizontal one, and the second turns it back, retracing ExE_x with an extra factor k2k^2. This example makes the spatial-curvature term in the wave equation visible.

Take the curl of Faraday’s equation. Because the medium is uniform and time independent, the spatial curl and time derivative can exchange order. Substitute Ampere’s equation for ∇×𝑯\nabla\times\mathbf{H}: ∇×(∇×𝑬)=−μ∂∂t(∇×𝑯)=−μϵ∂2𝑬∂t2.\begin{equation} \nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}) =-\mu\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\nabla\times\mathbf{H}) =-\mu\epsilon\frac{\partial^2\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}. \end{equation} The first curl produces a new vector field describing local circulation. Applying curl again measures the circulation of that resulting field. A vector-calculus identity expresses the result in terms of divergence and spatial curvature: ∇×(∇×𝑬)=∇(∇⋅𝑬)−∇2𝑬=−∇2𝑬.\begin{equation} \nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}) =\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E})-\nabla^2\mathbf{E} =-\nabla^2\mathbf{E}. \end{equation} The gradient ∇\nabla of a scalar points along its fastest spatial increase. Here it acts on the scalar divergence, which is zero everywhere in the chosen region, so that term vanishes. Equating the two expressions for the double curl leaves ∇2𝑬=μϵ∂2𝑬/∂t2\nabla^2\mathbf{E}=\mu\epsilon\,\partial^2\mathbf{E}/\partial t^2. Moving everything to one side produces the wave equation: ∇2𝑬−μϵ∂2𝑬∂t2=0.\begin{equation} \nabla^2\mathbf{E}-\mu\epsilon\frac{\partial^2\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}=0. \end{equation} The Laplacian ∇2\nabla^2 measures spatial curvature. For each Cartesian component it adds the second derivatives with respect to xx, yy, and zz, the three spatial coordinates. You can read the equation as a balance between spatial curvature and temporal acceleration of the field. For a sinusoidal wave, its known time dependence lets us express this balance using the complex field amplitude alone.

Differentiating ejωte^{j\omega t} once gives jωejωtj\omega e^{j\omega t}; twice gives −ω2ejωt-\omega^2e^{j\omega t}. Remove the shared time factor and the wave equation becomes the Helmholtz equation: ∇2𝑬̃+k2𝑬̃=0,k=ωμϵ.\begin{equation} \nabla^2\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}+k^2\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=0, \qquad k=\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}. \end{equation} It is the same wave physics written for a single frequency. The phase speed is 1/μϵ1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}; in vacuum this is cc. A field proportional to e−jkze^{-jkz} is a plane-wave solution travelling along +z+z under our time convention. A spherical far-field solution has the familiar e−jkR/Re^{-jkR}/R behaviour. The geometry changes the spreading; the phase-delay idea survives.

Fig. 9 shows why both solutions matter for antennas. Near a source, the fronts curve noticeably over a region a few wavelengths across. Far away, over a region of the same size, the spherical wave is practically a plane wave travelling along the line of sight, with its 1/R1/R amplitude nearly constant across the region. Every far-field calculation in the following chapters uses that local plane-wave picture: a receiving antenna sees a plane wave arriving from one direction, and a transmitting antenna’s distant observer sees each element along nearly parallel rays.

Transverse Fields Carry Power

Fig. 10 shows a linearly polarized plane wave: its electric field, magnetic field and propagation direction are mutually perpendicular. The two field curves rise and fall together, and the cross product 𝑬×𝑯\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H} points along the energy flow. Their physical amplitudes have different units, so the plotted curves divide each field by its own peak.

For the free-space plane wave, magnetic-field amplitude is Hpk=Epk/η0H_{\mathrm{pk}}=E_{\mathrm{pk}}/\eta_0, where η0=μ0/ϵ0≃377Ω\eta_0=\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon_0}\simeq377\ \Omega is the wave impedance. The time-averaged power density ⟨S⟩\langle S\rangle, in W/m2^2, is ⟨S⟩=|Ẽ|22η0=Erms2η0.\begin{equation} \langle S\rangle=\frac{|\widetilde E|^2}{2\eta_0} =\frac{E_{\mathrm{rms}}^2}{\eta_0}. \label{eq:fieldpower} \end{equation}(15) The first form uses a peak-amplitude phasor; the second uses the root-mean-square field Erms=Epk/2E_{\mathrm{rms}}=E_{\mathrm{pk}}/\sqrt2. The factor of two is a convention issue with a physical consequence. Always check whether a supplied amplitude is peak or RMS.

For example, a free-space peak field of 1010 V/m has peak magnetic field 10/377=0.026510/377=0.0265 A/m and average power density 100/(2×377)=0.133100/(2\times377)=0.133 W/m2^2. The units and the peak-to-RMS convention determine that numerical factor.

Add the Fields Before Asking About Power

Fig. 11 shows equal field contributions reinforcing, partly cancelling and cancelling completely as relative phase changes. Follow the green resultant first, then square its magnitude to read power. Coherent waves require that order because the phase-dependent cross term carries the interference.

Take two contributions at the same frequency and polarization. Let their phasors be Ẽ1\widetilde E_1 and Ẽ2\widetilde E_2. The total is Ẽtot=Ẽ1+Ẽ2\widetilde E_{\mathrm{tot}}=\widetilde E_1+\widetilde E_2; only then do we use |Ẽtot|2|\widetilde E_{\mathrm{tot}}|^2 to obtain power density. Expanding the squared magnitude shows exactly where interference lives: |Ẽ1+Ẽ2|2=|Ẽ1|2+|Ẽ2|2+2|Ẽ1||Ẽ2|cos⁡Δϕ.\begin{equation} |\widetilde E_1+\widetilde E_2|^2=|\widetilde E_1|^2+|\widetilde E_2|^2 +2|\widetilde E_1||\widetilde E_2|\cos\Delta\phi. \label{eq:crossterm} \end{equation}(16) Here Δϕ\Delta\phi is the phase of Ẽ2\widetilde E_2 minus the phase of Ẽ1\widetilde E_1. The first two terms are the separate powers; the third, the cross term, carries all of the dependence on relative phase. Equal in-phase fields double the amplitude and give four times the power density of one contribution. Equal opposite-phase fields cancel at that observation point.

Fig. 12 plots (16) for two equal fields. The coherent total swings between four times and zero times one input, while its average over all relative phases equals the sum of the two powers. That average explains when power addition is correct: sources with random, independent phases add in power because their cross terms average away. Antenna elements fed from one transmitter hold a fixed relative phase, so their cross terms survive, and those surviving cross terms are the antenna pattern.

The same source contributions reinforce in some directions and cancel in others. An antenna pattern maps the resulting directional distribution of radiation. Beamforming controls the relative phases and amplitudes across several sources to concentrate radiation in selected directions. Its power pattern follows from the squared magnitude of the combined field. For differently polarized fields, add the vector components and account for the polarization accepted by the receiving antenna.

One Source Moves: Why the Positional Phase Has a Plus Sign

Fig. 13 shows the path advantage created when a source moves toward the observer. Slide a plane perpendicular to the viewing direction through the origin and another through the source: every point on either plane is nearly equally far from a distant observer, so only the gap dd between the planes changes the path. The source can sit anywhere in three dimensions; only its projection onto the viewing direction matters. A shorter path means less propagation lag, which supplies the positive relative positional phase used in the array sum.

Now place several sources near a common origin OO. Figure 13 locates source SnS_n at position 𝒓n\mathbf{r}_n and observer PP at position R𝒒̂R\hat{\mathbf{q}}. Both position vectors start at OO and use the same three coordinate axes. A hat means a unit vector: 𝒒̂\hat{\mathbf{q}} has length one and tells us the observation direction. Here R=|OP|R=|OP| is the distance from the origin to the observer. The actual source-to-observer distance is Rn=|SnP|R_n=|S_nP|: Rn=|R𝒒̂−𝒓n|≃R−𝒒̂⋅𝒓n.\begin{equation} R_n=|R\hat{\mathbf{q}}-\mathbf{r}_n| \simeq R-\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n. \end{equation} The dot product d=𝒒̂⋅𝒓nd=\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n is the source’s displacement projected toward the observer, in metres. In Fig. 13, dd lies along the reference viewing direction. A source moved toward the observer has a positive projection and a shorter path.

The approximation comes from expanding the exact distance. Write Rn2=R2−2R𝒒̂⋅𝒓n+|𝒓n|2R_n^2=R^2-2R\,\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n+|\mathbf{r}_n|^2, factor out R2R^2, and use 1+x≃1+x/2−x2/8\sqrt{1+x}\simeq1+x/2-x^2/8 for small xx: Rn≃R−𝒒̂⋅𝒓n+|𝒓n|2−(𝒒̂⋅𝒓n)22R.\begin{equation} R_n\simeq R-\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n +\frac{|\mathbf{r}_n|^2-(\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n)^2}{2R}. \label{eq:rn-expansion} \end{equation}(18) The last term is the first one we drop. It equals |𝒓n|2sin⁡2ψ/(2R)|\mathbf{r}_n|^2\sin^2\psi/(2R), where ψ\psi is the angle between 𝒒̂\hat{\mathbf{q}} and 𝒓n\mathbf{r}_n, and it shrinks as 1/R1/R. Multiplied by kk, it becomes a phase error that is small once R≫|𝒓n|2/λR\gg|\mathbf{r}_n|^2/\lambda. Chapter II meets this same term again as the far-field distance rule.

Fig. 14 shows why amplitude and phase receive different treatment. Replacing 1/Rn1/R_n by 1/R1/R changes the amplitude by about |𝒒̂⋅𝒓n|/R|\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n|/R, below 1% beyond about a hundred wavelengths in this example. The phase is far less forgiving: the projection k𝒒̂⋅𝒓nk\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n stays the same size at every range, so it must be kept. A far-field calculation therefore uses one common 1/R1/R for every amplitude and the projected path for every phase.

Substitute that shorter distance into the propagation factor: e−jkRn≃e−jkRe+jk𝒒̂⋅𝒓n.\begin{equation} e^{-jkR_n}\simeq e^{-jkR}e^{+jk\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\mathbf{r}_n}. \end{equation} Substituting Rn≃R−dR_n\simeq R-d into −jkRn-jkR_n gives −jkR+jkd-jkR+jkd. The shorter path therefore supplies a positive positional phase kdkd relative to the reference origin. Every source shares nearly the same e−jkR/Re^{-jkR}/R spreading and delay. Their relative positional and feed phases are what remain to create the directional pattern. This is the bridge from travelling waves to antennas.

The chapter’s tools now travel together. A phasor stores amplitude and phase; a path difference ΔR\Delta R becomes a phase kΔRk\Delta R; coherent fields add before their power is computed, and the cross term of (16) is where every pattern comes from. The next chapter applies all three to an opening filled with radiating patches.

Sources

  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 6.007, “Lecture 19: Electromagnetic Waves,” phasor representation. Lecture slides.

chapters.title: An Opening Full of Waves Makes a Beam
chapters.label: sec:apertures
chapters.html:
Fig. 15 shows why an opening can make a beam. Along boresight every patch is the same distance from a plane perpendicular to the viewing direction, so the patches add in phase. Tilt the viewing direction and the distances form a ramp across the opening; the same patches now partly cancel. We will turn that picture into a surface sum.

An aperture is a surface across which we describe the radiating electric field. A horn mouth provides a physical opening. For a reflector, an imaginary plane across its mouth provides a useful aperture too. We describe both the field’s strength and its phase over that surface. “Uniform illumination” means the simplest idealization: the same field amplitude and phase throughout the opening, with zero outside.

Picture dividing the opening into tiny patches. Each patch contributes a wave toward the observer. At boresight, perpendicular to the aperture plane, equal-phase patches have equal relative travel distances. Their phasors line up. Move the observer off axis and one side has a shorter path than the other. The contributions progressively rotate relative to each other, reducing their sum. At particular angles they cancel.

For a point at horizontal aperture coordinate xx and vertical coordinate yy, let A(x,y)A(x,y) be its complex illumination relative to a chosen reference field. The observer’s direction has Cartesian components qx,qy,qzq_x,q_y,q_z in the aperture frame. Because the aperture lies in the xyxy plane, its position has z=0z=0. Our positional phase becomes k(xqx+yqy)k(xq_x+yq_y). A scalar far-field pattern is therefore proportional to F(qx,qy)∝∬𝒜A(x,y)ejk(xqx+yqy)dxdy.\begin{equation} F(q_x,q_y)\ \propto\ \iint_{\mathcal{A}} A(x,y) e^{jk(xq_x+yq_y)}\,dx\,dy. \end{equation} The region 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the opening. The integral is just a continuous version of “add the patches,” including their phases. The symbol ∝\propto means we have suppressed common amplitude factors. Normalizing by the boresight value makes the peak one for this equal-phase example. A phased array will replace this surface integral by a finite sum. The opening’s field and the far-field pattern form a spatial Fourier-transform pair: smooth or abrupt changes across the opening leave corresponding fingerprints in the beam [source].

A Strip Shows the Whole Mechanism

Fig. 16 carries out the patch sum for the simplest opening: a uniform strip of width DD, seen edge-on. Off boresight, each patch’s arrow turns slightly more than its neighbour’s, so the chain of arrows curls. The far-field magnitude is the straight-line distance from the chain’s start to its end.

The integral makes the picture exact. Let the strip occupy |x|≤D/2|x|\le D/2 with A(x)=1A(x)=1, and observe at angle θ\theta from boresight in the xzxz plane, so qx=sin⁡θq_x=\sin\theta. Then Fstrip(θ)∝∫−D/2D/2ejkxsin⁡θdx=Dsin⁡(Φ/2)Φ/2.\begin{equation} F_{\mathrm{strip}}(\theta)\propto\int_{-D/2}^{D/2}e^{jkx\sin\theta}dx =D\,\frac{\sin(\Phi/2)}{\Phi/2}. \label{eq:strip} \end{equation}(21) Here Φ=kDsin⁡θ\Phi=kD\sin\theta is the phase difference between the two edges, in radians. The first null occurs at Φ=2π\Phi=2\pi, where the far edge is exactly one wavelength farther from the observer than the near edge. Every patch then has a partner half a strip away whose path differs by λ/2\lambda/2; each pair cancels, and the chain closes into a full circle. That null sits at sin⁡θ=λ/D\sin\theta=\lambda/D. The half-power point sits at Φ≃2.78\Phi\simeq2.78, so the full half-power beamwidth of a long strip is about 0.886λ/D0.886\lambda/D radians. The first sidelobe reaches −13.3-13.3 dB.

Fig. 17 compares the strip with a circular opening of the same width. A disk is a stack of strips whose lengths follow the chord 2a2−x22\sqrt{a^2-x^2}, so its centre carries more weight than its edges. That built-in geometric taper moves the first null outward, from sin⁡θ=λ/D\sin\theta=\lambda/D to 1.22λ/D1.22\lambda/D, and lowers the first sidelobe from −13.3-13.3 to −17.6-17.6 dB. The Bessel-function pattern of the next subsection is the disk’s version of (21).

Radius, Diameter, and Size in Wavelengths

Fig. 18 shows the whole pattern of a circular opening. Because the disk looks the same from every azimuth, its beam is a dome and each sidelobe is a ring around it; one radial cut, in the lower panel, therefore describes every direction. A negative field in that cut is a phase reversal; the corresponding power remains nonnegative.

A circular aperture has radius aa, diameter D=2aD=2a, and physical area Aphys=πa2=πD2/4A_{\mathrm{phys}}=\pi a^2=\pi D^2/4. Radius, diameter, and area are linked by these geometric relations. The range RR from the previous section describes where the observer is; aa and DD describe the opening. The class ANT10 slides label their radius as RR; this guide uses aa for that radius to keep it distinct from propagation range. Thus the slide’s R=2λR=2\lambda is a diameter of 4λ4\lambda.

The important beam-size ratio is D/λD/\lambda: how many wavelengths fit across the opening. The edge-to-edge relative path off axis is approximately Dsin⁡θD\sin\theta, where θ\theta is the angle from boresight. In phase radians it is kDsin⁡θkD\sin\theta. A larger opening accumulates a large phase difference at a smaller angle, which is why its main beam is narrower. The larger opening spans more of a phase cycle across its surface at that angle.

For the disk, the same chord-weighted sum produces a Bessel function. Define the dimensionless angle coordinate u=kasin⁡θ=πDλsin⁡θ.\begin{equation} u=ka\sin\theta=\frac{\pi D}{\lambda}\sin\theta. \end{equation} The Bessel function J1(u)J_1(u) packages the wave contributions summed over the circular opening: each ring of patches contributes around a complete turn. For a uniformly illuminated disk, the normalized scalar field pattern is Fdisk(θ)=2J1(u)u.\begin{equation} F_{\mathrm{disk}}(\theta)=\frac{2J_1(u)}{u}. \label{eq:disk} \end{equation}(23) In the class scalar model, an additional projection, or obliquity, factor is retained [source]: Fn(θ)=cos⁡θFdisk(θ),pn(θ)=|Fn(θ)|2.\begin{equation} F_n(\theta)=\cos\theta\,F_{\mathrm{disk}}(\theta), \qquad p_n(\theta)=|F_n(\theta)|^2. \label{eq:classaperture} \end{equation}(24) Here FnF_n means normalized field, and pnp_n means normalized power. The subscript nn in these two names identifies normalization. Equation (24) is the course’s scalar model for the forward hemisphere, 0≤θ≤π/20\leq\theta\leq\pi/2. Other electromagnetic aperture models use different obliquity factors. Keep the stated model when comparing a plot or problem. Near boresight, cos⁡θ≃1\cos\theta\simeq1, so the disk-only approximation and class model agree closely. The radial cut in Fig. 18 uses the disk-only form.

At boresight u=0u=0, the written fraction has the form 0/00/0, with a finite limit. For small uu, J1(u)≃u/2J_1(u)\simeq u/2, hence 2J1(u)/u→12J_1(u)/u\to1. The field contributions are most in step at the center; the limiting value agrees with that picture. Numerical code evaluates this finite limit near zero.

Fig. 19 shows where the disk-only approximation is useful and where the class projection factor matters. Near the central beam the factor is close to one. At 60∘60^\circ it reduces power by cos⁡260∘=1/4\cos^2 60^\circ=1/4, or 6.026.02 dB, compared with the disk-only value at that same angle. Use the model specified in the problem; a familiar disk-only landmark does not silently replace the course model.

Read the Main Lobe, Half-Power Points, and Nulls

Fig. 20 shows exactly which two angles define beamwidth. The central peak, half-power crossings and first nulls identify different landmarks. The two panels use different vertical scales for the same power function, so they let us connect the physical ratio to its dB value.

The central peak is the main lobe. Smaller peaks beyond its zeros are sidelobes. A null is a direction of zero field in the ideal model. The first null of the disk-only pattern occurs at u≃3.83171u\simeq3.83171, which is sin⁡θ=1.22λ/D\sin\theta=1.22\lambda/D. The half-power crossing occurs earlier, at u≃1.61634u\simeq1.61634. The half-power crossing has relative power 0.50.5 and field magnitude 1/2≃0.7071/\sqrt2\simeq0.707. The first sidelobe instead peaks about 17.617.6 dB below the main lobe: approximately 0.01750.0175 of the peak power and 0.1320.132 of the peak field.

For a symmetric cut, the positive half-power angle θHP\theta_{\mathrm{HP}} is measured from boresight to one crossing. The full half-power beamwidth, ΘHP\Theta_{\mathrm{HP}}, spans the negative and positive crossings: θHP=sin⁡−1(1.61634λπD),ΘHP=2θHP.\begin{equation} \theta_{\mathrm{HP}}=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1.61634\lambda}{\pi D}\right), \qquad \Theta_{\mathrm{HP}}=2\theta_{\mathrm{HP}}. \end{equation} This expression uses the disk-only approximation and presumes the crossing exists in the visible angular range. Using 3.83171 in the same inverse-sine expression gives the one-sided first-null angle. For a large electrical aperture and small angles, the full HPBW is approximately 1.029λ/D1.029\lambda/D radians, or 58.96λ/D58.96\lambda/D degrees. The factor of two belongs to the full width, while the radians-to-degrees conversion is a separate step.

Relative power in decibels is pdB=10log⁡10pnp_{\mathrm{dB}}=10\log_{10}p_n. Since pn=|Fn|2p_n=|F_n|^2, the same relative value is 20log⁡10|Fn|20\log_{10}|F_n|. Half power is about −3.01-3.01 dB. Both logarithmic expressions represent the same relative ratio. A normalized pattern sets its own peak to 0 dB; absolute gain in dBi uses an isotropic radiator as its reference.

For a disk with D/λ=10D/\lambda=10, the one-sided half-power angle is 2.95∘2.95^\circ, so the full HPBW is 5.90∘5.90^\circ; the one-sided first-null angle is 7.01∘7.01^\circ. The 0.50.5 linear-power line and −3.01-3.01 dB line identify the same crossing.

A Softer Edge Changes the Sidelobes

Fig. 21 shows the aperture illumination beside its far-field consequence. Weakening the edge smooths the abrupt cut-off, lowers sidelobes and broadens the main peak. Compare patterns only after noting whether each curve has been normalized to its own peak.

A uniform opening ends abruptly. One way to reduce its sidelobes is to drive the edge less strongly than the center, called amplitude taper. This taper usually broadens the main beam and reduces peak directivity for the fixed aperture. The disk already displayed the effect in miniature: its chord weighting is a gentle geometric taper, and it lowered the first sidelobe from the strip’s −13.3-13.3 dB to −17.6-17.6 dB. A deliberate amplitude taper continues the same trade.

Increasing a uniform aperture’s diameter mostly squeezes its angular pattern inward. In the near-boresight disk-only model, the normalized sidelobe levels stay the same. Taper changes the distribution of contributions; size changes how quickly their relative phase builds with angle.

Fig. 22 shows the cost hidden when both curves in Fig. 21 are reset to 00 dB. Before reading the peaks, predict which illumination concentrates a fixed radiated watt more strongly. Full angular normalization gives peak directivities 984.7984.7 (29.9329.93 dBi) for the uniform disk and 749.9749.9 (28.7528.75 dBi) for the taper. Their full HPBWs are 5.90∘5.90^\circ and 7.20∘7.20^\circ. The taper spends about 1.181.18 dB of peak directivity to obtain lower sidelobes; no extra transmit watt has been added to either curve.

Amplitude taper is a general aperture design tool. In the GeorgiaTenna model, active feeds have equal magnitudes; a continuously graded amplitude taper cannot be inserted as an extra assignment control. Element selection and phase remain the permitted controls.

A Dish Is a Way to Create This Opening’s Field

Fig. 23 shows equal optical paths from a feed at the focus, around the whole bowl of the reflector, to one common plane. Those equal paths organize the phase at the mouth. The reflector therefore provides a practical way to create the aperture field described by the earlier integral.

The paraboloid’s job is to organize the phase supplied by a small feed. In a cross-section through its axis, the reflector surface is z=r2/(4F)z=r^2/(4F), where rr is distance from the axis and FF is the focal length, both in metres. Every point on a parabola is equally far from the focus and from a fixed line called the directrix; that property makes the path from the focus to the reflector and on to any plane across the mouth the same for every ray. Equal path gives equal propagation phase, so the mouth behaves like the aperture we have just described. Feed illumination, blockage, spillover, surface errors, and other losses determine how well a real dish achieves the ideal.

Fig. 24 shows how the feed’s own pattern becomes the aperture illumination of the previous subsection. Seen from the focus, the rim lies at the angle ψ0\psi_0 given by tan⁡(ψ0/2)=D/(4F)\tan(\psi_0/2)=D/(4F), here 64∘64^\circ. Radiation beyond ψ0\psi_0 misses the reflector; that lost fraction is spillover. Radiation inside ψ0\psi_0 lands with a strength set by the feed pattern and by the extra spreading over the longer path to the rim. Here the normalized feed power is Uf(ψ)/Uf(0)=cos⁡qψU_f(\psi)/U_f(0)=\cos^q\psi on 0≤ψ≤π/20\leq\psi\leq\pi/2; its field magnitude is proportional to cos⁡qψ\sqrt{\cos^q\psi}. The angle ψ\psi is measured from the feed axis toward the reflector. A broad q=1q=1 feed illuminates the edge at −6.4-6.4 dB but spills 19.2% of its power. A narrow q=4q=4 feed spills only 1.6% but tapers the edge to −17.2-17.2 dB, which widens the beam and wastes part of the opening. The best aperture efficiency lies between these extremes, typically with the edge illuminated roughly 10 dB below the centre; together with blockage and surface errors, this trade is why practical dishes reach efficiencies near the ηa=0.60\eta_a=0.60 used below. The azimuthal 2π2\pi factor cancels from the spilled fraction: PspillPfeed=∫ψ0π/2cos⁡qψsin⁡ψdψ∫0π/2cos⁡qψsin⁡ψdψ=cos⁡q+1ψ0.\begin{equation} \frac{P_{\mathrm{spill}}}{P_{\mathrm{feed}}} =\frac{\int_{\psi_0}^{\pi/2}\cos^q\psi\sin\psi\,d\psi} {\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^q\psi\sin\psi\,d\psi} =\cos^{q+1}\psi_0. \label{eq:audit-ant-spill} \end{equation}(26) The lower curve also includes the focus-to-aperture spreading: its relative field is cos⁡qψ(1+cos⁡ψ)/2\sqrt{\cos^q\psi}(1+\cos\psi)/2. Thus its dB axis is 20log⁡1020\log_{10} of a field ratio, while the shaded integral counts power.

Collect Power and Scale the Frequency

Fig. 25 shows a narrower angular pattern when more wavelengths fit across the same opening. The collecting area and the angular concentration answer different questions. We use effective area to connect incident power density to received power, then obtain gain from that area.

Define effective collecting area AeA_e as received available power divided by the incident power density under the stated alignment and polarization conditions. It has units m2^2. If ηa\eta_a is the overall aperture efficiency used in this model, then Ae=ηaAphys=ηaπD24.\begin{equation} A_e=\eta_a A_{\mathrm{phys}}=\eta_a\frac{\pi D^2}{4}. \end{equation} Efficiency is a dimensionless fraction. Effective area expresses how efficiently that geometric opening collects power under the stated conditions. In the same matched convention, the dimensionless gain GG is related to effective area by G=4πAeλ2=ηa(πDλ)2,GdBi=10log⁡10G.\begin{equation} G=\frac{4\pi A_e}{\lambda^2} =\eta_a\left(\frac{\pi D}{\lambda}\right)^2, \qquad G_{\mathrm{dBi}}=10\log_{10}G. \end{equation} Gain compares directional performance with an ideal isotropic reference. The “i” in dBi identifies that reference. Each physical loss enters the link budget once. A gain calculated with aperture efficiency already includes the losses represented by that efficiency.

The class engineering estimate G≃33000/(Θ1Θ2)G\simeq33000/(\Theta_1\Theta_2) uses two orthogonal full half-power beamwidths Θ1\Theta_1 and Θ2\Theta_2, both in degrees. The empirical coefficient incorporates the stated degree units, beam shape and efficiency convention of that engineering estimate. HPBW alone does not establish radiation efficiency or the complete pattern integral. The following lossless comparison concerns directivity; the running link continues to use the gain obtained from AeA_e above. A higher-gain antenna is less forgiving of pointing error because the intended receiver can move down the side of its narrower main lobe. The relevant pointing error is the full angle between the boresight and receiver directions, determined by their unit vectors.

Fig. 26 explains the coefficient 33,000. If an antenna sent its power uniformly into a solid angle ΩA\Omega_A and nowhere else, its directivity would be 4π/ΩA4\pi/\Omega_A: the whole sphere divided by the part the beam fills. The sphere holds 4π4\pi sr =4π(180/π)2≃41,253=4\pi(180/\pi)^2\simeq41{,}253 square degrees, so a beam Θ1×Θ2\Theta_1\times\Theta_2 degrees would give 41,253/(Θ1Θ2)41{,}253/(\Theta_1\Theta_2). A real pattern has rounded edges and sidelobes. Replacing their integral by a coefficient is a beam-shape approximation: 33,00033{,}000 corresponds here to an effective solid angle about 41,253/33,000=1.2541{,}253/33{,}000=1.25 times the HPBW rectangle. That factor is not universal and does not independently measure radiation loss. For a uniformly illuminated 1 m disk at 10 GHz, D/λ=33.3D/\lambda=33.3 and ΘHP=1.77∘\Theta_{\mathrm{HP}}=1.77^\circ. The beamwidth estimate gives 10,550, while the ideal large-aperture value (πD/λ)2(\pi D/\lambda)^2 is 10,970: agreement within 0.20.2 dB under this lossless comparison. In contrast, the specified ηa=0.60\eta_a=0.60 receiving dish has gain 6580, about 2.052.05 dB below that width-based estimate. Keep its stated efficiency convention when using either calculation; applying total aperture efficiency again to a width rule can duplicate pattern losses already represented by its beam shape. Chapter IV reaches the same idea from the other direction: its pattern integral BB is the beam solid angle.

For example, D=1D=1 m at 1010 GHz gives λ≃0.030\lambda\simeq0.030 m. With ηa=0.60\eta_a=0.60, Ae=0.471A_e=0.471 m2^2 and G≃6580G\simeq6580, or 38.1838.18 dBi. This dish is the receiving antenna of the running example. Doubling frequency leaves that collecting area unchanged in this fixed-efficiency model, raises gain by 6.026.02 dB and approximately halves beamwidth.

Check the Far-Field Approximation

Fig. 27 shows the curvature error behind the far-field distance rule. Increasing range makes the rays more nearly parallel across the aperture. Decide which phase error is acceptable before treating the parallel-ray pattern as sufficiently accurate.

Finally, all these angular patterns presume the far field. A common engineering distance scale is RF≃2Dmax⁡2/λR_F\simeq2D_{\max}^2/\lambda, where DmaxD_{\max} is the antenna’s largest dimension and RFR_F is the far-field screening distance. This approximate criterion screens for a small phase error from wavefront curvature across the antenna; the required accuracy determines how much phase error is acceptable. We have been adding almost-parallel far-field rays; close to the aperture, their actual geometry matters more.

Fig. 28 shows where the D2D^2 comes from. The centre of an aperture of width DD lies a distance RR from the observer, and the edge lies R2+(D/2)2≃R+D2/(8R)\sqrt{R^2+(D/2)^2}\simeq R+D^2/(8R) away. The excess δ=D2/(8R)\delta=D^2/(8R) is the curvature term of (18) with |𝒓n|=D/2|\mathbf{r}_n|=D/2 perpendicular to the viewing direction. Its phase is kδ=πD2/(4λR)k\delta=\pi D^2/(4\lambda R), which equals π/8\pi/8 at R=2D2/λR=2D^2/\lambda.

For the same 11 m aperture and 0.0300.030 m wavelength, RF≃66.7R_F\simeq66.7 m. In the paraxial estimate, the edge-to-centre path excess is Dmax⁡2/(8R)D_{\max}^2/(8R); multiplying by kk gives the phase error plotted in Fig. 27. At RFR_F it is π/8\pi/8 radians, or 22.5∘22.5^\circ. Required phase accuracy can justify a larger observation range.

An opening of width DD therefore concentrates its power into a beam roughly λ/D\lambda/D radians wide, with sidelobes set by how abruptly its illumination ends, and a dish builds that opening with a curved reflector. The next chapter builds the same opening from discrete elements whose phases can be changed electronically.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, ANT10 and dish/array lectures; supplied October 22–29, 2026 notes and transcripts. The course scalar obliquity convention is retained.

  • Brigham Young University, ECEn 665, “Antennas and Propagation for Wireless Communications,” aperture distributions. Lecture notes. Supplementary check of aperture summation and taper intuition.

chapters.title: An Array Is an Aperture You Can Reprogram
chapters.label: sec:arrays
chapters.html:
Fig. 29 shows the two available controls: choose contributing sites and rotate their feed phases. The active arrows have equal length, while their angles differ. The array turns those feed settings into a directional interference pattern without mechanically reshaping the opening.

A dish uses a shaped reflector to arrange the phase across an opening. An array arranges that phase electronically: place several radiating elements at known positions, then control the amplitude and phase of each feed. Changing their relative phases steers the interference pattern while the hardware stays still. This is electronic beam steering.

Picture a distant listener. Every active element contributes a field at that location. We choose a direction, calculate the amplitude and phase of each arriving contribution, and add the fields. Repeating that calculation over the viewing directions builds the antenna pattern.

Give Every Element a Position and a Feed

Fig. 30 shows a positional phase advance cancelled by a feed phase delay in the chosen direction. Each element contributes one complex arrow after both phases have been included. We now give positions, viewing directions and feed settings precise symbols so the picture becomes a computable sum.

Let NN be the number of elements. The index nn labels one element, and its position relative to the array’s chosen origin is the vector 𝒓n\boldsymbol{r}_n, measured in metres. The unit vector 𝒒̂\hat{\boldsymbol{q}} points from the array toward a far-away observer. The hat identifies a unit vector: its length is one, so it supplies the viewing direction.

The feed of element nn has a relative magnitude AnA_n and a phase ϕn\phi_n, in radians. Package them in the complex number an=Anejϕna_n=A_ne^{j\phi_n}. The excitation weight ana_n describes how that element is driven. Using the previously developed e+jωte^{+j\omega t} convention, the element’s positional phase is +k𝒒̂⋅𝒓n+k\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_n, where k=2π/λk=2\pi/\lambda is the wavenumber and λ\lambda is wavelength. The dot product projects position onto the viewing direction. Multiplying metres by radians per metre gives a phase in radians.

Now the array factor, abbreviated AFAF, is simply the sum of these weighted contributions: AF(𝒒̂)=∑n=1Nanejk𝒒̂⋅𝒓n.\begin{equation} AF(\hat{\boldsymbol{q}})=\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n e^{jk\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_n}. \label{eq:arr-general} \end{equation}(29) The summation sign means “do this for every element and add.” For similarly oriented copies of a common element, the total far-field pattern is the common element field pattern multiplied by this array factor. If EelementE_{\mathrm{element}} denotes that common field contribution under the chosen reference excitation, then Etotal=EelementAF.\begin{equation} E_{\mathrm{total}}=E_{\mathrm{element}}AF. \label{eq:arr-product} \end{equation}(30) This separation assumes a common element and polarization model, with coupling handled as specified by that model. Mutual coupling describes how one element’s electromagnetic field affects the currents on nearby elements; practical arrays account for it through their element and feed models.

Suppose the intended beam direction is 𝒒̂0\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}_0. The subscript zero identifies the selected direction. We want the phase in every term of the sum to be the same there. Choose ϕn=−k𝒒̂0⋅𝒓n.\begin{equation} \phi_n=-k\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}_0\cdot\boldsymbol{r}_n. \label{eq:arr-steer} \end{equation}(31) At 𝒒̂=𝒒̂0\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}=\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}_0, feed phase plus positional phase is zero for each element. The field phasors line up, giving constructive interference. The steering-law sign follows from the traveling-wave convention.

A phase added equally to every feed rotates the entire field sum by the same amount. It changes the overall timing reference of the field but leaves |AF|2|AF|^2, and therefore the power pattern, unchanged. Steering requires relative phase changes across the array.

Two Elements Already Make a Beam

Fig. 31 shows that spacing and one relative feed phase already decide where two elements reinforce. Every pattern is a surface of revolution: two points on a line look the same from every azimuth around that line, so the pattern depends only on the angle θ\theta from the axis. Put both on the zz axis, a distance dd apart, and let β\beta be the upper element’s feed phase minus the lower one’s. The upper element’s path toward an observer at angle θ\theta from +z+z is shorter by dcos⁡θd\cos\theta, so its total relative phase is ψ=kdcos⁡θ+β\psi=kd\cos\theta+\beta, and AF=1+ejψ,|AF|=2|cosψ2|.\begin{equation} AF=1+e^{j\psi},\qquad |AF|=2\left|\cos\frac{\psi}{2}\right|. \label{eq:arr-two} \end{equation}(32) Power peaks where ψ\psi is a multiple of 2π2\pi and vanishes where ψ\psi is an odd multiple of π\pi. With d=λ/2d=\lambda/2 and β=0\beta=0, ψ=πcos⁡θ\psi=\pi\cos\theta: the paths match broadside (θ=90∘\theta=90^\circ), while along the axis the half-wavelength path difference supplies π\pi and the fields cancel. With d=λ/2d=\lambda/2 and β=π\beta=\pi the roles swap: the feed’s 180∘180^\circ cancels broadside, and along the axis the path’s 180∘180^\circ restores agreement. With d=λ/4d=\lambda/4 and β=−π/2\beta=-\pi/2, ψ=(π/2)(cos⁡θ−1)\psi=(\pi/2)(\cos\theta-1). Toward +z+z the quarter-wave path advantage exactly repays the quarter-cycle feed lag; toward −z-z the two add to π\pi and cancel. The pair has a preferred endfire maximum toward +z+z and a null toward −z-z. At broadside its power remains half the maximum, so the back-axis null does not confine all radiation to a single ray or hemisphere.

A Straight Line Makes the Bookkeeping Friendlier

Fig. 32 shows how equally spaced elements create a main beam, ordinary sidelobes and, at wider spacing, an additional fully coherent direction. Both patterns steer to the same target. The repeated geometry lets one adjacent phase difference describe the whole line.

Fig. 33 shows what that angular cut means in space. A line of elements can only distinguish directions by their angle from the line, so every direction at the same θ\theta receives the same field. The beam steered to 60∘60^\circ is therefore a whole cone, and the plotted curve in Fig. 32 is one slice through it. A second array dimension can distinguish directions around that cone, as the planar example below shows.

Start with a uniform linear array. “Uniform” here means equally spaced elements, equal feed magnitudes, and a constant phase increment between adjacent feeds. Put the line along the zz axis, let dd be adjacent spacing in metres, and measure the observation angle θ\theta from the positive zz axis. The position of element nn, now numbered from 00 to N−1N-1, is nd𝒛̂nd\hat{\boldsymbol{z}}, where 𝒛̂\hat{\boldsymbol{z}} is the unit vector along the line.

An observer at angle θ\theta sees an adjacent projected displacement dcos⁡θd\cos\theta. Let β\beta be the feed phase of one element minus the feed phase of its previous neighbor. The total adjacent phase difference, called ψ\psi, is ψ=kdcos⁡θ+β,AF=∑n=0N−1ejnψ.\begin{equation} \psi=kd\cos\theta+\beta,\qquad AF=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{jn\psi}. \label{eq:arr-psi} \end{equation}(33) There are two ingredients in ψ\psi: geometry supplies kdcos⁡θkd\cos\theta, and the electronics supplies β\beta. Each successive contribution turns another ψ\psi radians in the complex plane.

If ψ=0\psi=0, all NN unit contributions add to NN. The same is true when ψ\psi is any whole multiple of 2π2\pi, because one complete turn returns to the same point. At other angles the arrows fan around and partially cancel. The sum is a geometric series with ratio ejψe^{j\psi}: ∑n=0N−1ejnψ=1−ejNψ1−ejψ=ej(N−1)ψ/2sin⁡(Nψ/2)sin⁡(ψ/2).\begin{equation} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{jn\psi}=\frac{1-e^{jN\psi}}{1-e^{j\psi}} =e^{j(N-1)\psi/2}\,\frac{\sin(N\psi/2)}{\sin(\psi/2)}. \end{equation} The second form factors ejNψ/2e^{jN\psi/2} from the numerator and ejψ/2e^{j\psi/2} from the denominator and uses ejx−e−jx=2jsin⁡xe^{jx}-e^{-jx}=2j\sin x. The leading exponential has magnitude one, so it only sets the phase reference. Taking magnitudes gives the familiar normalized result: |AF|N=|sin⁡(Nψ/2)Nsin⁡(ψ/2)|.\begin{equation} \frac{|AF|}{N} =\left|\frac{\sin(N\psi/2)}{N\sin(\psi/2)}\right|. \label{eq:arr-ula} \end{equation}(35) Division by NN makes a fully coherent peak equal to one. Squaring gives a peak-normalized power shape. At a coherent direction, evaluate the quotient by its limit: the original sum gives AF=NAF=N, so the normalized magnitude is one.

Fig. 34 shows the geometric series as arrows. Each element’s arrow turns ψ\psi more than its neighbour’s, so the chain curls. When Nψ=2πN\psi=2\pi, the arrows close a regular polygon and the sum vanishes; the first nulls therefore sit at ψ=±2π/N\psi=\pm2\pi/N, and the main lobe spans 4π/N4\pi/N in ψ\psi. More elements give a narrower lobe in ψ\psi for the same reason a wider aperture gives a narrower beam. This is the discrete version of the closing circle in Fig. 16.

“Broadside” and “endfire” describe directions relative to the array. Broadside to a line is perpendicular to it: θ=90∘\theta=90^\circ. Endfire lies along the line: θ=0∘\theta=0^\circ or 180∘180^\circ. An in-phase line has β=0\beta=0 and reinforces broadside. To reinforce a chosen angle θ0\theta_0, set β=−kdcos⁡θ0\beta=-kd\cos\theta_0.

A sidelobe is an additional local bump from partial reinforcement. A grating lobe is a replica where the phase progression has gone through another complete turn and all elements reinforce again. To check for replicas, use an integer ℓ\ell, positive, negative, or zero, and solve kdcos⁡θ+β=2πℓ,−1≤cos⁡θ≤1.\begin{equation} kd\cos\theta+\beta=2\pi\ell, \qquad -1\leq\cos\theta\leq1. \label{eq:arr-replicas} \end{equation}(36) The inequality keeps only real viewing directions. Check every integer that gives a visible direction.

Fig. 35 turns the replica check into a picture. As θ\theta sweeps from 180∘180^\circ to 0∘0^\circ, cos⁡θ\cos\theta runs from −1-1 to 11 and ψ\psi sweeps the window from β−kd\beta-kd to β+kd\beta+kd. Steering sets β\beta and so slides the window; spacing sets its width 2kd2kd. The pattern seen in angle is the slice of the periodic array factor inside that window. A grating lobe appears when the window reaches a neighbouring peak at ψ=±2π\psi=\pm2\pi. For a beam steered to θ0\theta_0, with β=−kdcos⁡θ0\beta=-kd\cos\theta_0, the peaks stay outside when kd(1+|cos⁡θ0|)<2πkd(1+|\cos\theta_0|)<2\pi: dλ<11+|cos⁡θ0|.\begin{equation} \frac{d}{\lambda}<\frac{1}{1+|\cos\theta_0|}. \label{eq:arr-nograting} \end{equation}(37) Broadside steering allows spacing just under λ\lambda; steering to 60∘60^\circ requires d<0.667λd<0.667\lambda, which the 0.8λ0.8\lambda example violates; steering to endfire requires d<λ/2d<\lambda/2. Half-wavelength spacing satisfies the strict condition for every steering angle 0<θ0<π0<\theta_0<\pi. At exact endfire it reaches equality and the opposite endfire endpoint also becomes fully coherent, as the bottom panel shows. It remains a useful starting spacing for scanning, with that endpoint exception and the practical element and coupling models included.

Fig. 36 shows a second cost of steering. The outermost centres of NN sites span (N−1)d(N-1)d, while the long-array beamwidth approximation uses an effective aperture length approximately NdNd. Seen from θ0\theta_0, that effective length presents a projected width Ndsin⁡θ0Nd\sin\theta_0, and the beam width follows the projected width: for a long array away from endfire, the full half-power beamwidth is about 0.886λ/(Ndsin⁡θ0)0.886\lambda/(Nd\sin\theta_0) radians, the strip result of Chapter II with DD replaced by the projected length. Sixteen half-wave elements give 6.4∘6.4^\circ at broadside, 7.4∘7.4^\circ at 60∘60^\circ and 13.0∘13.0^\circ at 30∘30^\circ.

For a concrete steering setting, let d=λ/2d=\lambda/2 and θ0=60∘\theta_0=60^\circ. Then β=−π/2\beta=-\pi/2 radians. At the target, ψ=0\psi=0 and eight unit field contributions give AF=8AF=8. At broadside, ψ=−π/2\psi=-\pi/2 and the eight equally spaced phasors cancel. The squared array factor is a relative power shape; absolute gain still needs the normalization developed below.

The Element Still Gets a Vote

Fig. 37 shows the element power pattern multiplying the array interference pattern. An axial element null remains a null even when the array factor reinforces there. Steering the feed phases cannot supply radiation in a direction where the adopted element field is zero.

An array’s radiation combines placement, feed interference, and the angular response of each element. Since fields multiply as in (30), the power shape contains |Eelement|2|AF|2|E_{\mathrm{element}}|^2|AF|^2. A zero in the common element field therefore remains a zero for every finite array factor.

Fig. 38 shows why a cosine appears for a zz-directed line while a sine appears for an xyxy-plane grid. The operation is unchanged: project the physical separation onto the viewing vector. For a line step d𝒛̂d\hat{\mathbf{z}} this gives dcos⁡θd\cos\theta; for a planar step dx𝒙̂d_x\hat{\mathbf{x}} it gives dxsin⁡θcos⁡ϕd_x\sin\theta\cos\phi. At broadside to the plane, predict both in-plane path projections before choosing feed phases: they are zero.

A Plane Gives Us Two Steering Directions

Fig. 39 shows a phase ramp across a two-dimensional grid and the pencil beam it produces. The two grid directions let the feeds select both uxu_x and uyu_y. For an element at (x,y,0)(x,y,0), the path projection is xux+yuyxu_x+yu_y. Reflecting the viewing direction across the array plane changes only uzu_z, so it leaves every feed’s phase sum unchanged. The full-space array factor has a mirror beam behind the plane. The October 29 half-space element model suppresses that rear response; the figure shows its forward beam [source].

Now spread the elements over the xyxy plane and choose +z+z as forward boresight. Broadside to this plane means along its normal. This differs from broadside to the earlier zz-axis line, so draw the object before interpreting the word.

In this antenna frame, θ\theta is angle from +z+z, and ϕ\phi is the azimuth around zz measured from +x+x toward +y+y. Define two direction cosines, uxu_x and uyu_y, as the xx and yy components of the viewing unit vector: ux=sin⁡θcos⁡ϕ,uy=sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ.\begin{equation} u_x=\sin\theta\cos\phi,\qquad u_y=\sin\theta\sin\phi. \label{eq:arr-dircos} \end{equation}(38) These dimensionless quantities are the viewing vector’s projections onto the two array axes. On the forward hemisphere the remaining component is uz=1−ux2−uy2u_z=\sqrt{1-u_x^2-u_y^2}. Thus physically visible forward directions lie inside ux2+uy2≤1u_x^2+u_y^2\leq1.

Fig. 40 shows what these coordinates are. Shine a light down the array normal: the shadow of the unit viewing vector on the array plane has components (ux,uy)(u_x,u_y) and length sin⁡θ\sin\theta. Every forward direction casts its shadow inside the unit disk; boresight maps to the centre and the horizon to the rim, where equal steps in θ\theta crowd together. Because the positional phase depends linearly on uxu_x and uyu_y, the array factor of a fixed amplitude mask translates in this disk under ideal phase steering. The complete radiation pattern also contains the fixed element pattern and the visible-disk boundary; it need not translate unchanged. The crowding of constant-θ\theta circles near the rim is the planar version of the scan broadening in Fig. 36.

Let dx,dyd_x,d_y be grid spacings in metres. Integers m,nm,n label a grid location (mdx,ndy,0)(md_x,nd_y,0), and amna_{mn} is its complex feed weight. The general sum becomes AF(ux,uy)=∑m∑namnejk(mdxux+ndyuy).\begin{equation} AF(u_x,u_y)=\sum_m\sum_n a_{mn} e^{jk(md_xu_x+nd_yu_y)}. \label{eq:arr-planar} \end{equation}(39) To select direction (ux0,uy0)(u_{x0},u_{y0}), assign feed phase ϕmn=−k(mdxux0+ndyuy0)\phi_{mn}=-k(md_xu_{x0}+nd_yu_{y0}). It is the same cancellation idea as before, now with a phase ramp across both grid directions. A filled rectangle with separable feed settings factors into two line-array sums. For a thinned grid or arbitrary phase map, evaluate the actual active-element sum.

For half-wavelength spacings, target (ux0,uy0)=(0.3,−0.2)(u_{x0},u_{y0})=(0.3,-0.2) requires a feed increment of −54∘-54^\circ along xx and +36∘+36^\circ along yy. Its off-axis angle is sin⁡−10.32+(−0.2)2=21.1∘\sin^{-1}\sqrt{0.3^2+(-0.2)^2}=21.1^\circ. The coordinates are direction cosines, rather than distances or angles in degrees.

Fig. 41 shows the separate roles of steering and the element. Predict the element multiplier at the new target: 1−0.72=0.511-0.7^2=0.51, compared with one at broadside. The complete peak can also shift slightly away from the array-factor target. Its absolute directivity must still be found from the full angular integral, rather than by resetting each product to the same peak. The illustrated element is a teaching model; the homework’s forward-isotropic element has a different element factor.

With a single beam formed and steered, the antenna side of the story is complete. The remaining question is what that beam delivers on the ground.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, ANT10 and dish/array lectures; supplied October 22–29, 2026 notes and transcripts. The course scalar obliquity convention is retained.

chapters.title: Turn a Beam Into a Link on the Ground
chapters.label: sec:link
chapters.html:
Fig. 42 shows the complete chain for one geographic cell. Follow its ray and range into the antenna calculation, then carry the resulting gain into the power calculation. Only after the available received power is known do we make a coverage decision.

The pattern is an angular object. A coverage map is a geographic object. Joining them means answering two questions for each ground point: Which way is it from the satellite? How far away is it? The look-angle geometry supplies both quantities.

Look Angles Belong to a Particular Observer

Fig. 43 puts the Earth-centred triangle and the station's local horizon in one scene. The line of sight leaves the station; its tilt above the horizon plane is the elevation, and the direction of its shadow on that plane, measured from North, is the azimuth. These are observer-dependent angles, so we first state the coordinate frame.

At a ground station, the local frame is East, North, Up. Let the ground and satellite positions in one common Earth-centered frame be 𝒓g\boldsymbol{r}_g and 𝒓s\boldsymbol{r}_s, both in metres. The subscript gg means ground and ss means satellite. The line-of-sight displacement from ground toward satellite is 𝒅g=𝒓s−𝒓g\boldsymbol{d}_g=\boldsymbol{r}_s-\boldsymbol{r}_g. Its length is slant range R=∥𝒅g∥R=\|\boldsymbol{d}_g\|, where the double bars mean Euclidean length. Divide by RR to obtain the viewing unit vector 𝒒̂g\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}_g.

After rotating that vector into the station’s East-North-Up axes, call its components qE,qN,qUq_E,q_N,q_U. Elevation ElE_l measures upward from the local horizon. Azimuth AzAz starts at north and increases toward east. Both follow from the components: El=atan2⁡(qU,qE2+qN2),Az=atan2⁡(qE,qN).\begin{equation} E_l=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(q_U,\sqrt{q_E^2+q_N^2}\right), \qquad Az=\operatorname{atan2}(q_E,q_N). \label{eq:arr-look} \end{equation}(40) The two-argument arctangent uses both signs to choose the correct quadrant and returns an angle in radians. Convert azimuth to the interval 00 to 2π2\pi if desired. At exact zenith the viewing vector points straight up. Its horizontal projection is zero, so every horizontal azimuth refers to the same upward direction and azimuth is undefined.

For the spherical-Earth triangle in Fig. 43, the satellite’s outward component relative to the station is rscos⁡γ−rer_s\cos\gamma-r_e, and its horizontal component toward the satellite subpoint is rssin⁡γr_s\sin\gamma. Dividing both by rsr_s leaves a useful equivalent expression: El=atan2⁡(cosγ−re/rs,sinγ).\begin{equation} E_l=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\cos\gamma-r_e/r_s,\sin\gamma\right). \label{eq:arr-elevation} \end{equation}(41) Here rer_e and rsr_s are geocentric radii: distances from Earth’s center. Satellite altitude is rs−rer_s-r_e in this spherical model. A negative elevation means the line of sight is below the ideal geometric horizon. This equation and the component equation tell the same geometric story. Mountains, refraction, and an operational elevation mask require additional modeling.

The central angle and the slant range follow from the station’s latitude LgL_g and east longitude ℓg\ell_g and the satellite subpoint (Ls,ℓs)(L_s,\ell_s). Spherical trigonometry and the law of cosines give cos⁡γ=cos⁡Lgcos⁡Lscos⁡(ℓs−ℓg)+sin⁡Lgsin⁡Ls,R=re2+rs2−2rerscos⁡γ.\begin{align} \cos\gamma&=\cos L_g\cos L_s\cos(\ell_s-\ell_g)+\sin L_g\sin L_s,\\ R&=\sqrt{r_e^2+r_s^2-2r_er_s\cos\gamma}. \label{eq:arr-slant} \end{align}(43) A geostationary satellite has Ls=0L_s=0, so cos⁡γ=cos⁡Lgcos⁡(ℓs−ℓg)\cos\gamma=\cos L_g\cos(\ell_s-\ell_g).

Fig. 44 applies these formulas to a geostationary link. Place the satellite at Atlanta’s longitude, the starting point suggested in class, and the station at Atlanta’s latitude, 33.75∘33.75^\circ N. Then γ=33.75∘\gamma=33.75^\circ, (41) gives El=atan2⁡(0.8315−0.1513,0.5556)=50.8∘E_l=\operatorname{atan2}(0.8315-0.1513,\,0.5556)=50.8^\circ, and (43) gives R=37,031R=37{,}031 km. These are the direction and range of the running example; the link budget below uses them. At the same longitude the GEO satellite lies due south of Atlanta, so its ground-station azimuth is 180∘180^\circ.

Reverse the Ray and Change the Frame

Fig. 45 shows the same segment viewed from its two ends. The ground station points toward the satellite, while the satellite array radiates toward the ground. Reversing the common-frame ray and then rotating it into the antenna frame keeps those two angle conventions consistent.

The satellite’s array looks the other way along that segment. Its outgoing unit vector toward the ground is 𝒒̂s=𝒓g−𝒓sR=−𝒒̂g.\begin{equation} \hat{\boldsymbol{q}}_s=\frac{\boldsymbol{r}_g-\boldsymbol{r}_s}{R}=-\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}_g. \label{eq:arr-reverse} \end{equation}(44) The last equality compares vectors expressed in the same common frame. Reverse the ray first, then rotate it into the satellite antenna frame to read ux,uyu_x,u_y. Ground-station azimuth and elevation use the station’s horizon and north reference; antenna-frame θ,ϕ\theta,\phi use the satellite’s array axes.

Fig. 46 shows the rotation as a set of signed projections, rather than an unexplained change of coordinates. For the spherical Earth and geocentric latitude LgL_g, east-positive longitude ℓg\ell_g supplies the unit basis 𝒆̂=(−sin⁡ℓg,cos⁡ℓg,0),𝒏̂=(−sin⁡Lgcos⁡ℓg,−sin⁡Lgsin⁡ℓg,cos⁡Lg),𝒖̂=(cos⁡Lgcos⁡ℓg,cos⁡Lgsin⁡ℓg,sin⁡Lg).\begin{align} \hat{\mathbf{e}}&=(-\sin\ell_g,\ \cos\ell_g,\ 0),\\ \hat{\mathbf{n}}&=(-\sin L_g\cos\ell_g,\ -\sin L_g\sin\ell_g,\ \cos L_g),\\ \hat{\mathbf{u}}&=(\cos L_g\cos\ell_g,\ \cos L_g\sin\ell_g,\ \sin L_g). \label{eq:audit-ant-enu-basis} \end{align}(47) The common-frame station position is 𝒓g=re𝒖̂\mathbf{r}_g=r_e\hat{\mathbf{u}}. Project the common-frame unit ray onto each basis direction: (qE,qN,qU)=(𝒆̂⋅𝒒̂g,𝒏̂⋅𝒒̂g,𝒖̂⋅𝒒̂g).\begin{equation} (q_E,q_N,q_U)=(\hat{\mathbf{e}}\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{q}}_g, \hat{\mathbf{n}}\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{q}}_g, \hat{\mathbf{u}}\!\cdot\!\hat{\mathbf{q}}_g). \label{eq:audit-ant-enu-projection} \end{equation}(48) For Atlanta the result is approximately (0,−0.633,0.774)(0,-0.633,0.774): southward and upward. Substitution into the look-angle equation gives Az=180∘Az=180^\circ and El=50.76∘E_l=50.76^\circ.

For any chosen right-handed antenna basis (𝒙̂s,𝒚̂s,𝒛̂s)(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_s,\hat{\mathbf{y}}_s,\hat{\mathbf{z}}_s), the same dot products give (ux,uy,uz)(u_x,u_y,u_z) from the reversed ray 𝒒̂s\hat{\mathbf{q}}_s. Here choose 𝒛̂s=−𝒓s/rs\hat{\mathbf{z}}_s=-\mathbf{r}_s/r_s toward nadir, 𝒙̂s\hat{\mathbf{x}}_s eastward, and 𝒚̂s=𝒛̂s×𝒙̂s\hat{\mathbf{y}}_s=\hat{\mathbf{z}}_s\times\hat{\mathbf{x}}_s. The resulting components are (0,−0.0957,0.9954)(0,-0.0957,0.9954), giving off-axis angle cos⁡−1(uz)=5.49∘\cos^{-1}(u_z)=5.49^\circ. Rotating the normal to the target makes the scan angle zero. This angle is measured at the satellite; it is not the ground elevation’s complement because the local normals differ.

Turn a Relative Pattern Into Radiation Intensity

Fig. 47 shows the missing physical step between an interference image and a link budget. The coherent sum first produces a relative power shape. Multiplying by a scale with units W/sr produces intensity, and the total radiated power will determine that scale.

Let ana_n be relative feed weights, so AFAF is a dimensionless complex field sum. Squaring its magnitude gives a dimensionless interference power shape. If gel(θ,ϕ)g_{\mathrm{el}}(\theta,\phi) is the common element’s relative power pattern, define the complete relative pattern w(θ,ϕ)=gel(θ,ϕ)|AF(θ,ϕ)|2.\begin{equation} w(\theta,\phi)=g_{\mathrm{el}}(\theta,\phi)|AF(\theta,\phi)|^2. \label{eq:arr-relative-power} \end{equation}(49) It describes where radiation goes, but its scale does not yet specify watts. Choose a constant CC with units W/sr and write U=CwU=Cw, where UU is physical radiation intensity in watts per steradian. For example, AF=1+jAF=1+j has |AF|2=2|AF|^2=2; if gel=0.5g_{\mathrm{el}}=0.5, then w=1w=1. A scale C=2C=2 W/sr makes U=2U=2 W/sr in that direction. To choose CC from a specified radiated power, integrate the whole pattern next. The November 12 class makes this normalization the starting point for absolute array gain [source].

Count Solid Angle Before Adding Directional Power

Fig. 48 shows on the sphere itself why an equal step in polar angle and azimuth is not an equal-area patch everywhere. The equatorial patch spans twice the solid angle of the illustrated near-pole patch. We therefore weight directional intensity by solid angle before adding powers.

The symbol Ω\Omega denotes direction on a sphere. A steradian measures area on a unit sphere; on a sphere of radius RR, the corresponding area is R2dΩR^2d\Omega. Here θ\theta is polar angle from +z+z, in radians, and ϕ\phi is azimuth around that axis. A small cell has meridional side RdθR\,d\theta and azimuthal side Rsin⁡θdϕR\sin\theta\,d\phi. Therefore dΩ=dAR2=sin⁡θdθdϕ.\begin{equation} d\Omega=\frac{dA}{R^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi. \label{eq:arr-solid-angle} \end{equation}(50) At the pole, a full azimuthal sweep shrinks to a point; at the equator it follows the largest ring. That geometry supplies the sine weight. For a pattern value UU in W/sr, UdΩU\,d\Omega is power in watts into that cell. Summing those weighted powers over 0≤θ≤π0\leq\theta\leq\pi and 0≤ϕ<2π0\leq\phi<2\pi gives the radiated total. For example, the figure’s near-pole cell subtends 0.03040.0304 sr and the equatorial cell 0.06080.0608 sr, although their angle increments match.

Normalize the Pattern to Obtain Directivity

Fig. 49 shows two beams with the same relative peak but different angular concentration; seen in three dimensions, the narrower one plainly occupies less of the sphere. The narrower shape must have a larger physical peak when both radiate the same total power. Directivity measures precisely that peak-to-spherical-average ratio.

Integrating intensity over the full sphere gives total radiated power PradP_{\mathrm{rad}}: Prad=∫4πU(Ω)dΩ,Ddir(Ω)=4πU(Ω)Prad.\begin{equation} P_{\mathrm{rad}}=\int_{4\pi}U(\Omega)\,d\Omega,\qquad D_{\mathrm{dir}}(\Omega)=\frac{4\pi U(\Omega)}{P_{\mathrm{rad}}}. \label{eq:arr-directivity} \end{equation}(51) DdirD_{\mathrm{dir}} is dimensionless directivity: intensity divided by the spherical average. Its subscript distinguishes it from aperture diameter DD. Define the relative-pattern integral B=∫4πwdΩB=\int_{4\pi}w\,d\Omega. Its steradian bookkeeping gives C=PradB,U=PradBw,Ddir=4πwB.\begin{equation} C=\frac{P_{\mathrm{rad}}}{B},\qquad U=\frac{P_{\mathrm{rad}}}{B}w, \qquad D_{\mathrm{dir}}=\frac{4\pi w}{B}. \label{eq:arr-shape-normalization} \end{equation}(52) The constant field scale cancels from directivity. Doubling every feed doubles AFAF and multiplies both ww and BB by four, leaving DdirD_{\mathrm{dir}} unchanged. When ww is scaled to a peak of one, BB is the beam solid angle ΩA\Omega_A of Fig. 26, and the peak directivity is 4π/B4\pi/B: the sphere divided by the solid angle the beam effectively fills. A peak-normalized plot discards BB; it therefore supplies beam shape without the absolute directivity needed for a link budget.

In the forward-only model, the backward hemisphere contributes zero, while the entire forward pattern, including sidelobes, belongs in BB. For w=cos⁡mθw=\cos^m\theta on the forward hemisphere, substitution of x=cos⁡θx=\cos\theta gives B=2π/(m+1)B=2\pi/(m+1). Thus m=2m=2 gives peak directivity 6, or 7.787.78 dBi; m=8m=8 gives 18, or 12.5512.55 dBi. Both retain zero backward radiation, and both integrate their directivity over the sphere to 4π4\pi.

Put watts on the first example: if Prad=12P_{\mathrm{rad}}=12 W and w=cos⁡2θw=\cos^2\theta, then C=18/π=5.73C=18/\pi=5.73 W/sr. Boresight intensity is 5.735.73 W/sr, spherical-average intensity is 12/(4π)=0.95512/(4\pi)=0.955 W/sr, and their ratio is 6. Gain additionally includes radiation efficiency: G=ηradDdirG=\eta_{\mathrm{rad}}D_{\mathrm{dir}}. If ηrad=0.80\eta_{\mathrm{rad}}=0.80, accepted transmit power is 1515 W, radiated power is 1212 W and peak gain is 4.84.8 (6.816.81 dBi). Using accepted power with gain or radiated power with directivity gives the same link; include that loss once. The homework’s ideal lossless model has ηrad=1\eta_{\mathrm{rad}}=1, so G=DdirG=D_{\mathrm{dir}}.

Fig. 50 shows where the efficiency belongs. The accepted 1515 W already becomes 1212 radiated watts through ηrad=0.80\eta_{\mathrm{rad}}=0.80, and directivity 6 becomes gain 4.8 through that same efficiency. Either 15×4.815\times4.8 or 12×612\times6 supplies the link’s numerator. Applying the loss on both routes at once would count it twice. The receiving AeA_e is likewise used with the efficiency convention already included in its definition.

For the assigned forward-isotropic planar elements, there is also an exact normalization check that retains distant sidelobes. If ρnm=∥𝒓n−𝒓m∥\rho_{nm}=\|\mathbf{r}_n-\mathbf{r}_m\| is pair separation in metres, the coherent pair integral gives Q=∑n∑manam*sin⁡(kρnm)kρnm,B=2πQ,Ddir=2|AF|2Q.\begin{align} Q&=\sum_n\sum_m a_na_m^*\frac{\sin(k\rho_{nm})}{k\rho_{nm}},\\ B&=2\pi Q,\qquad D_{\mathrm{dir}}=\frac{2|AF|^2}{Q}. \label{eq:arr-pair-normalization} \end{align}(54) The zero-separation fraction has limit one. The conjugate am*a_m^* and the cross terms preserve phase interference; QQ is real and dimensionless. Summing individual element powers alone is an approximation unless the integrated cross terms vanish.

The pair term has a direct meaning. Expanding |AF|2=∑n∑manam*ejk𝒒̂⋅(𝒓n−𝒓m)|AF|^2=\sum_n\sum_ma_na_m^*e^{jk\hat{\boldsymbol{q}}\cdot(\boldsymbol{r}_n-\boldsymbol{r}_m)} produces one cross term for each pair of elements, exactly as in (16). Averaged over every direction on the sphere, the exponential of a pair separated by ρnm\rho_{nm} averages to sin⁡(kρnm)/(kρnm)\sin(k\rho_{nm})/(k\rho_{nm}).

Fig. 51 shows that average. At every nonzero integer multiple of λ/2\lambda/2 it is zero: such pairs redistribute power between directions without changing the total, so the total radiated power is the plain sum of element powers. A straight half-wavelength line has only those nonzero pair separations. For unit-magnitude active weights its QQ equals the number of active elements; in the general weighted case the surviving diagonal contribution is ∑n|an|2\sum_n|a_n|^2. A square grid also contains diagonal pairs λ/2\lambda/\sqrt2 apart, where the average is −0.217-0.217. A 2×22\times2 half-wavelength square therefore has Q=4+4(−0.217)=3.13Q=4+4(-0.217)=3.13 from its four ordered diagonal pairs, and broadside directivity 2(16)/3.13=10.22(16)/3.13=10.2 (10.1 dBi), above the 8 that a plain power sum would predict. Four equal in-phase elements on a half-wavelength straight grid have Q=4Q=4: at broadside AF=4AF=4, relative power is 16 and absolute directivity is 2(16)/4=82(16)/4=8, or 9.039.03 dBi. These are three different quantities describing the same direction. The full-pattern integral and this exact pair check avoid any need to assume that all power lies near Georgia.

Fig. 52 shows why the diagonal correction appears four times even though there are only two drawn diagonals: both (n,m)(n,m) and (m,n)(m,n) occur. The four self pairs are also retained, with the limit sin⁡(kρ)/(kρ)=1\sin(k\rho)/(k\rho)=1 at ρ=0\rho=0. Predict what changes if one feed phase reverses: the geometric distances remain fixed, but products anam*a_na_m^* involving that feed change sign, so QQ and the pattern must both be recomputed.

Give the Beam a Transmit Power and a Range

Fig. 53 shows gain concentrating the transmitted power and a receiver collecting part of the resulting density. The lower plot isolates range: doubling it reduces received power by four. We combine those two antenna gains and the geometric spreading into Friis' equation.

Let PtP_t be power delivered to the transmitting antenna, in watts. Let GtG_t be its linear gain toward the receiver, and GrG_r the receiver’s linear gain back toward the transmitter. In free space, the transmitted power spreads over spherical area 4πR24\pi R^2, with directional gain concentrating it. A matched receiving antenna has effective area Ae,r=Grλ2/(4π)A_{e,r}=G_r\lambda^2/(4\pi). Multiply incident power density by that area and we obtain Friis’ equation: Pr=PtGt4πR2Ae,r=PtGtGr(λ4πR)2.\begin{equation} P_r=\frac{P_tG_t}{4\pi R^2}\,A_{e,r} =P_tG_tG_r\left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi R}\right)^2. \label{eq:arr-friis} \end{equation}(55) PrP_r is available received power in watts. This version assumes far-field free-space propagation, matched polarization, appropriate pointing gains, and matching at the receiving antenna; additional propagation or implementation losses need their own factors. Gain is dimensionless, and λ/R\lambda/R is a ratio of lengths, so the result has the same power unit as PtP_t.

Read Power References in Decibels
