Fig. 54 shows three powers written against watt and milliwatt references. The two numbers at each point describe the same physical power. Keeping that reference explicit prevents a 30 dB error when converting a received-power threshold.

Decibels turn the multiplication into addition. Define free-space path loss LFS=20log⁡10(4πR/λ)L_{\mathrm{FS}}=20\log_{10}(4\pi R/\lambda) in dB. Express power relative to one watt as PdBW=10log⁡10(P/1W)P_{\mathrm{dBW}}=10\log_{10}(P/1\,\mathrm{W}) and gain relative to an isotropic radiator as GdBi=10log⁡10GG_{\mathrm{dBi}}=10\log_{10}G. Then Pr,dBW=Pt,dBW+Gt,dBi+Gr,dBi−LFS.\begin{equation} P_{r,\mathrm{dBW}}=P_{t,\mathrm{dBW}}+G_{t,\mathrm{dBi}}+G_{r,\mathrm{dBi}}-L_{\mathrm{FS}}. \label{eq:arr-db} \end{equation}(56) The milliwatt reference gives dBm instead: PdBm=PdBW+30P_{\mathrm{dBm}}=P_{\mathrm{dBW}}+30. These are different reference levels for the same power. A power ratio uses 10log⁡1010\log_{10}; a corresponding field-amplitude ratio uses 20log⁡1020\log_{10} because power depends on squared field magnitude. Keep the impedance and field convention consistent when making that comparison.

Fig. 55 puts the running example into (56). The satellite delivers Pt=10P_t=10 W, or 10.010.0 dBW, to an antenna with an illustrative 3030 dBi toward Atlanta; for the array, this number would come from the normalized directivity above. The receiving antenna is the 1 m, ηa=0.60\eta_a=0.60 dish of Chapter II, with 38.238.2 dBi at λ=0.030\lambda=0.030 m. The slant range is 37,03137{,}031 km, so LFS=20log⁡104π(3.7031×107)0.030=203.8dB,\begin{equation*} L_{\mathrm{FS}}=20\log_{10}\frac{4\pi(3.7031\times10^7)}{0.030}=203.8\ {\mathrm{dB}}, \end{equation*} and Pr=10.0+30.0+38.2−203.8=−125.6P_r=10.0+30.0+38.2-203.8=-125.6 dBW, or −95.6-95.6 dBm: about 2.7×10−132.7\times10^{-13} W. Chapter VII compares this power with the receiver’s noise.

Connect the Georgiatenna Design Steps

Fig. 56 shows how a completed power map becomes a weighted score. First classify each original cell as inside or outside the service region, then compare its received power with the threshold. The toy example makes the unequal miss and spill penalties visible before combining them algebraically.

The assignment is a practical meeting place for all these ideas. For every map cell, geometry gives a range and satellite-frame direction. The element model and actual active-element phases give a field sum. Full angular normalization turns its shape into gain. The link equation gives received power, and the threshold turns that into a coverage decision. Verify coverage at every required map cell, using its own direction and range.

The November 3 clarification leaves the GEO longitude as a design choice and permits the array normal to point toward Georgia; the instructor suggested Atlanta’s longitude as a convenient starting point. The GEO satellite’s subpoint remains at zero latitude. The array’s pointing direction is a separate orientation choice, which sets the antenna frame used in the phase calculation [source].

The specified model uses equal magnitudes for active elements, permitted off-elements, and controllable phases on the prescribed grid. Turning elements off changes the effective aperture; changing relative phases reshapes its interference. With equal active-element magnitudes, the available design controls are element selection and phase. The original full-credit brief asks for at least 100 elements. The November 10 discussion calls NN the total installed count and describes a one-element submission as partial credit; state the installed/active interpretation explicitly and use the final scoring definition [source] [source].

On the illustrative raster, two missed interior cells contribute 2×100=2002\times100=200 penalty units, while four covered exterior cells contribute only four. The fixed-raster count penalty is J=100PGNC+POGCJ=100P_{\mathrm{GNC}}+P_{\mathrm{OGC}}; the conditional score is 1/[N+100J]1/[\sqrt{N+100}J] when the correctness flag is one. Keep the original raster dimensions when comparing designs. Convert a counted area to square kilometres separately using a stated cell-area convention, and correct the source Georgia latitude sign without altering its original data [source].

The classroom score penalizes uncovered Georgia cells, unwanted coverage elsewhere, and element count. Transmit power is unrestricted by that score, so practical spacecraft evaluation also needs a separate power assessment. The useful study goal is to understand which stage changes when one design choice changes: position alters geometry; phases alter the pattern; transmit power scales the resulting received-power map.

The propagation story is now complete. Geometry gives each ground cell a direction and a range, the coherent sum and its normalization give the gain in that direction, and Friis’ equation gives the watts that arrive. The next three chapters ask what those watts carry and how a receiver reads it.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, November 3 and 5, 2026 class notes, original board images and Notability transcripts. Direct-sequence spread spectrum, GPS signal structure, Earth-fixed ranging and timing precision. Local source files are retained in the course reference folders.

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, November 10 and 12, 2026, original notes 23. ECE 6390 11_10 and 24. ECE 6390 11_12, with the corresponding local Notability transcripts. The notes and recordings are primary course sources; unclear automatic-transcription arithmetic is not used as a verified numerical result.

  • ECE 6390, “GEO Georgiatenna,” supplied assignment and October 29 handwritten clarifications.

chapters.title: Give the Signal a Digital Description
chapters.label: sec:digital
chapters.html:
Fig. 57 shows the three decisions needed to transmit a camera image or sensor voltage: which times to record, which amplitude labels to store, and how to describe those labels economically. Follow the arrows from a continuous input toward the bit stream before assigning a rate to any stage.

We have followed a wave across space. Now imagine being responsible for what the wave carries: perhaps a camera image, a microphone recording, or a stream of spacecraft measurements. To prepare this information for transmission, we first choose how to represent it.

A digital recorder performs three connected jobs. Sampling decides when to look. Quantization decides which amplitude to record. Compression decides how economically to describe the resulting data. Each stage controls a different part of the recorded description. The supporting VID3–VID4 material supplies this part of the story [source].

Sampling: Record the Signal at Selected Times

Fig. 58 shows the recording problem in time and frequency: identical sample values can hide different between-sample oscillations. The receiver needs a bandwidth restriction and a sufficiently fast sample clock to choose the intended continuous signal.

Let x(t)x(t) be an analog signal, such as a voltage measured in volts. Time tt is continuous and measured in seconds: the signal has a value even between the instants when we inspect it. Let fsf_s be the sampling rate in samples per second. Uniform sampling means the time between snapshots is the sampling interval TsampleT_{\mathrm{sample}}: Tsample=1fs,x[n]=x(nTsample).\begin{equation} T_{\mathrm{sample}}=\frac{1}{f_s},\qquad x[n]=x(nT_{\mathrm{sample}}). \end{equation} The integer nn counts snapshots. Square brackets in x[n]x[n] remind us that this is a sequence indexed by whole numbers; parentheses in x(t)x(t) describe a signal that exists at every time. Ideal sampling preserves the exact amplitude at each selected instant. Quantization will supply the finite amplitude precision in the next stage.

Reconstructing the signal between snapshots requires a restriction on how fast the original can vary. A signal’s spectrum describes its content at different frequencies. For a real baseband signal, that content is centered around zero frequency. Say its highest occupied positive frequency is BB hertz; BB is its one-sided baseband bandwidth. A hertz is one cycle per second.

In the ideal band-limited model, the safe side of the Nyquist boundary is fs>2B.\begin{equation} f_s>2B. \end{equation} Under the model’s assumptions, the complete sample sequence contains enough information to identify the original band-limited signal. A practical anti-alias filter also needs a transition band between the frequencies it passes and rejects, which calls for a sampling rate above 2B2B. At the exact boundary, the phase of an edge-frequency sinusoid can produce ambiguous samples.

Reconstruction uses the sample sequence together with the band limit: place a sinc pulse at each sample time, scale it by the sample value, and add, x(t)=∑nx[n]sinc⁡(t−nTsampleTsample),sinc⁡(v)=sin⁡πvπv.\begin{equation} x(t)=\sum_n x[n]\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\frac{t-nT_{\mathrm{sample}}}{T_{\mathrm{sample}}}\right),\quad \operatorname{sinc}(v)=\frac{\sin\pi v}{\pi v}. \label{eq:rep-reconstruct} \end{equation}(59)

Fig. 59 shows (59) at work. An unweighted sinc pulse equals one at its own sample time and zero at every other sample time. The infinite, sample-weighted sum in (59) therefore reconstructs the band-limited signal exactly under the ideal assumptions. The plotted 121-term approximation passes through the displayed samples but retains the small between-sample residual shown below it. Chapter VI reuses this same zero-crossing property to pack transmitted symbols closely without letting them interfere at decision times.

Figure 58 shows two waveforms passing through the same sample values while completing different numbers of oscillations between them. They become aliases: distinct analog inputs with the same samples. In frequency language, sampling makes repeated copies of the spectrum, spaced by fsf_s. If neighboring copies overlap, their contributions cannot generally be separated from the samples alone.

A one-line calculation shows which complex inputs collide. A complex sinusoid at frequency ff produces samples ej2πfn/fse^{j2\pi fn/f_s}; replacing ff by f+mfsf+mf_s for any integer mm multiplies each sample by ej2πmn=1e^{j2\pi mn}=1. Keep its signed alias first: fsigned=f−mfs,−fs/2≤fsigned<fs/2.\begin{equation} f_{\mathrm{signed}}=f-mf_s,\qquad -f_s/2\le f_{\mathrm{signed}}<f_s/2. \end{equation} For a real sinusoid we may report the positive apparent frequency fa=|fsigned|f_a=|f_{\mathrm{signed}}|, provided we also keep the corresponding phase. A negative signed frequency conjugates a real cosine’s phasor when expressed at a positive frequency. For instance, at fs=12f_s=12 samples/s, ej2π9n/12=e−j2π3n/12,\begin{equation} e^{j2\pi9n/12}=e^{-j2\pi3n/12}, \end{equation} while the +3+3 Hz complex sequence rotates the other way. Their zero-phase real cosine projections agree; the imaginary sine projections have opposite signs.

Fig. 60 shows the real-frequency magnitude as a zig-zag and the complex sign in the sample traces. With fs=12f_s=12 samples/s, 2 Hz lies in the first zone; 9, 15 and 21 Hz all have a real apparent-frequency magnitude of 3 Hz. Their signed aliases are −3-3, +3+3 and −3-3 Hz. An anti-alias filter removes out-of-band energy before sampling so the intended first-zone input can be reconstructed.

An anti-alias filter therefore belongs before the sampler. It suppresses frequencies outside the intended recording band. Increasing amplitude precision afterward preserves those same sample values more accurately; the ambiguity between aliased inputs remains. A physical sample-and-hold circuit also holds each recorded voltage for a short time, producing a staircase-like output. That holding operation changes the spectral envelope; precise reconstruction may need filtering and compensation for its frequency-dependent attenuation. It is a separate effect from aliasing.

Quantization: Giving Each Snapshot an Allowed Value

Fig. 61 shows what happens when a recorder must replace a continuously varying voltage with one of eight allowed labels. The staircase and error plot identify two different design questions: how finely to resolve an in-range sample, and how much input range to provide before clipping.

Now we have selected the times. We still need a finite set of amplitude labels. Let bqb_q be the number of bits per sample. Since each bit has two possible values, the number of available labels is L=2bqL=2^{b_q}. For example, three bits provide eight labels. Each binary label identifies one reconstruction voltage recorded by the quantizer.

The course notes use uniformly spaced output levels that include the lowest and highest allowed voltages, VminV_{\min} and VmaxV_{\max}. With LL levels, there are L−1L-1 gaps between the endpoints. Their spacing, called the quantization step Δ\Delta, is therefore Δ=Vmax−VminL−1=Vmax−Vmin2bq−1.\begin{equation} \Delta=\frac{V_{\max}-V_{\min}}{L-1} =\frac{V_{\max}-V_{\min}}{2^{b_q}-1}. \end{equation} Here Δ\Delta is in volts. This is the same counting idea as fence posts: eight posts make seven gaps. Another common quantizer divides the range into LL equal bins, giving bin width (Vmax−Vmin)/L(V_{\max}-V_{\min})/L. The stated quantizer convention determines which count applies.

Call the rounded voltage xqx_q and the input at that instant xx. Define the quantization error as eq=xq−xe_q=x_q-x. Nearest-level rounding keeps the error within half a step, provided the input is inside the allowed range: |eq|≤Δ2.\begin{equation} |e_q|\le\frac{\Delta}{2}. \end{equation} Outside that range, the recorder clips at an endpoint. The error can then grow far beyond half a step. For the three-bit quantizer of Fig. 61, Δ=2/7=0.286\Delta=2/7=0.286 V and every in-range error stays within ±0.143\pm0.143 V.

For a sufficiently fine quantizer and a suitable changing input, a useful model treats the in-range error as roughly uniform between −Δ/2-\Delta/2 and +Δ/2+\Delta/2. Its mean is then zero and its variance, the average squared error, is σq2≃Δ212.\begin{equation} \sigma_q^2\simeq\frac{\Delta^2}{12}. \end{equation} The symbol σq2\sigma_q^2 has units of volts squared. This approximation is useful when a varying input samples many quantization steps. Steady inputs, coarse quantization, and clipping can produce correlated or nonuniform errors.

The quantization signal-to-noise ratio, or SQNR, compares wanted signal power with quantization-error power. The notes’ rule of thumb is about 6bq6b_q dB. The practical takeaway is the trend: one additional bit approximately halves the amplitude step and quarters the modeled error power, and 10log⁡104=6.0210\log_{10}4=6.02 dB, so SQNR improves by about 6 dB per bit when the other assumptions stay the same. Nonuniform quantization devotes smaller amplitude steps to selected parts of the input range. Companding implements this idea by compressing the amplitude range before uniform quantization and expanding it after reconstruction.

Fig. 62 shows why companding helps. Speech and many sensor signals spend most of their time at small amplitudes. The compressor stretches small inputs and squeezes large ones, so uniform steps after the compressor correspond to fine steps for quiet inputs and coarse steps for loud ones. The error then stays roughly proportional to the signal, which keeps the SQNR nearly constant over a wide range of input levels.

Recording more snapshots and recording more precise snapshots both cost bits. If nchn_{\mathrm{ch}} independent channels are each sampled at fsf_s, with bqb_q bits per sample, the raw pulse-code-modulation rate is RPCM=nchfsbq.\begin{equation} R_{\mathrm{PCM}}=n_{\mathrm{ch}}f_sb_q. \end{equation} RPCMR_{\mathrm{PCM}} is measured in bits per second. The units tell the story: channels times samples per second per channel times bits per sample. This count excludes headers and other overhead. Two audio channels sampled at 44.1 kHz with 16 bits per sample, for example, produce 2×44,100×16=1.4112\times44{,}100\times16=1.411 Mbit/s.

Compression: Describe the Same Data More Cleverly

Fig. 63 shows two ways to shorten a digital description: count repetitions, or assign short words to frequent source symbols. The practical problem is to save transmitted bits while preserving the level of information fidelity the application requires.

Repeated or predictable values offer opportunities for a shorter description. Run-length encoding can replace repeated values by a count and a value. Dictionary methods reuse descriptions of recurring sequences. A Huffman code gives shorter bit strings to more probable symbols. These are different ways of exploiting a pattern in the digital input.

“Lossless” means the decoder can reconstruct the exact digital input to the compressor. The reconstructed values therefore retain the precision supplied by the earlier quantizer. “Lossy” means some of that digital information is deliberately discarded. Image and video codecs often transform data into coefficients and then quantize those coefficients. A reversible transform reorganizes the data; quantizing or discarding its coefficients introduces loss. Color subsampling can also discard color detail while retaining more brightness detail.

The entropy formula describes how predictable a source is. Suppose there are KK possible source symbols, indexed by i=1,…,Ki=1,\ldots,K, and symbol ii occurs with probability pip_i. Their probabilities sum to one. The source entropy is H=−∑i=1Kpilog⁡2pi.\begin{equation} H=-\sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i\log_2p_i. \end{equation} HH is measured in bits per source symbol. The quantity −log⁡2pi-\log_2p_i assigns more information to a rarer event; multiplying by pip_i and adding computes its average. A symbol that is almost certain gives little new information. A surprising one gives more. The zero-probability term is taken as zero by a limit.

For a particular code, let ℓi\ell_i be the number of bits in the codeword for symbol ii. Its average length is ℓ¯=∑ipiℓi\overline{\ell}=\sum_i p_i\ell_i. Individual codewords have integer lengths, while their probability-weighted average can be fractional. Entropy provides an average-rate benchmark for lossless coding under the stated source model: no symbol-by-symbol lossless code can average fewer than HH bits per symbol. Actual file size also includes counts, codebooks, and headers. When that overhead exceeds the saved data, the file grows; alternating values, for example, produce very short runs.

Fig. 64 builds the code and checks it against the entropy. The Huffman recipe merges the two least probable entries, treats the merged pair as one entry with their combined probability, and repeats until one entry remains. Labelling each branch 0 or 1 and reading from the root gives A = 0, B = 10, C = 110 and D = 111. Every symbol sits at a leaf, so no codeword begins another, which is the prefix property. For probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1, H=−∑pilog⁡2pi=1.846,ℓ¯=∑piℓi=1.90\begin{equation*} H=-\sum p_i\log_2p_i=1.846,\qquad \overline\ell=\sum p_i\ell_i=1.90 \end{equation*} bits per symbol, against 2 bits for fixed-length labels. The code comes within 3% of the entropy bound.

Finally, define the compression factor before using it. Here let 𝒞=Rraw/Rinfo\mathcal{C}=R_{\mathrm{raw}}/R_{\mathrm{info}}, where RrawR_{\mathrm{raw}} is the uncompressed data rate and RinfoR_{\mathrm{info}} is the compressed information rate, both in bits per second. Then Rinfo=Rraw𝒞.\begin{equation} R_{\mathrm{info}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{raw}}}{\mathcal{C}}. \end{equation} For the four-symbol source, Huffman coding gives 𝒞=2/1.90=1.05\mathcal{C}=2/1.90=1.05 relative to fixed two-bit labels, and the entropy bound limits symbol-by-symbol coding to 2/1.846=1.082/1.846=1.08. Large compression factors come from sources with far more predictability, such as images with smooth regions or video frames that repeat their neighbours. Compression removes representational redundancy, improving the efficiency of the source description. Channel coding adds structured redundancy: relationships the receiver can use to detect or correct errors. The bit stream is now ready; the next chapter gives each group of bits a physical pulse.

Sources

  • G. D. Durgin, ECE 6390, supplied VID1–VID4 notes and optional foundational review videos. Analog video is background review; sampling, quantization, and source encoding form the digital representation chapters.

chapters.title: Let Pulses Overlap, Then Listen at the Right Moment
chapters.label: sec:pulses
chapters.html:
Fig. 65 shows why a usable digital radio waveform can be smooth and overlapping even though its symbols are discrete choices. Each colored pulse is one symbol’s contribution; their sum must deliver the intended values at the receiver’s decision instants.

The compressed data eventually becomes a sequence of transmission symbols. For now, think of each symbol as an amplitude choice; the next section adds the two-dimensional I/Q picture. Each symbol chooses a value from a transmission alphabet. The pulse shape gives that value its waveform and can extend across several symbol intervals [source].

Let RsR_s be the symbol rate in symbols per second, and let T=1/RsT=1/R_s be the symbol interval in seconds. This TT measures the time between transmitted symbols; TsampleT_{\mathrm{sample}} earlier measured the time between analog-input samples. The sampling and transmission stages set these two intervals according to their respective rate requirements.

Use ama_m for the amplitude of symbol number mm, and p(t)p(t) for one pulse shape. A shifted copy p(t−mT)p(t-mT) is centered at symbol mm’s time. Adding those shifted, weighted copies gives a baseband waveform: xbb(t)=∑mamp(t−mT).\begin{equation} x_{\mathrm{bb}}(t)=\sum_m a_m p(t-mT). \end{equation} The subscript “bb” means baseband. The sum sign means all the contributing symbols are added. With a dimensionless normalized pulse shape, ama_m and xbbx_{\mathrm{bb}} have the same amplitude units, such as volts. Complex-valued ama_m will later hold the two quadrature components.

A Rectangular Pulse Reveals the Time–Bandwidth Link

Fig. 66 shows why sending faster edges consumes more spectrum. A pulse has both a time description and a frequency description; the November 12 class uses that pair to connect pulse shape with occupied bandwidth [source].

Choose a unit-height rectangular pulse p(t)=1p(t)=1 for |t|<T/2|t|<T/2 and zero elsewhere. Here TT is duration in seconds and pp is dimensionless. Its Fourier transform is P(f)=∫−∞∞p(t)e−j2πftdt=Tsinc⁡(fT).\begin{equation} P(f)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(t)e^{-j2\pi ft}\,dt =T\operatorname{sinc}(fT). \end{equation} The integration variable tt is time; ff is frequency in Hz. The exponential is dimensionless because ftft counts cycles. Integrating a dimensionless pulse over seconds gives PP units of seconds. The normalized definition is sinc⁡(x)=sin⁡(πx)/(πx)\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x), with its limiting value one at zero.

The transform describes field or voltage amplitude. A power spectrum uses its squared magnitude, |P(f)|2=T2sinc⁡2(fT)|P(f)|^2=T^2\operatorname{sinc}^2(fT). For independent, zero-mean symbols of mean squared amplitude 𝔼|am|2\mathbb{E}|a_m|^2 sent every TT seconds, Sx(f)=𝔼|am|2T|P(f)|2.\begin{equation} S_x(f)=\frac{\mathbb{E}|a_m|^2}{T}|P(f)|^2. \end{equation} The expectation 𝔼\mathbb{E} means a probability-weighted average. With symbols measured in volts, SxS_x has units V2^2/Hz. A deterministic pulse has an energy spectrum; a continuing random symbol stream has a power spectral density under these assumptions.

For T=1μT=1~\mus the first nulls occur at ±1\pm1 MHz: the full main lobe is 2 MHz wide. Halving TT doubles those frequencies. A first-null width describes the main lobe; the rectangular pulse’s sidelobes extend to arbitrarily high frequency. A triangular pulse obtained by convolving rectangles instead has a sinc-squared amplitude transform and a sinc-to-the-fourth power envelope. This is the time–frequency connection behind the fast rectangular-chip model used later for spreading codes.

Put the FFT on the Correct Frequency Grid

Fig. 67 shows the two numerical traps emphasized on November 17: knowing which frequency belongs to each FFT value, and putting the zero-frequency component in the expected place [source]. These matter when checking a pulse against a spectral mask or using a Fourier transform to calculate an aperture pattern.

Take NN samples pn=p(nΔt)p_n=p(n\Delta t), spaced by Δt\Delta t seconds. The sampling rate and the Fourier-bin spacing are fs=1Δt,Δf=fsN=1NΔt.\begin{equation} f_s=\frac{1}{\Delta t},\qquad \Delta f=\frac{f_s}{N}=\frac{1}{N\Delta t}. \end{equation} The ordinary unnormalized forward DFT is Xk=∑n=0N−1pne−j2πkn/NX_k=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}p_n e^{-j2\pi kn/N}. Multiplication by Δt\Delta t gives the Riemann-sum approximation to the continuous Fourier transform: P(fk)≃ΔtXk.\begin{equation} P(f_k)\simeq \Delta t\,X_k. \end{equation} The approximation concerns a sampled, finite observation window; sufficiently rapid sampling and a sufficiently long window are still needed. For voltage samples, XkX_k has volts under this convention, while PP has V s. A continuing random stream’s PSD needs the symbol statistics and the normalization already stated in Fig. 66; a plotted FFT magnitude alone is not a PSD.

For even NN, native FFT order starts at DC, runs through positive frequencies, then stores the negative-frequency bins. The Nyquist bin is conventionally labeled −fs/2-f_s/2 in a full two-sided grid. Applying fftshift to both the frequency vector and the transform puts the negative frequencies first and DC in the center. It reorders the same information [source]. In the figure, N=64N=64 and Δt=0.05\Delta t=0.05 s give fs=20f_s=20 Hz and Δf=0.3125\Delta f=0.3125 Hz. Adding zeros before the FFT produces a denser plotted grid but does not lengthen the measured pulse record or resolve features the original window could not distinguish.

Zero ISI at Decision Times

Fig. 68 shows the receiver’s timing requirement: at the correct decision time the neighboring pulse contributions vanish, while a quarter-symbol timing error lets them enter the sample. The design target is therefore the value of the combined response at specified instants.

The transmitted pulse, the propagation channel, and the receiver filter all shape the final response. Call their combined normalized response g(t)g(t). Choose the receiver’s time origin to include the common system delay, so symbol nn is read at t=nTt=nT. Let w[n]w[n] be the noise in that decision sample. The receiver reads y[n]=∑mamg((n−m)T)+w[n].\begin{equation} y[n]=\sum_m a_m g((n-m)T)+w[n]. \end{equation} Here nn identifies the symbol being decided, while mm runs over every symbol that might contribute. The desired term has m=nm=n, giving ang(0)a_ng(0). Terms with m≠nm\ne n are contributions from neighboring symbols.

To isolate the desired symbol at each decision time, normalize its response to one and require the neighboring responses to be zero: g(0)=1,g(kT)=0for every nonzero integer k.\begin{equation} g(0)=1,\qquad g(kT)=0\quad\text{for every nonzero integer }k. \end{equation} The integer kk counts symbol intervals away from a pulse’s center. These are the zero-intersymbol-interference, or zero-ISI, conditions. Figure 65 shows these conditions in the individual pulses and their sum. Between decisions, the overlapping pulses form the continuous waveform. At the decision instants, their zero crossings isolate the desired symbols. A timing error moves the decision away from the zeros, allowing neighboring symbols to interfere.

Pulse Tails and Bandwidth

Fig. 69 shows the price of shortening a pulse’s distant tails: the raised-cosine spectrum occupies a wider band as rolloff increases. A designer chooses that tradeoff while preserving the regularly spaced zeros needed for symbol decisions.

An ideal example is the normalized sinc response g(t)=sinc⁡(t/T)g(t)=\operatorname{sinc}(t/T), using sinc⁡(x)=sin⁡(πx)πx,sinc⁡(0)=1.\begin{equation} \operatorname{sinc}(x)=\frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x},\qquad \operatorname{sinc}(0)=1. \end{equation} In this definition xx is a dimensionless argument, such as t/Tt/T. Nonzero integer arguments make the numerator zero. The apparent division by zero at the origin has the limit one. That is why sinc pulses can overlap while preserving the samples: it is the same property that reconstructed a sampled signal in Fig. 59, now used to transmit symbols.

For the peak-normalized combined response, the formula is gRC(t)=sinc⁡(t/T)cos⁡(παt/T)1−(2αt/T)2,0≤α≤1.\begin{equation} g_{\mathrm{RC}}(t)=\operatorname{sinc}(t/T) \frac{\cos(\pi\alpha t/T)}{1-(2\alpha t/T)^2},\quad 0\le\alpha\le1. \end{equation} The pulse argument t/Tt/T and rolloff α\alpha are dimensionless, and gRC(0)=1g_{\mathrm{RC}}(0)=1. At t=±T/(2α)t=\pm T/(2\alpha), use the continuous limit (π/4)sinc⁡[1/(2α)](\pi/4)\operatorname{sinc}[1/(2\alpha)] rather than dividing two zeros. With α=0\alpha=0 the expression reduces to sinc. The November 12 board formula uses T=1/(2f0)T=1/(2f_0) and α=κ\alpha=\kappa, with a leading scale 2f02f_0; that amplitude convention changes the peak scale, not the zero locations or normalized shape [source].

The ideal sinc stretches forever in both time directions. A real system needs a delayed, finite approximation, and sharp truncation changes the behavior. A raised-cosine combined response makes a more practical bandwidth-versus-tail tradeoff. Its rolloff factor α\alpha runs from zero to one. Increasing α\alpha spends additional bandwidth while making distant pulse tails decay more quickly. The spectrum’s one-sided baseband edge is (1+α)Rs/2(1+\alpha)R_s/2 Hz. A real RF signal translated around a positive carrier occupies both sides of that carrier, giving the usual full occupied-width model BRF=(1+α)Rs.\begin{equation} B_{\mathrm{RF}}=(1+\alpha)R_s. \end{equation} Here BRFB_{\mathrm{RF}} is bandwidth in hertz.

Read Timing Margin From an Eye Diagram

Fig. 70 shows what the extra bandwidth of a larger rolloff buys. An eye diagram overlays many short slices of the received waveform, all aligned to the symbol clock. At the correct decision instant every trace passes exactly through +1+1 or −1-1: zero ISI. The open region between the upper and lower bundles is the eye. Its vertical clearance shows the displayed waveform’s amplitude margin at a chosen sampling time, while horizontal clearance shows its timing tolerance. A finite collection of random traces samples these margins; a guaranteed all-pattern bound requires examining every allowed neighboring-symbol contribution.

A quarter symbol late, the neighbours’ tails no longer pass through zero. In the plotted realization the smallest observed half-opening is 0.120.12 for α=0.25\alpha=0.25 and 0.640.64 for α=1\alpha=1. A half-opening is the distance from zero to the nearer trace; the full vertical eye opening is twice that distance. With the desired symbol fixed, the worst interfering sign pattern is found by adding the absolute values of the other pulse contributions, not by taking a minimum over this random sample. Rolloff therefore trades bandwidth, 1.25Rs1.25R_s against 2Rs2R_s, for timing tolerance and reduced distant-tail contributions in a finite filter.

A Matched Filter Recognizes a Pulse

Fig. 71 shows a receiver comparing a noisy segment with a known pulse template. Time reversal and conjugation arrange the convolution so matching pieces add at one chosen decision instant; the goal is a reliable amplitude estimate at that instant.

If we know what an isolated pulse should look like, we can compare a noisy received segment with that template. Multiply corresponding values and add them. A matching pulse builds a large score because its weighted contributions reinforce. For zero-mean white noise, the noise contributions cancel in expectation. The filter maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio at the chosen decision instant.

The earlier p(t)p(t) describes a dimensionless shaping pulse. Here the filter sees a physical received pulse. Let vr(t)v_r(t) be its voltage across load resistance RLR_L and use pr(t)=vr(t)/RLp_r(t)=v_r(t)/\sqrt{R_L}, measured in W\sqrt{\mathrm{W}}. Its squared integral is then energy in joules. For this known pulse in additive white noise, let h(t)h(t) describe how the receiver filter responds to a very short input. This is its impulse response. Choose the decision time T0T_0 in seconds and a constant KK to set the desired gain. A star on a complex value means conjugation: reverse the sign of its imaginary component. The matched-filter impulse response is h(t)=Kpr*(T0−t).\begin{equation} h(t)=Kp_r^*(T_0-t). \end{equation} A real pulse needs only the time reversal and delay. Figure 71 uses an asymmetric real pulse so the reversal is visible.

A filter computes convolution, which slides a time-reversed copy of its impulse response across the input. Reversing the template in hh compensates for that reversal. If the received waveform in the same power-normalized units is rE(t)r_E(t) and τ\tau is a dummy time variable, the output at T0T_0 becomes y(T0)=K∫rE(τ)pr*(τ)dτ.\begin{equation} y(T_0)=K\int r_E(\tau)p_r^*(\tau)\,d\tau. \end{equation} The integral adds matching products over the pulse. With a noise-free matching input rE=prr_E=p_r, it becomes Ep=∫|pr|2dtE_p=\int|p_r|^2dt, measured in joules. For an input rE=aprr_E=a p_r, choosing K=1/EpK=1/E_p makes the output an estimate of the relative amplitude aa. This physical template and the earlier dimensionless shaping pulse have different units.

Matched filtering optimizes an isolated pulse’s decision SNR under the white-noise assumptions. For this real received pulse in real white noise of two-sided density N0/2N_0/2, the signal score is EpE_p and the output noise variance is (N0/2)Ep(N_0/2)E_p when K=1K=1. Their ratio is SNRMF=Ep2(N0/2)Ep=2EpN0.\begin{equation} \mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{MF}}=\frac{E_p^2}{(N_0/2)E_p}=\frac{2E_p}{N_0}. \end{equation} It depends on the pulse energy alone; every known pulse shape with the same energy can reach it under these assumptions. In the next chapter, two unit-energy I/Q coordinates each carry a noise variance N0/2N_0/2; combining their signal energies gives the symbol metric Es/N0E_s/N_0. Stating the real or complex convention keeps the factor of two attached to the quantity it describes.

Let Transmit and Receive Filters Share the Shaping

Fig. 72 shows how a practical pair creates the received pulse used in the earlier eye diagrams. The transmitter controls emitted spectrum, while the receiver also collects energy with a matched filter. Sharing the response lets the same pair meet both goals [source].

For the ideal flat channel, write PTX(f)P_{\mathrm{TX}}(f) for the transmit-filter response and HRX(f)H_{\mathrm{RX}}(f) for the receive-filter response. Choose matched root-raised-cosine responses so that GRC(f)=PTX(f)HRX(f).\begin{equation} G_{\mathrm{RC}}(f)=P_{\mathrm{TX}}(f)H_{\mathrm{RX}}(f). \end{equation} Multiplication in frequency corresponds to convolution in time. The combined response gRC(t)g_{\mathrm{RC}}(t) has gRC(0)=1g_{\mathrm{RC}}(0)=1 and zeros at nonzero integer multiples of TT after accounting for the common delay. The individual RRC pulses need not have those same zeros. Matched filtering selects a high-SNR sample for an isolated known pulse; zero ISI describes the combined stream response at all the symbol decisions. Channel distortion, finite filters and clock error can disturb that ideal result.

Find the Packet and Align the Decision Clock

Fig. 73 shows the timing problem behind every matched-filter sample: a receiver must first find where the packet starts, then keep its decisions aligned with the transmitter’s symbol intervals. The November 12 discussion connects this synchronization operation with the correlation already used for spreading codes [source].

A packet can contain a known preamble or header pattern. Let p[k]p[k] be its dimensionless reference samples, let r[k]r[k] be received complex-baseband samples in volts, and let NhN_h be the number of reference samples. A trial integer offset qq gives the average correlation C[q]=1Nh∑k=0Nh−1r[k+q]p*[k].\begin{equation} C[q]=\frac1{N_h}\sum_{k=0}^{N_h-1}r[k+q]p^*[k]. \end{equation} The star denotes complex conjugation. The receiver searches the magnitude of this score across possible offsets; with this normalization the score has voltage units. If the ADC interval is TADCT_{\mathrm{ADC}} seconds, one offset step represents TADCT_{\mathrm{ADC}} seconds. The figure uses a toy sampled pattern; practical preambles, oversampling, carrier-offset estimation and interpolation refine the estimate.

After estimating a start time t̂0\widehat t_0 and symbol interval T̂\widehat T, the receiver schedules decision nn at t̂n=t̂0+nT̂,en=(t̂0−t0)+n(T̂−T).\begin{equation} \widehat t_n=\widehat t_0+n\widehat T,\quad e_n=(\widehat t_0-t_0)+n(\widehat T-T). \end{equation} The integer nn counts symbols and ene_n is timing error in seconds. An initial offset affects every decision; an interval mismatch accumulates along the packet. For T=1μT=1~\mus and a 10-parts-per-million interval error, T̂−T=10\widehat T-T=10 ps. After 1000 symbols the accumulated error is 10 ns, or 0.01T0.01T. Tracking can update the clock estimate rather than allowing that drift to grow. The matched filter improves the chosen sample’s SNR; synchronization chooses and maintains the appropriate sample times. With pulses shaped, filtered and sampled at the right instants, the remaining choice is which values each pulse may carry.

chapters.title: Give the Bits a Ride on a Radio Wave
chapters.label: sec:modulation
chapters.html:
Fig. 74 shows the work a modem must perform between an information-bit stream and an RF link. The transmitter protects, maps, shapes and upconverts the data; the receiver needs a compatible frequency reference, timing, filtering and decision process to recover it.

The digital data is represented by a stream of bits. A modulator maps groups of bits to allowed radio waveforms; a demodulator recognizes the chosen waveform after it has traveled through the channel. Together they are a modem. A codec compresses and decompresses the information; a modem sends and receives its physical representation. These names identify the information-processing and radio-waveform stages [source].

Choose Rate, Pulse and Constellation Together

Fig. 75 shows why specifying a bit rate alone does not specify a digital radio signal. The application sets an information-rate need; the designer must also choose how often symbols arrive, what shape each contributes, and which complex amplitudes the symbols may take [source].

The same baseband construction connects all three choices: xbb(t)=∑mamp(t−mT),T=1/Rs.\begin{equation} x_{\mathrm{bb}}(t)=\sum_m a_m p(t-mT),\qquad T=1/R_s. \end{equation} The integer mm identifies a symbol; ama_m is its chosen I/Q value, pp is the normalized pulse, and RsR_s is the symbol rate in symbols/s. With dimensionless pp, both ama_m and xbbx_{\mathrm{bb}} have the same amplitude units. The shift mTmT places that pulse at its symbol time. Selecting RsR_s changes the time scale, selecting pp changes the transitions and spectrum, and selecting the constellation restricts the available ama_m values.

For example, QPSK supplies four alternatives and therefore two coded bits per symbol. At 1 Msymbol/s it carries 2 Mbit/s before coding and other overhead. With raised-cosine rolloff α=0.25\alpha=0.25, the ideal RF width is (1+α)Rs=1.25(1+\alpha)R_s=1.25 MHz. Each number answers a different question: how many labels per second, how many bits per label, and how much radio bandwidth the chosen pulse requires.

Two Knobs Called I and Q

Fig. 76 shows one allowed complex symbol and the two real carrier components that create it. A practical radio needs control of both amplitude and phase; two perpendicular coordinates provide that control while keeping the emitted voltage real.

Start with a carrier, a rapidly oscillating cosine at frequency fcf_c hertz. Here the subscript cc means carrier, and tt is time in seconds. We can multiply that cosine by a slowly changing amplitude I(t)I(t). We can also use a sine at the same frequency, shifted a quarter cycle from the cosine, with a second weight Q(t)Q(t). These weights are called the in-phase and quadrature components. Under our chosen complex-exponential convention, the real transmitted voltage is s(t)=I(t)cos⁡(2πfct)−Q(t)sin⁡(2πfct).\begin{equation} s(t)=I(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct)-Q(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct). \end{equation} The letter ss names the transmitted signal, and II and QQ have the same voltage units as ss in this expression. The minus sign is a convention that follows directly from taking the real part of [I(t)+jQ(t)]ej2πfct.\begin{equation} [I(t)+jQ(t)]e^{j2\pi f_ct}. \end{equation} Multiply the two factors using Euler’s formula: the real terms are Icos⁡(2πfct)I\cos(2\pi f_ct) and −Qsin⁡(2πfct)-Q\sin(2\pi f_ct). Taking the real part therefore gives the transmitted voltage in the equation above. A book using a different quadrature convention may write a plus sign; its receiver must use the matching convention.

Think of I+jQI+jQ as one point on a plane. Its horizontal coordinate selects the cosine weight; its vertical coordinate selects the negative-sine weight. If AA is the point’s distance from the origin and φ\varphi its angle, then I=Acos⁡φI=A\cos\varphi and Q=Asin⁡φQ=A\sin\varphi. For fixed weights, their sum is Acos⁡(2πfct+φ)A\cos(2\pi f_ct+\varphi). The two weights select the amplitude and phase of the resulting radio waveform.

Fig. 77 shows how a receiver with a synchronized carrier recovers the two weights. Multiply s(t)s(t) by 2cos⁡(2πfct)2\cos(2\pi f_ct) and use 2cos⁡2x=1+cos⁡2x2\cos^2x=1+\cos2x and 2sin⁡xcos⁡x=sin⁡2x2\sin x\cos x=\sin2x: 2s(t)cos⁡(2πfct)=I+Icos⁡(4πfct)−Qsin⁡(4πfct).\begin{equation} 2s(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct)=I+I\cos(4\pi f_ct)-Q\sin(4\pi f_ct). \end{equation} The first term is the wanted baseband weight; the other two oscillate at 2fc2f_c, and a low-pass filter removes them. Multiplying by −2sin⁡(2πfct)-2\sin(2\pi f_ct) instead leaves QQ plus its own 2fc2f_c terms. The cosine and sine are orthogonal over each carrier cycle, so each branch recovers its own weight with no leakage from the other. If the receiver oscillator leads the transmitter by ϵ\epsilon, the recovered point rotates by −ϵ-\epsilon. For example, a 90∘90^\circ lead turns a transmitted (I,Q)=(1,0)(I,Q)=(1,0) into (0,−1)(0,-1) under this mixer convention.

Separate Carrier Alignment From Symbol Timing

Fig. 78 shows why recovering the carrier and finding the symbol clock are separate tasks. Both affect the decision, but they change different parts of the measurement.

With the receiver oscillator ahead in phase by ϵ\epsilon, the recovered complex value is multiplied by e−jϵe^{-j\epsilon}. A constant offset rotates the constellation; a frequency offset makes that angle accumulate over time. A timing offset instead samples g(t)g(t) away from its intended zero-ISI grid, admitting adjacent-symbol contributions. Carrier tracking estimates the oscillation’s phase and frequency; symbol timing estimates where to sample the pulse. Correcting one leaves the other task to be completed.

A Carrier Frequency Error Keeps Rotating the Point

Fig. 79 shows why a header that aligns the constellation once does not by itself hold the alignment throughout the packet. The November 17 example is a one-part-per-million mismatch at 1 GHz, which is a 1 kHz carrier-frequency error [source].

Let Δf=fLO−fc\Delta f=f_{\mathrm{LO}}-f_c be receiver-reference frequency minus transmitter frequency, in hertz. If the receiver starts ahead in phase by ϵ0\epsilon_0, its phase error is ϵ(t)=ϵ0+2πΔft.\begin{equation} \epsilon(t)=\epsilon_0+2\pi\Delta f\,t. \end{equation} With the guide’s cosine/minus-sine convention, its recovered complex baseband is multiplied by e−jϵ(t)e^{-j\epsilon(t)}. The fixed phase correction needed at the packet start grows into a time-dependent correction. A known header can help estimate both ϵ0\epsilon_0 and Δf\Delta f; multiplying by the estimated inverse rotation compensates them. Residual frequency error and random phase noise remain practical tracking tasks. At 1 kHz, even an initially perfect phase estimate slips by 90∘90^\circ in only 0.250.25 ms. Sampling the pulse at the correct symbol times is a separate requirement.

Turn RF Voltage Into Symbol Energy

Fig. 80 shows the change of units behind an energy-normalized constellation. Start with actual I/Q voltages; finish with coordinates whose squared length records how much energy arrived during the symbol.

For constant II and QQ over an illustrative symbol interval TT, with an integer number of carrier cycles and load resistance RLR_L, averaging the squared RF voltage gives C=I2+Q22RL,Es=CT.\begin{equation} C=\frac{I^2+Q^2}{2R_L},\qquad E_s=CT. \end{equation} The cross term averages to zero and each carrier’s squared average is one half. Using unit-energy carrier functions gives coordinates aI=IT2RL,aQ=QT2RL.\begin{equation} a_I=I\sqrt{\frac{T}{2R_L}},\qquad a_Q=Q\sqrt{\frac{T}{2R_L}}. \end{equation} These coordinates have units J\sqrt{\mathrm{J}}, so aI2+aQ2=Esa_I^2+a_Q^2=E_s. For one isolated symbol with a real dimensionless shaping pulse p(t)p(t), use its equivalent squared-pulse duration 𝒯p=∫|p(t)|2dt,Es=I2+Q22RL𝒯p.\begin{equation} \mathcal{T}_p=\int |p(t)|^2dt,\qquad E_s=\frac{I^2+Q^2}{2R_L}\mathcal{T}_p. \end{equation} Here 𝒯p\mathcal{T}_p is in seconds. With carrier-cycle averaging, the general coordinate scale is aI=I𝒯p/(2RL)a_I=I\sqrt{\mathcal{T}_p/(2R_L)} and aQ=Q𝒯p/(2RL)a_Q=Q\sqrt{\mathcal{T}_p/(2R_L)}. A unit-height rectangular pulse gives 𝒯p=T\mathcal{T}_p=T, producing the illustrated formula. A shaped pulse uses its own squared integral instead. The geometric point stays the same after a common scale change; the units and energy accounting become explicit.

In a two-coordinate, unit-energy basis, real AWGN of two-sided density N0/2N_0/2 projects onto independent noise samples nIn_I and nQn_Q, each with variance N0/2N_0/2 in joules. The total complex noise energy has mean N0N_0. Dividing the coordinates by Es\sqrt{E_s} makes average signal energy one and gives per-axis variance N0/(2Es)N_0/(2E_s). The running example’s carrier power is 2.73×10−132.73\times10^{-13} W; at 2 Msym/s, T=0.5μT=0.5~\mus and Es=1.37×10−19E_s=1.37\times10^{-19} J. Its relative noise standard deviation is therefore N0/(2Es)=0.121\sqrt{N_0/(2E_s)}=0.121, the scale used in the noisy constellation below. This connects the physical link power to the same decisions drawn on the normalized axes.

Why a Carrier Creates Sidebands

Fig. 81 shows how multiplying a low-frequency message by a carrier moves its spectral content to two neighboring RF frequencies. This translation is what lets a baseband waveform use an antenna and a chosen radio band.

Before choosing digital symbols, take a quick analog detour to see what multiplication does. Let a simple message be m(t)=cos⁡(2πfmt)m(t)=\cos(2\pi f_mt), with dimensionless amplitude and message frequency fmf_m in hertz. Use a carrier at frequency fcf_c hertz, higher than fmf_m, and let AcA_c be its reference voltage amplitude in volts. Multiplying the message by the carrier gives sAM(t)=Acm(t)cos⁡(2πfct)s_{\mathrm{AM}}(t)=A_cm(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct). The subscript AM labels this amplitude-modulated waveform. The cosine product identity reveals its ingredients: sAM(t)=Ac2cos⁡[2π(fc−fm)t]+Ac2cos⁡[2π(fc+fm)t].\begin{equation} s_{\mathrm{AM}}(t)=\frac{A_c}{2}\cos[2\pi(f_c-f_m)t] +\frac{A_c}{2}\cos[2\pi(f_c+f_m)t]. \end{equation} The message tone has become two RF tones: a lower sideband at fc−fmf_c-f_m and an upper sideband at fc+fmf_c+f_m. Each cosine has amplitude Ac/2A_c/2 volts. A general message contains many frequencies, so each produces shifted contributions around the carrier. That is how a low-frequency message moves to a radio-frequency band. This particular example is double-sideband suppressed-carrier modulation: the zero-mean message places the transmitted power in the two sidebands, shown in Figure 81. Conventional AM adds a constant offset to the message, introducing a carrier component at fcf_c. The simple product picture is also the basis for the receiver’s mixing operation above.

Fig. 82 follows the November 17 board from a message spectrum to its radio-channel width [source]. With a real message m(t)m(t) and a cosine carrier, multiplication gives S(f)=[M(f−fc)+M(f+fc)]/2S(f)=[M(f-f_c)+M(f+f_c)]/2, where M(f)M(f) is the message transform. If M(f)M(f) ends at ±B\pm B and fc>Bf_c>B, the positive RF band runs from fc−Bf_c-B to fc+Bf_c+B. Its width is 2B2B. The cluster around −fc-f_c is the conjugate mirror, S(−f)=S*(f)S(-f)=S^*(f), required for a real transmitted voltage. Counting it again would double the assigned radio bandwidth.

Each positive-frequency sideband of this real message carries the information needed to recover the other. Keeping the upper sideband and its negative-frequency mirror gives an ideal single-sideband signal of width BB. Coherent mixing, low-pass filtering and gain adjustment recover the message. A vestigial-sideband filter eases the transition near the carrier by retaining a small part of the lower sideband. In the drawn example it passes 2.75 to 4 MHz. Its mirrored transition slopes add to a constant after coherent mixing, so message frequencies retain the same relative gain. A general I/Q signal can put independent information in the two baseband coordinates; arbitrarily dropping a sideband from that signal can discard information.

Choose the Symbol Constellation

Fig. 83 shows the central energy-versus-throughput choice: fitting more symbol alternatives into the same average energy leaves smaller gaps between neighboring decisions. Read each point as a permitted I/Q value before reading its bit label.

Choose a finite set of allowed I/Q points and we have a constellation. Each allowed point is a symbol. If the menu contains MM equally usable choices, where MM is a power of two, each symbol can label log⁡2M\log_2 M bits. Binary phase-shift keying, BPSK, has two opposite phases and carries one bit per symbol. Quadrature phase-shift keying, QPSK, has four phases and carries two. Phase-shift keying, PSK, changes phase; quadrature amplitude modulation, QAM, uses both amplitude and phase. Amplitude-and-phase-shift keying, APSK, arranges choices on multiple rings.

A larger constellation can label more bits per symbol. To compare its noise tolerance with another constellation, use the same average symbol energy: the same average energy spent during one symbol interval. In an energy-normalized I/Q picture, that means the same average squared distance from the origin. Adding choices within this energy budget generally reduces the spacing between neighboring points. A smaller gap requires a smaller noise displacement to cross a decision boundary.

Put numbers on the gap. With average symbol energy EsE_s, the QPSK points sit at (±1,±1)Es/2(\pm1,\pm1)\sqrt{E_s/2}, so neighbours are dmin=2Es=1.41Esd_{\min}=\sqrt{2E_s}=1.41\sqrt{E_s} apart. 16-QAM uses levels ±1\pm1 and ±3\pm3 on each axis, scaled by Es/10\sqrt{E_s/10} so the average energy stays EsE_s; its neighbours are dmin=2Es/10=0.63Esd_{\min}=2\sqrt{E_s/10}=0.63\sqrt{E_s} apart. Restoring the QPSK spacing would take (1.41/0.63)2=5(1.41/0.63)^2=5 times the symbol energy, about 7.0 dB, in exchange for twice the bits per symbol.

Gray labeling is useful because neighboring-point errors are common at reasonably good signal quality: a one-step mistake can then corrupt one bit instead of several. Differential schemes encode changes between successive phases, reducing dependence on an absolute phase reference, with their own performance tradeoffs.

Fig. 84 shows what the constellation’s labels do after the geometric decision. Keep one word through the complete step instead of changing alphabets between the bit stream and the point.

On each axis, assign increasing levels (−3,−1,+1,+3)/10(-3,-1,+1,+3)/\sqrt{10} the Gray labels (00,01,11,10)(00,01,11,10). Put the I bits first and the Q bits second. Word 1101 selects (+1,−1)/10(+1,-1)/\sqrt{10}. The shown illustrative noise vector (0.42,0.10)(0.42,0.10) in the normalized coordinates moves it to approximately (0.736,−0.216)(0.736,-0.216). The nearest I level is now 3/103/\sqrt{10}, labeled 10, while the Q label remains 01. The decision is 1001: one symbol error and one bit error. This single chosen displacement illustrates labeling; it is separate from the statistical AWGN trial that follows.

Frequency-shift keying, FSK, represents labels by selecting among carrier frequencies. The optional review’s minimum-shift-keying convention uses two tones with full separation Rb/2R_b/2, where RbR_b is the transmitted binary bit rate in bits/s. Each tone lies Rb/4R_b/4 from their center frequency. Minimum-shift keying, MSK, maintains continuous phase; the two-tone separation and the single-tone deviation are different quantities. Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing, OFDM, uses many subcarriers. If TuT_u is a useful symbol duration in seconds, adjacent subcarriers spaced by 1/Tu1/T_u hertz are orthogonal over that interval. Their spectra may overlap while their ideal decision measurements remain separable. A guard interval adds time, so it also consumes some net throughput.

Encode the Change Between Successive Phases

Fig. 85 shows the information moving from a point’s absolute angle to the angle between consecutive points. In ordinary coherent QPSK, a word labels one allowed phase; in differential QPSK, DQPSK, it labels a phase increment [source].

Use the lecture’s illustrative mapping 10↦0,11↦+π/2,00↦−π/2,01↦π.\begin{equation} 10\mapsto0,\quad 11\mapsto+\pi/2,\quad 00\mapsto-\pi/2,\quad 01\mapsto\pi. \end{equation} These labels are a declared convention; another implementation may assign them differently. For selected increment Δϕk\Delta\phi_k, transmit ϕk=(ϕk−1+Δϕk)mod⁡2π,sk=Esejϕk.\begin{equation} \phi_k=(\phi_{k-1}+\Delta\phi_k)\bmod2\pi,\qquad s_k=\sqrt{E_s}\,e^{j\phi_k}. \end{equation} The subscript kk counts symbols, and EsE_s is symbol energy in joules. A reference symbol supplies the starting phase; after that, the same word can lead to different absolute phases depending on the preceding symbol. The plot unwraps angles only to make the sequence easy to follow.

For a noise-free received value rk=ske−jϵkr_k=s_ke^{-j\epsilon_k}, multiplication by the previous value’s conjugate gives rkrk−1*=Esej(Δϕk−ϵk+ϵk−1).\begin{equation} r_kr_{k-1}^*=E_s e^{j(\Delta\phi_k-\epsilon_k+\epsilon_{k-1})}. \end{equation} A constant unknown carrier phase cancels. Frequency offset still contributes a phase step of magnitude 2π|Δf|Ts2\pi|\Delta f|T_s between symbols of duration TsT_s, and symbol-clock alignment remains necessary. With noise present, the previous received symbol is also noisy: comparing two samples costs detection performance relative to an appropriate coherent reference. Differential encoding and differential detection are separate choices; this comparison describes the two-sample differential receiver discussed in class.

Distinguish a Fixed Rotation From Alternating Phase Sets

Fig. 86 shows two uses of a 45∘45^\circ angle that look similar on a board but describe different operations. The November 17 notes first rotate the axial QPSK drawing into the quadrants, then introduce a differential variant [source].

A fixed rotation replaces every point ss by sejπ/4se^{j\pi/4}. Four choices remain four choices, and the minimum distance and ideal coherent AWGN performance stay the same after the receiver aligns its reference. It is still two bits per symbol. Gray labels can be carried along with the rotation without changing neighboring-bit relationships.

In π/4\pi/4-DQPSK, the allowed changes are Δϕ∈{±π/4,±3π/4}\Delta\phi\in\{\pm\pi/4,\pm3\pi/4\}. Successive symbols alternate between two four-point sets separated by 45∘45^\circ [source]. There are eight possible phase locations across time, but only four permitted next steps from any current phase, so the rate remains two bits per symbol. Direct 180∘180^\circ symbol-to-symbol jumps are avoided. The exact continuous envelope between symbol instants still depends on pulse shaping; equal-radius constellation endpoints alone do not guarantee a constant-envelope RF waveform.

Noise Moves the Received Point

Fig. 87 shows what a decision does with noise. The receiver’s matched-filter sample is the transmitted point plus a random displacement. In additive white Gaussian noise, the in-phase and quadrature displacements are independent Gaussian variables, each with variance N0/2N_0/2 on the energy-normalized scale. The best decision for equally likely points chooses the nearest allowed point. For square constellations that rule reduces to separate thresholds on II and QQ, placed halfway between neighbouring levels.

At the running example’s Es/N0=15.3E_s/N_0=15.3 dB, the noise standard deviation is 0.12Es0.12\sqrt{E_s} per axis. QPSK’s boundaries lie 0.71Es0.71\sqrt{E_s} from each point, almost six standard deviations away; this realization has no errors among its 3000 QPSK symbols. The 16-QAM boundaries lie only 0.32Es0.32\sqrt{E_s} away, about 2.6 standard deviations, and 34 of its 3000 symbols cross a decision boundary. The comparison fixes average symbol energy, rather than information-bit rate or energy per useful bit.

Symbol-error rate, SER, counts wrong symbol decisions; bit-error rate, BER, counts wrong bits after those decisions are mapped back to labels. Gray labeling makes a nearest-neighbor mistake change one bit along the crossed axis. The figure’s counted mapped-bit errors are still before channel decoding. Under the stated coherent AWGN model, theoretical SER is finite: approximately 5.10×10−95.10\times10^{-9} for QPSK and 0.01340.0134 for 16-QAM at the unrounded operating point [source]. The observed counts are samples of that random process, rather than error-free guarantees.

The rate ledger below assumes a half-rate code to illustrate bookkeeping. Its code, decoder and error target are unspecified, so post-decoder BER and frame-error rate, FER, have not been evaluated. A demonstrated coded operating point requires those additional choices and a corresponding performance curve.

Multipath Makes Some Frequencies Harder Than Others

Fig. 88 shows the broadband-link problem raised in the November 12 discussion: echoes that add at one frequency can cancel at another. A single wideband waveform therefore passes through peaks and nulls rather than one constant channel gain [source].

Model a direct path and one echo with relative voltage amplitude aa and excess delay τ\tau seconds. The impulse response and frequency response are hch(t)=δ(t)+aδ(t−τ),Hch(f)=1+ae−j2πfτ.\begin{align} h_{\mathrm{ch}}(t)&=\delta(t)+a\delta(t-\tau),\\ H_{\mathrm{ch}}(f)&=1+a e^{-j2\pi f\tau}. \end{align} Here δ(t)\delta(t) is the unit-area impulse, with units 1/s, and HchH_{\mathrm{ch}} is a dimensionless voltage-transfer ratio. The exponential gives the echo’s frequency-dependent phase. For a real positive aa, |Hch(f)|2=1+a2+2acos⁡(2πfτ).\begin{equation} |H_{\mathrm{ch}}(f)|^2=1+a^2+2a\cos(2\pi f\tau). \end{equation} This power-transfer ratio repeats every 1/τ1/\tau Hz. Equal-strength paths, a=1a=1, can cancel completely at f=(2q+1)/(2τ)f=(2q+1)/(2\tau), where qq is any integer. A 1μ1~\mus excess delay gives a 1 MHz spacing between successive fading cycles. The plotted a=0.9a=0.9 leaves deep but nonzero nulls.

OFDM divides the band into many orthogonal narrow subcarriers. Over a useful symbol interval TuT_u, spacing Δf=1/Tu\Delta f=1/T_u makes the ideal carrier basis functions orthogonal.

Fig. 89 shows why the subcarriers can overlap. A tone that lasts TuT_u seconds has a sinc-shaped spectrum with zeros every 1/Tu1/T_u hertz from its centre. Spacing the subcarriers by exactly 1/Tu1/T_u puts every neighbour’s zero at each subcarrier’s centre. This is the zero-ISI idea of Chapter VI moved from time to frequency. With a 1 μ\mus echo the channel gain repeats every 1 MHz, while LTE’s 15 kHz subcarriers are each narrow enough to see a nearly constant gain. A cyclic prefix at least as long as the modeled channel delay spread can preserve that useful structure under the usual synchronized, approximately time-invariant channel assumptions. Each subcarrier then has its own gain and signal quality, which can inform equalization and resource or bit allocation. The prefix consumes time, and a deep null still costs useful signal energy. This connects the class’s LTE example to pulse design, rate overhead, and channel-dependent adaptation without assuming that every frequency is equally useful.

Follow One Bit Stream Through the Rate Ledger

Fig. 90 shows why a single application can have several different rates along one link. Compression, protection and constellation mapping change different counts, so a bandwidth calculation must follow the stream through every conversion.

We have already separated sampling, quantization and compression. Now keep the bookkeeping alive through the radio. Let RrawR_{\mathrm{raw}} be the digital bit rate before compression, in bits/s, and 𝒞\mathcal{C} the compression factor defined as raw rate divided by compressed rate. The information rate after compression is Rinfo=Rraw/𝒞R_{\mathrm{info}}=R_{\mathrm{raw}}/\mathcal{C}. This definition matters because people sometimes use the phrase “compression ratio” in the reverse direction.

Channel coding adds structured redundancy to help a receiver correct errors. Define code rate rc=kc/ncr_c=k_c/n_c: the encoder accepts kck_c information bits and sends ncn_c coded bits. Both counts are dimensionless integers, so 0<rc≤10<r_c\le1 for the usual redundancy-adding code. The transmitted coded-bit rate is therefore Rcoded=Rinforc.\begin{equation} R_{\mathrm{coded}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{info}}}{r_c}. \end{equation} A rate-one-half code sends two coded bits per information bit. Dividing by one-half increases the transmitted rate; this is a different operation from compression. Here that rate is an assumed accounting choice, with no particular code or decoder performance implied.

The modulator packs log⁡2M\log_2 M coded bits into each symbol. Its symbol rate RsR_s, in symbols/s or baud, is Rs=Rcodedlog⁡2M,Rinfo=rcRslog⁡2M.\begin{equation} R_s=\frac{R_{\mathrm{coded}}}{\log_2 M},\qquad R_{\mathrm{info}}=r_cR_s\log_2 M. \end{equation} The subscript ss means symbol. One symbol takes T=1/RsT=1/R_s seconds. Each symbol groups log⁡2M\log_2 M coded bits. The ADC sample interval belongs to the earlier sampling stage and is set by its sampling rate.

Follow the numbers in Fig. 90. A 12 Mbit/s raw stream compressed by 𝒞=3\mathcal{C}=3 leaves Rinfo=4R_{\mathrm{info}}=4 Mbit/s. A rate-1/21/2 code doubles it to Rcoded=8R_{\mathrm{coded}}=8 Mbit/s. 16-QAM packs four coded bits per symbol, so Rs=2R_s=2 Msym/s, and a rolloff of 0.250.25 gives BRF=2.5B_{\mathrm{RF}}=2.5 MHz. These are the rates the running example uses below.

Recall the raised-cosine pulse picture in Fig. 69. With rolloff α\alpha, the ideal full RF bandwidth is BRF=(1+α)RsB_{\mathrm{RF}}=(1+\alpha)R_s. Here BRFB_{\mathrm{RF}} is measured in hertz and α\alpha is dimensionless. Higher constellation order can reduce the symbol rate needed to carry a fixed information rate. Its smaller decision spacing also requires better signal quality for a given error rate. In a real rate calculation, pilots, framing and guard intervals also take resources. The compact rate equations above deliberately omit those overheads.

Power, Noise Density and Energy Tell the Same Story in Different Units

Fig. 91 shows the two products behind receiver-quality calculations: noise density times bandwidth gives noise power, and average carrier power times a symbol interval gives symbol energy. The problem is to compare the link budget with a performance threshold using the same reference quantity.

The antenna and path-loss calculation give us received carrier power. Call that power CC, measured in watts. The receiver also collects noise. Let N0N_0 be the equivalent noise power spectral density, in watts per hertz, using a convention consistent with the receiver’s noise bandwidth BNB_N in hertz. If the density is approximately flat over that bandwidth, the collected noise power is N=N0BN.\begin{equation} N=N_0B_N. \end{equation} Here NN denotes receiver noise power. The carrier-to-noise ratio C/NC/N is dimensionless. Widening the receiver’s bandwidth collects more noise under this model at fixed carrier power.

Fig. 92 shows why the pulse’s occupied edges do not automatically specify receiver noise power. Every frequency contributes noise weighted by the squared receive-filter gain; the equivalent rectangle preserves that area.

With a consistent two-sided complex-baseband frequency coordinate and receive transfer function HRX(f)H_{\mathrm{RX}}(f), define the equivalent noise bandwidth as BN=∫−∞∞|HRX(f)|2df|HRX(0)|2.\begin{equation} B_N=\frac{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H_{\mathrm{RX}}(f)|^2\,df}{|H_{\mathrm{RX}}(0)|^2}. \end{equation} This integral has units of hertz. It describes noise area referred to the stated center-frequency gain; the signal power used in C/NC/N must use the same measurement reference. The later running C/NC/N example explicitly assumes a flat 2.52.5 MHz noise-measurement bandwidth. Its occupied RF width is also 2.52.5 MHz, but that equality is a chosen measurement assumption. The actual RRC matched filter’s noise area can differ, as the upper panel shows. The separate quantities C/N0C/N_0 and Es/N0E_s/N_0 do not require equating the occupied and noise bandwidths.

Thermal noise sets N0N_0. A receiver whose total noise equals that of a matched resistor at the system noise temperature TsysT_{\mathrm{sys}}, in kelvin, has N0=kBTsys,kB=1.38×10−23J/K,\begin{equation} N_0=k_BT_{\mathrm{sys}},\qquad k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}\ {\mathrm{J/K}}, \end{equation} where kBk_B is Boltzmann’s constant; in decibels, kBk_B is −228.6-228.6 dBW/(K⋅\cdotHz). At Tsys=290T_{\mathrm{sys}}=290 K, N0=4.0×10−21N_0=4.0\times10^{-21} W/Hz, or −204.0-204.0 dBW/Hz. Antenna noise, cable loss and the amplifier’s noise figure all raise TsysT_{\mathrm{sys}}.

Dividing carrier power by noise density produces C/N0C/N_0, which has units of hertz. It is a useful bandwidth-independent link quantity under the flat-noise model. To calculate it from a measured C/NC/N, restore the bandwidth used for that measurement: CN0=CNBN.\begin{equation} \frac{C}{N_0}=\frac{C}{N}B_N. \end{equation} Next ask how much energy we receive during one symbol. Average energy equals average power times time, so Es=CT=C/RsE_s=CT=C/R_s, where EsE_s is symbol energy in joules. Dividing by the noise density gives EsN0=C/N0Rs.\begin{equation} \frac{E_s}{N_0}=\frac{C/N_0}{R_s}. \end{equation} The hertz in C/N0C/N_0 cancels the symbols-per-second time scale numerically; symbol counts are dimensionless. The result is an energy ratio. Likewise, allocating the carrier energy to information bits gives Eb,infoN0=C/N0Rinfo,\begin{equation} \frac{E_{b,\mathrm{info}}}{N_0}=\frac{C/N_0}{R_{\mathrm{info}}}, \end{equation} where Eb,infoE_{b,\mathrm{info}} is energy per information bit. Energy per coded bit instead uses RcodedR_{\mathrm{coded}} in the denominator. Use the bit definition stated by the performance table.

In logarithmic units, C/N0C/N_0 is commonly written in dB-Hz. To obtain Es/N0E_s/N_0 in dB, subtract 10log⁡10Rs10\log_{10}R_s, entering the numerical symbol rate in symbols/s. To obtain Eb,info/N0E_{b,\mathrm{info}}/N_0 in dB, subtract 10log⁡10Rinfo10\log_{10}R_{\mathrm{info}}, with the information rate in bits/s. Convert the available link quantity to the performance table’s metric before comparing thresholds. C/NC/N uses noise power accumulated over bandwidth; Es/N0E_s/N_0 uses energy accumulated over a symbol interval.

Fig. 93 completes the running example, retaining extra digits in the teaching ledger. The Atlanta dish received C≃−125.631C\simeq-125.631 dBW. With Tsys=290T_{\mathrm{sys}}=290 K, N0≃−203.975N_0\simeq-203.975 dBW/Hz, so C/N0≃78.344C/N_0\simeq78.344 dB-Hz, or 78.378.3 dB-Hz after final rounding. The rate ledger’s 22 Msym/s gives Es/N0=15.334E_s/N_0=15.334 dB; its 44 Mbit/s information rate gives Eb,info/N0=12.324E_{b,\mathrm{info}}/N_0=12.324 dB. The independently assumed 2.52.5 MHz noise-measurement bandwidth gives C/N=14.365C/N=14.365 dB. Calculation uses unrounded inputs before rounding the reported result. Fig. 87 showed finite symbol-decision trials at that energy ratio.

Adaptation: Make the Best Choice the Link Can Support

Fig. 94 shows a link selecting higher-throughput modes only after signal quality clears their thresholds. Fade, distortion and uncertainty determine which step is presently usable and how much extra margin the choice should retain.

Adaptive modulation and coding, often called ACM, selects a modulation-and-code combination, or MODCOD, that the present link can support. A robust mode trades throughput for a greater chance of correct reception. A faster mode earns its extra throughput only when the received signal clears its required threshold and the chosen design margin. Margin is the extra allowance for uncertainty and changing conditions, measured in the same dB metric as the threshold.

A rain fade reduces received carrier power. Amplifier backoff reduces the operating power relative to a reference maximum and can improve waveform fidelity by reducing nonlinear distortion. Amplitude-varying waveforms can be especially sensitive to that distortion. Choose the operating point by weighing the available carrier power against the distortion the waveform can tolerate. Apply fade and backoff consistently to the stated reference power before testing the mode thresholds.

An ideal additive-white-Gaussian-noise channel provides a benchmark for the maximum reliable information rate. For bandwidth BB hertz and in-band signal-to-noise ratio SNR\mathrm{SNR} in linear units, its capacity is Ccap=Blog⁡2(1+SNR).\begin{equation} C_{\mathrm{cap}}=B\log_2(1+\mathrm{SNR}). \end{equation} The symbol CcapC_{\mathrm{cap}} means capacity in bits/s, while CC above denotes carrier power in watts. Capacity sets the theoretical ceiling for reliable information delivery under the stated channel model. Coding, overhead, hardware, and synchronization determine the throughput of a practical system.

Fig. 95 reads the capacity formula backwards. A spectral efficiency of η\eta bits/s per hertz needs an SNR of at least 2η−12^\eta-1: 0 dB for one, 4.8 dB for two, 11.8 dB for four. Each step of a mode ladder like Fig. 94 sits some decibels to the right of this ideal curve. In the running example, C/N=14.4C/N=14.4 dB, a linear ratio of 27.3, in 2.5 MHz gives Ccap=2.5×106log⁡2(28.3)=12.1C_{\mathrm{cap}}=2.5\times10^6\log_2(28.3)=12.1 Mbit/s. The 44 Mbit/s design is below that ideal ceiling; the rate ratio alone establishes no practical fade margin or post-decoder error rate. At 1.61.6 bit/s/Hz the Shannon lower bound is approximately 3.083.08 dB in-band SNR. A real MODCOD must be compared with its own required threshold at the chosen error target, using the same metric as the available link. Its usable margin would be MdB=(Es/N0)available,dB−(Es/N0)required,dB.\begin{equation} M_{\mathrm{dB}}=\left(E_s/N_0\right)_{\mathrm{available,dB}} -\left(E_s/N_0\right)_{\mathrm{required,dB}}. \end{equation} The required term remains unspecified for this assumed half-rate code. Capacity therefore checks an ideal limit; a measured or modeled code-and-decoder curve establishes a practical operating threshold.

The digital chain is now complete: sample, quantize and compress; protect with a code; map bits to I/Q symbols; shape, upconvert and transmit; then filter, synchronize and decide. Navigation reuses the same machinery, a known waveform, correlation and precise timing, with a different goal: the arrival time itself becomes the measurement.

Pulse shaping, Fourier-bin grids, I/Q, carrier offset, QPSK, Gray labeling and differential phases. Mathematical statements are checked separately from imperfect automatic wording.

The notes and recordings are primary course sources; unclear automatic-transcription arithmetic is not used as a verified numerical result.
